usage: A rebuke to someone harming his own support or kindred, reminding him that the loss will return to him as grief.
igbo: Mmadụ anaghị egbu onye ọ ga-ebe

meaning: [uncertain] Mmakwara never goes first — something always goes ahead of it.
literal: Mmakwara does not lead the way.
usage: Used to say that a great thing does not begin itself, or to point to what must come before an act.
igbo: Mmakwara anaghị ebu ụzọ

meaning: [uncertain] When the masquerade falls, its blade is finished — once a man of power is brought down, the power goes out of him with the fall.
literal: If the masquerade falls into the ogwugwu, its knife is spoiled.
usage: Said over the downfall of someone who was feared or admired, marking how quickly his strength leaves him.
igbo: Mmanwụ daa ogwugwu mma ya arụọ

meaning: [uncertain] When wine meets someone it knows, it ... — the line is corrupt, but the drift seems to be that drink behaves differently toward those it recognizes.
literal: Wine sees a person it knows, it ... ugwu.
usage: Used of drink and familiarity, when a person's dealings with those he knows turn out unlike his dealings with strangers.
igbo: Mmanya hụ onye ọ ma, o bee ugwu

meaning: An injury done to a rich man is counted as worse than killing him — what is taken from him is taken as his life.
literal: The spoiling of a rich man is more than his killing.
usage: Said to warn someone off cheating or shaming a wealthy man, since the loss will be pursued as though a life had been taken.
igbo: Mmebụ ọgaranya ka ogbugbu ya

meaning: [uncertain] The finishing of the cocoyam is not the chicken that goes with it — the end of the work is not the same thing as its reward.
literal: The finishing of cocoyam is not its chicken.
usage: Said when someone mistakes the conclusion of a task for the benefit that should come with it.
igbo: Mmecha ede abụghị ọkụkọ ya

meaning: The water that dragged off the snail dragged off the puppy too — a sweeping calamity does not stop to choose its size, but takes the small and the helpless together.
literal: Water drew and snail drew puppy.
usage: Said when trouble carries off more than the one it was aimed at, or to warn that no one is too small or too tough to be swept up.
igbo: Mmiri dọrọ na eju dọọrọ nwa nkịta

meaning: [uncertain] When water has taken the bag, calling it a bag is finished — once the harm is done, the thing is no longer what it was.
literal: Water touched bag, calling it bag is finished.
usage: Said over something ruined past recovery, when its old name no longer fits what is left.
igbo: Mmiri maa akpa, akpọ ya akpa agwụ

meaning: Water can wash the foot that trod the dirt, but it cannot wash back a word already spoken from the mouth — what has been said cannot be unsaid.
equivalent: A word spoken is past recalling.
literal: Water washes the foot that trod, it will not wash the word that was spoken in the mouth.
usage: A warning to someone about to speak carelessly, or a rebuke to one who has spoken and now wants it taken back.
igbo: Mmiri machie ụkwụ a zọrọ azọ, ọ gaghị amachi okwu ekwuru n'ọnụ

meaning: [uncertain] The water that knows the ugo is the water that washes its body — only one who knows a person can rightly handle him.
literal: Water knew ugo, washed ugo's body.
usage: Said when a matter is best left to someone familiar with the person or thing concerned.
igbo: Mmiri mara ugo sara ugo ahụ

meaning: Water is what turns soap into foam: nothing gets done by one thing alone, and the helper deserves as much credit as the effort.
literal: Water is helping soap to foam.
usage: Said to invite someone to lend a hand, or to praise the quiet helper without whom the work would never have come out.
igbo: Mmiri na-enyere ncha aka agba ụfụfụ

meaning: [uncertain] If the water has swallowed the elephant, the tortoise plucking its leaves is left asking whether it will fly or whether it will sink — when the strong go under, the weak can only wonder how they will escape.
literal: Water swallowed elephant, as tortoise saw and was breaking off ọgọdọ, will it fly or will it swim?
usage: Used as a warning when the fall of someone great shows that no one is safe.
igbo: Mmiri riri enyi ka mbe huru na awa ọgọdọ, ọ ga-efe efe ka ọ ga-awụ awụ?

meaning: The same source serves everyone: the great take what they need from it in their own measure, and so do the small.
literal: The water the eagle used to wash its hands is the water the ugbala used to wash its body.
usage: Said to settle a quarrel over who deserves more, reminding the parties that one shared thing feeds all of them.
igbo: Mmiri ugo jiri kwọọ aka ka ugbala jiri saa ahụ

meaning: Whoever lends you the power to do a thing is expected to help you carry what comes of it; help that stops halfway is no help.
literal: The spirit that led the child, if it killed an ele, will it help it or will it carry it for it?
usage: A rebuke to an elder or patron who set someone on a task and then walked away from the consequences.
igbo: Mmụọ kpara nwata ọ gbagbuo ele, ga enyere ya aka ọ maburu ya

meaning: People are destroyed by the very things they give themselves to; the spirits a person serves are the ones that kill him.
literal: The spirits they are worshipping are killing them.
usage: Said with a shake of the head about someone whose chosen attachments are ruining him.
igbo: Mmụọ ndị na-efe na-egbu ha

meaning: [uncertain] What a person leaves behind after eating shows who he is — the remains on the dish betray the one who eats beyond his share.
literal: It is by the leftovers on the ụkwa that one knows the person of much food.
usage: A dry remark about a greedy eater or a covetous person whose behaviour gives him away.
igbo: Na ntụtụ ụkwa ka e ji ama onye ụbụ nri

meaning: Growth comes with the years; a child washes and grows one year at a time, and nothing worthwhile arrives all at once.
literal: It is year by year that a child washes its body.
usage: A consolation to someone impatient for a child, a harvest, or a slow improvement to arrive.
igbo: N'afọ n'afọ ka nwata na-asa ahụ

meaning: Patience is the road the world is travelled on; the one who can wait is the one who goes far.
literal: Patience is the journey of the world.
usage: Said to steady a person who is in a hurry and tempted to force a matter open.
igbo: Ndidi bu ije ụwa

meaning: Each lives by the other — the water is the fish's life, and the fish is the water's life; no one thrives apart from what sustains him.
literal: Life of water, life of fish.
usage: Said of two people or peoples so bound together that harm to one is harm to the other.
igbo: Ndụ mmiri, ndụ azụ

meaning: Nothing sells itself at home; you must get up and move about if you want the goat sold.
literal: It is by going about that one sells a young goat.
usage: An encouragement to a trader or a job-seeker to stop sitting still and take the matter out into the world.
igbo: Ngagharị ka e ji ere nwa mkpi

meaning: [uncertain] Showing up where people gather is what brings a full belly home — you are fed by attending, not by staying away.
literal: Gathering a meeting brings a belly of rice.
usage: Said lightly to urge someone to come along to a gathering rather than keep to himself.
igbo: Ngakọ meeting na-ebuta ụbụ rice

meaning: [uncertain] What has been covered over is uncovered again once there is need of it — nothing set aside is lost for good.
literal: Ngala covered the mat; when it is wanted, it is uncovered.
usage: A consolation to someone who has put a thing away or been put aside, promising it can still be brought out.
igbo: Ngala kpuchie ute, agụọ ekpughee ya

meaning: An elder runs after the straying cow, but he runs with dignity — even a needed, unseemly act is done with self-respect intact.
literal: It is with pride that an elder runs after a cow.
usage: Said to defend or to tease an elder who has been seen doing something beneath his station for gain.
igbo: Nganga ka okenye ji agbara ehi ọsọ

meaning: Abandon the place that shelters you and you are caught in the open; leaving your cover is how you are taken.
literal: The lizard left the base of the tree; the hand caught it.
usage: A warning to someone restless to leave a safe position for no good reason.
igbo: Ngwere hapụ ukwu osisi, aka akpara ya

meaning: Lizards all lie flat the same way, so no one can tell whose belly is aching — outward likeness hides what each person is carrying inside.
literal: All lizards lie flat the same; we do not know the one the belly is hurting.
usage: Said to soften someone's judgment of others, or to explain why a person who looks fine may be suffering.
igbo: Ngwere niile makpu amakpu anyị amaghị nke afọ na-arụ

meaning: Outward achievements or associations do not change what a person fundamentally is.
literal: The lizard that climbed the kola nut is not a child.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who thinks a feat or a new association has made them something they are not.
igbo: Ngwere rịrị ọjị abụzighi nwa

meaning: [uncertain] When you set out on your own and fall, you have no one to blame but yourself, since you were your own trainer.
literal: The lizard said that it falls from the top, says there is no one who raised it, let it raise its own self.
usage: Used as a rebuke to someone who wants to blame others after a self-chosen risk goes wrong.
igbo: Ngwere sị na-elu daa, si enweghi onye toro ya, ya too onye ya

meaning: A matter that can be unravelled patiently should not be forced open; rough handling creates a debt you must answer for.
literal: A bundle that will be untied piece by piece, splitting it with the hand is answering for it.
usage: Used as a warning to handle a delicate matter patiently rather than with force.
igbo: Ngwugwu a ga-atọpe atọpe, ịwa ya aka bụ ịza

meaning: You can run, but you can't hide.
equivalent: You can run, but you can't hide.
literal: The nkakwu bird hides so that the vulture will not carry it; the vulture said it is carrying the nkakwu.
usage: Used to say that a person cannot escape a pursuer or fate by hiding.
igbo: Nkakwụ na-ezo ka udele ghara ibu ya, udele o kwuru na ya na-ebu nkakwụ

meaning: [uncertain] What a person has is what he holds in his hand; people can only rely on what is truly theirs.
literal: What a person holds is how he holds in hand.
usage: Used to say that each person must depend on what is actually in their own possession.
igbo: Nke onye ji ka o ji ana aka

meaning: As you sow, so shall you reap.
equivalent: As you sow, so shall you reap.
literal: What a person ate is what he carries.
usage: Used to remind someone that they must bear the consequences of their own actions.
igbo: Nke onye riri ka o bu

meaning: If you chase two rabbits, you will catch neither.
equivalent: If you chase two rabbits, you will catch neither.
literal: A dog answers two calls at one time and also breaks a calabash.
usage: Used as a warning against divided attention or trying to satisfy two demands at once.
igbo: Nkịta na-aza oku abụo ofu mgbe, na-etiwakwa agba

meaning: Everyone does the same dirty thing, but only the one caught with it in hand is condemned.
literal: All dogs eat shit, but is it the one seen with shit in its mouth that is the shit-eater?
usage: Used to expose selective blame when many are guilty but only one is singled out.
igbo: Nkịta nile na-eri nshi, ka ma ọ bụ nke ahụrụ nshi n'ọnụ bụ ori nshi

meaning: Give someone the means to gather, and they will take everything they can.
literal: The dog took a bag, shit finished in the bush.
usage: Used to describe someone who, once given an opportunity or tool, exploits it greedily.
igbo: Nkịta nyara akpa, nshi gwụ n'ọhia

meaning: [uncertain] The lowly one does the dirty work while the powerful one profits or takes action.
literal: The dog finished eating shit, the king sold a goat.
usage: Used to comment on a situation where one person bears the shame and another gains.
igbo: Nkịta richaa nshi, eze ree ewu

meaning: Having something does not mean knowing how to use it well.
literal: The dog says that those who have tails do not know how to sit with a tail.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who has an advantage but handles it poorly.
igbo: Nkịta sị ndi nwere ọdụ amaghi anọdi ọdụ

meaning: [uncertain] People attach themselves to the wealthy for gain, and when they are denied, they make noise.
literal: The dog said it knows why it follows a big-bellied person; it did not drink, it barked.
usage: Used to expose a hanger-on whose loyalty is really self-interest.
igbo: Nkịta sị ya ma ihe ya ji eso onye afọ ukwu, ọ nyụghị anyụ, ọ gbọọ agbọọ

meaning: A possession you cannot reach or enjoy is of no use to you.
literal: A dog does not chew a bone tied around its neck.
usage: Used to console or mock someone who has something but cannot benefit from it.
igbo: Nkịta anaghị ata ọkpụkpọ a nyawara ya n'olu

meaning: The resources of a place serve the people of that place.
literal: The firewood that is in the land cooks food for the land.
usage: Used to encourage using local resources for the good of the community.
igbo: Nkụ dị na mba na-eghere mba nri

meaning: When the powerful make a threatening move, the vulnerable live in fear.
literal: The stone goes up, fear strikes the pot of water.
usage: Used to describe the anxiety of the weak when the strong are on the move.
igbo: Nkume laa elu, ụjọ tụwa ite mmiri

meaning: Promises made by someone of no consequence, or made in a moment of intimacy, are not to be trusted; they are easily broken.
equivalent: Promises are like pie crusts, made to be broken.
literal: The promise that a nobody makes to a person is like a promise made to a woman on the bed.
usage: A warning not to rely on words spoken by someone who lacks the power or standing to keep them.
igbo: Nkwa ofeke kwere mmadụ dịka nkwa ekwere nwaanyị n'elu akwa

meaning: The young learn how to live by watching their elders; children copy what their parents do.
literal: The mother goat is chewing akụgbara; her young ones are looking at her mouth.
usage: Used to remind parents that their example teaches children what to do and how to behave.
igbo: Nne ewu na-ata akụgbara, ụmụ ya ana-ele ya anya n'ọnụ

meaning: The size of the task determines the size of the preparation or support it requires; great matters demand great resources, small matters small ones.
literal: A big fish brings big firewood; a small fish brings small firewood.
usage: Said to justify spending or preparing according to the scale of what is being undertaken.
igbo: Nnukwu azụ kpata nnukwu nkụ, obere azụ kpata obere nkụ

meaning: When a great or mysterious person lingers too long in public, even the lowliest observer learns what he is really like; overexposure strips away awe.
equivalent: Familiarity breeds contempt.
literal: A big masquerade that overstays in the arena, even a small woman knows the work/dance it performed.
usage: A warning to those in high or mysterious positions not to overstay and cheapen their own prestige.
igbo: Nnukwu mmanwụ nọkaria n'ọgbọ obere nwaanyi amara ọrụ ọ gbara

meaning: One who takes a high or conspicuous place must be ready to show what he can do; privilege brings the obligation to perform.
literal: The bird that perched on the igu tree is looking for the dance it will dance.
usage: Used to remind someone who has risen to a prominent position that he must now prove himself.
igbo: Nnụnụ benyere n'ọdụ igu na-achọ egwu ọ ga-agba

meaning: [uncertain] No matter how far or high one goes, one remains tied to the ground of one's origin; the exact word 'okpokikuwe' is unclear, so the sense is not certain.
literal: The bird that flew from the ground and flew into okpokikuwe should still be on the ground.
usage: A caution about remembering one's roots and not imagining that elevation changes one's fundamental nature.
igbo: Nnụnụ fepuru n'ala fenye n'okpokikuwe ka nọkwa n'ala

meaning: [uncertain] One should not answer a call or take on a challenge that is beyond one's reach; the phrase 'akwa ọtụrụkpọkpọ' is unclear.
literal: A bird whose head does not reach its hand does not go to the akwa ọtụrụkpọkpọ.
usage: A warning to avoid joining in something that is too big for one's strength or ability.
igbo: Nnụnụ isi akaghị aka anaghị eje akwa ọtụrụkpọkpọ

meaning: [uncertain] One should not enter a fight or contest that exceeds one's strength; the exact word 'ọtụrụkpokpo' is unclear, but the point is to know one's limits.
equivalent: Don't bite off more than you can chew.
literal: A bird whose head does not reach its hand does not go to the ọtụrụkpokpo fight.
usage: A warning not to engage in a battle or undertaking that is beyond one's capacity.
igbo: Nnụnụ isi na-akaghị aka anaghị aga ọgụ ọtụrụkpokpo

meaning: [uncertain] When the hunter grows deadly accurate, the prey must grow cleverer still; a threat sharpens the wits of the one it threatens.
literal: The bird of flight says that ever since the hunter learned to shoot without missing the hand, it too has learned things that are not anywhere.
usage: Said when someone must quickly learn new tricks because an opponent or rival has become far more skilled.
igbo: Nnụnụ ufe si kamgbe dinta mụtara igba ehieghi aka, yanwa amụta ife ebeghi ebe

meaning: You can tell where a person will end up from where they have already been found; settled habits betray a person's future haunts.
literal: The bird that has perched, one knows from the tree where it will perch.
usage: A dry remark about someone whose old habits make their next move easy to predict.
igbo: Nnụnụ tụọ nkwe a mara n’osisi ọ ga-ebe

meaning: Coming events cast their shadows before: the small habits and bearing of a person already announce what they will grow into.
equivalent: Coming events cast their shadows before.
literal: A child who will kill his father's cow, they know him by the strutting of his legs.
usage: Said of a child whose manner already hints at the kind of adult they will become, often as a warning to the parents.
igbo: Nnwa ga-egburu nna ya ehi, a na-ama ya n'agaramije ụkwụ ya

meaning: To know and honour one's father is to be joined to the whole line of ancestors; respect for a parent opens the door to the elders who came before.
literal: The child who knows his father has known the ancestors.
usage: Used to urge a young person to respect and learn from their father, since that links them to all who went before.
igbo: Nnwa maara nna ya amarago ndị ichie

meaning: Do not attempt the later stage when the first has not yet been mastered; steps must be taken in their order.
equivalent: Don't run before you can walk.
literal: The first child has not walked, is it the second who will run?
usage: A rebuke to someone reaching for an advanced task before they have managed the first one.
igbo: Nnwa mbụ ejeghi ije, ọ bụ nke abụọ ga-agba ọsọ?

meaning: Where the people do not stand as one, a small and unworthy fellow ends up ruling over them.
literal: In a town where one is not, mbele becomes king.
usage: Said bitterly when a community's quarrelling has handed power to someone nobody respects.
igbo: N'obodo otu na-adịghị, mbele na-abụ eze

meaning: Even the least portion scraped from the pot finds its way to the mouth it belongs to; what is due to a person is not lost, however small.
literal: The food scraped at the corner of the pot lands at the corner of the mouth.
usage: A consolation to someone who seems to have been given the smallest share, and a reminder that small portions still reach their owner.
igbo: Nri akụkụtara na nkọnkọ ite na-ala na nkọnkọ ọnụ

meaning: Once something has been shared out to the community, it is no longer the property of one person.
literal: Food that has become public is no longer one person's own.
usage: Used when someone tries to reclaim something that has already been given or shared out to others.
igbo: Nri bọrọ ọra abụghịzi ofu onye nwe

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is garbled; a reliable meaning cannot be given from this form.
literal: The dung that one remembers the body today.
usage: Uncertain; avoid using until the correct form is known.
igbo: Nshi a na-echetera arụ taa

meaning: Some tasks cannot be done with bare hands; they require the proper means.
literal: Excrement does not come out by hand; if it does not use sight, it uses water.
usage: Used to advise that a messy or difficult matter needs the right approach, not bare-handed effort.
igbo: Nshị anaghị agba aka apụta, o jighi ahụrụ, o jiri mamiri

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb is obscure; it may warn that a persistent noise or boastfulness can lead to one's downfall, but this is a guess.
literal: Nshịkọ said 'egwuruegwu' until the point of scratching the back; someone has killed it.
usage: Uncertain; best avoided unless the proverb is known in context.
igbo: Nshịkọ sị egwuruegwu rue nke ịchịfe aka azụ, onye egwusala ya

meaning: Someone who boasts of great deeds can still end up in a small, embarrassing failure.
literal: Nshịkọ said that it dug a big stream, dug a small stream, and then fell water into a woman's soup pot.
usage: Used to deflate a boaster who claims grand achievements but is caught in a petty mishap.
igbo: Nshịkọ sị na ya gwuru iyi ukwu, gwuo iyi nta, ma daa mmiri n'ite ofe nwaanyị

meaning: [uncertain] It may be about being torn between two demands or trying to serve two masters at once.
literal: Nshịkọ said his in-law and his chi asked him for work at one time; he then used it to carry two heads.
usage: Uncertain; used when someone is caught between competing obligations.
igbo: Nshịkọ sị ọgọ ya na chi ya yọrọ ya ọrụ ofu mgbe, ya were buru isi abụọ

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb is garbled; it may warn about hearing falsehood or gossip, but the sense is unclear.
literal: The ear will hear a thing that is not, unless it is more than a hat.
usage: Uncertain; avoid using until the correct form is known.
igbo: Ntị ga-anụ ihe abụghị ma ọ ha ka okpu ata

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is obscure; no reliable meaning can be given from this form.
literal: Ntukwu carried wrestling; awọ will be fish and reach the ground.
usage: Uncertain; best avoided unless the proverb is known in context.
igbo: Ntukwu buru mgba, awọ ga-abụ azụ eru ala

meaning: You cannot take full account of something when one part refuses to cooperate.
literal: Ntukwu is counting the lizard, but the tail does not allow it.
usage: Used when someone tries to control or account for a matter but one element keeps escaping them.
igbo: Ntukwu na-agụ ngwere ma ọdụ ekweghi ya

meaning: A child of noble stock does not behave basely.
literal: A leopard cub does not eat grass.
usage: Used to remind someone of their good lineage or to rebuke a person of standing for base behavior.
igbo: Nwa agụ anaghị ata ahịhịa

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is garbled; it likely means that a child cannot teach or precede an elder in what the elder already knows.
literal: A child does not lead his father to learn to be a firstborn.
usage: Used to rebuke a child who tries to instruct an elder.
igbo: Nwa anaghị ebu nna ya ụzọ amụta di ọkpara

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb is garbled; a reliable meaning cannot be given from this form.
literal: Nwa anwụ is barking, nwa ebu is barking; who then gathered the child to look?
usage: Uncertain; best avoided unless the proverb is known in context.
igbo: Nwa anwụ na-agọ, nwa ebu na-agọ, onye zi gbakpọrọ nwa atanị anya?

meaning: A lamb that wants to grow horns will find it hard; one should not aspire to what is beyond one's nature.
literal: A lamb is seeking to grow horns; it will be hard for it.
usage: Used to caution someone against ambitions beyond their nature or station.
igbo: Nwa atụrụ na-achọ ipu mpi, ekwu ga-esi ya ike

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled; it appears to continue the warning about a lamb wanting horns, but the second half is unclear.
literal: A lamb is seeking to grow horns, and it refuses ebila as ekwu is to it.
usage: Uncertain; best avoided unless the proverb is known in context.
igbo: Nwa atụrụ na-achọ ipu mpi, ya jụkwa ebila ka ekwu dị ya

meaning: When one returns home, one remembers the nurture one received.
literal: A calf has returned to the ground; it drank its mother's milk.
usage: Used when someone comes home after a long absence and is reminded of their roots.
igbo: Nwa ehi hulọta ala ọṅụrụ nne ya ara

meaning: Acting before the proper time spoils one's chance to act when the time comes; premature eagerness only injures the eager one.
literal: The young antelope broke its leg in dancing before the time for dancing came.
usage: Used to warn someone against rushing an action before its proper time.
igbo: Nwa mgbada gbajiri ụkwụ ya n'egwu tupu oge eji agba egwu eruo

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb cautions that even a young one should look carefully before making a bold move toward a parent or elder; discretion should come before boldness.
literal: The young he-goat looked carefully and ran to its mother.
usage: Said as a caution to a young person about acting boldly toward an elder.
igbo: Nwa mkpi lechara anya gbaa nne ya

meaning: People of different kinds or backgrounds should not harm one another; each side must respect the other.
equivalent: Live and let live.
literal: A spirit child should not maltreat a human child; a human child should not maltreat a spirit child.
usage: Used to urge mutual respect and restraint between two people or groups.
igbo: Nwa mmụọ emegbula nwa mmadụ, nwa mmadụ emegbula nwa mmụọ

meaning: If you refuse to take part in what is offered or required at the start, you cannot expect to enjoy the comfort or reward that comes later.
literal: The puppy did not eat the afterbirth; let it be denied fire.
usage: Said to someone who refuses the initial share and then expects the later benefit.
igbo: Nwa nkịta erighi ụna, ya anyara ọkụ

meaning: A mother's child will always be somewhere away from home; children travel and settle in other lands, yet the bond remains.
literal: A mother's child is in a foreign land.
usage: Said to comfort a mother whose child has travelled or settled far away.
igbo: Nwa nne dị na mba

meaning: Do not feel too secure enjoying yourself in another's place, because something of your own—danger or obligation—is waiting for you elsewhere.
literal: A bird's chick that is dancing in a dove's nest has something drumming for it in the forest.
usage: Said to warn someone against getting too comfortable in another's place.
igbo: Nwa nnụnụ na-agba egwu n'akwa nduru, nwere ihe na-akụrụ ya egwu n'ime ọhịa

meaning: Everyone must act within the limits of their own strength or ability; do not attempt more than you can.
equivalent: Cut your coat according to your cloth.
literal: The young nza bird will dance ụbara as far as its strength allows.
usage: Said to remind someone to work within their own capacity rather than compete beyond it.
igbo: Nwa nza ga-agba ụbara oke ike ya ha

meaning: A little comfort can make a small person arrogant, so that they even challenge their own god.
equivalent: Set a beggar on horseback and he'll ride to the devil.
literal: When the young nza bird is full, it tells its chi to come out to wrestle.
usage: Used as a rebuke when a person of small means becomes arrogant after a little comfort.
igbo: Nwa nza rijuo afọ, ọ sị chi ya pụta mgba

meaning: Do not take a co-wife's or another person's courteous greeting as licence to treat her with disrespect.
equivalent: Don't mistake kindness for weakness.
literal: A woman does not take the fact that her husband's wife greeted her well and then call her an in-law.
usage: Said to warn against treating a co-wife's or neighbour's politeness as submission.
igbo: Nwaanyị anaghị eji na nwunye di ya kwere ya ekele ofuma were kpowa ya ọgọ

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb appears to warn that outrunning one's mate to a husband brings a dangerous or burdensome outcome; the exact sense is unclear because the line is corrupt.
literal: A woman who went before her mate to the husband has in her hand firewood and fire.
usage: Used as a warning about rushing ahead of one's peer to a man or advantage.
igbo: Nwaanyị buru ibe ya ụzọ gaa di na-aka ya enwe kanka eku na nkanka ọkụ

meaning: One who is determined to quarrel will manufacture a pretext, however petty.
equivalent: He who wants to beat a dog will always find a stick.
literal: If a woman seeks a quarrel with her husband's wife, she says to her, give me oil so I can chew akwụ.
usage: Said when someone is clearly looking for a quarrel and seizing on a flimsy excuse.
igbo: Nwaanyị chọwa nwunye di ya okwu, o sị ya nye ya mmanụ ka o were taa akwụ

meaning: [uncertain] Only by exerting oneself—running—does one discover the burden destiny has placed on one; strength is revealed in action.
literal: A woman with strong legs will know the load her chi placed on her if she runs.
usage: Said to encourage someone to test their strength and discover what they can bear.
igbo: Nwaanyị ike ukwu ga-ama ibu chi ya bunyere ya ma ọsọ suru

meaning: Experience and comparison teach one to know which option is better.
equivalent: Experience is the best teacher.
literal: A woman who married two husbands knows which is better.
usage: Said when someone speaks from experience about which choice is better.
igbo: Nwaanyị lụrụ dị naabụ, ọ mara nke ka mma

meaning: [uncertain] The line seems to say that a woman who knows ụkwa is aware that work is going on; the proverb is obscure as written.
literal: A woman who is experiencing ụkwa knows that work is being done.
usage: Said when the person involved knows the effort underway better than an onlooker.
igbo: Nwaanyị na-ama ụkwa na ọrụ na-eme

meaning: A woman in labour may scream, but it is the inexperienced young girls she frightens; those who know childbirth are not alarmed.
literal: A woman giving birth and shouting, it is young girls she is threatening.
usage: Said when a woman's cries in labour are meant to warn or frighten the inexperienced.
igbo: Nwaanyị na-amụ nwa na-eti mkpu bu ụmụagbọbia ka ọ na-eyi egwu

meaning: Anything attractive that is put out in the open will draw the eager eyes of those ready to take it.
literal: A woman selling ogiri, and the flies have sharp eyes.
usage: Said with a wry shrug when a person's wares or good fortune attract a crowd of greedy watchers.
igbo: Nwaanyị na-ere ogiri ma ijiji anya pịara

meaning: A woman who behaves well and works hard is never turned away by her husband; good conduct earns a person their place.
literal: A woman of good work, her husband does not reject her food.
usage: Praise for a diligent, well-mannered wife, or encouragement that good behaviour secures acceptance.
igbo: Nwaanyị olu oma, di anaghị ajuru ya nri

meaning: Someone who has done the very same thing turns round and blames his companion for doing it.
equivalent: The pot calling the kettle black.
literal: A child who has carried firewood says his mate carried his in the bad bush.
usage: Thrown at a hypocrite who faults another for a fault he shares.
igbo: Nwata akpakarịrị n'nkụ sị ibe ya kpara n'ajọ ohịa

meaning: [uncertain] The child who out-gathered his mate claims he gathered his firewood in the bad bush, where wood is scarce — the one who achieves more claims the harsher conditions.
literal: A child who carried firewood more than his mate says that he carried in the bad bush.
usage: Used when someone boasts of an achievement by insisting on how hard his circumstances were.
igbo: Nwata kpakarịa ibe ya n'nkụ asị na-ọkpara n'ajọ ohịa

meaning: Someone who has been carried all the way has no idea how long the road is for the person doing the walking.
literal: A child carried on the back does not know that the journey is far.
usage: Said to or about someone who judges another's effort without ever having borne the load.
igbo: Nwata a kwọ n'azụ amaghị na ije dị anya

meaning: Someone who is carried never feels the ache of the road, so he cannot speak to the hardship of those who walk it.
literal: A child carried on the back does not know that the journey is painful.
usage: A mild reproach to a pampered person who underestimates another's suffering.
igbo: Nwata a kwọ n'azụ amaghị na ije dị ụfụ

meaning: The one carried along feels nothing of the weariness that the journey puts on the body of the one who walks.
literal: A child carried on the back does not know that the journey hurts the body.
usage: Said to remind a sheltered listener that ease in one place is labour in another.
igbo: Nwata a kwọ n'azụ amaghị na ije na-ara ahụ

meaning: A child who tries to lift his own father off the ground only gets the man's cloth hanging over his eyes: reaching past your strength brings you hurt, not honour.
literal: A child lifts his father up; the loincloth covers his eyes.
usage: A warning to someone taking on what is far beyond his strength or station.
igbo: Nwata bulie nna ya elu, ọgọdọ awuchie ya anya

meaning: Whoever handles fire and a blade cannot come away unmarked; if the fire does not burn him, it will singe him.
equivalent: If you play with fire, you get burned.
literal: A child carries fire and holds a machete; if the fire did not burn him, it singed him.
usage: A warning to someone flirting with danger and expecting to escape it whole.
igbo: Nwata buru ọkụ jide mma, ọkụ ereghi ya mma eyie ya

meaning: The news a child is bursting to shout to the whole world is told to his mother first.
literal: A child wants to cry out in the public square; he tells his mother that things are happening.
usage: Said fondly when a child's excitement spills out first to the person closest to him.
igbo: Nwata chọọ ịgba ama ọ sị nne ya na ihe na-eme

meaning: A man keeps hunting the very thing that killed his father and mother, and ends up digging their grave with his own hands.
literal: The mushroom that killed his mother, killed his father, he is still looking for mushroom; with his own hand he digs the grave.
usage: A sharp rebuke to someone who will not learn from the ruin of his own people and rushes to the same end.
igbo: Nwata ero gburu nne ya, gbuo nna ya, ya ka na-achọ ero, ji aka ya egwu ala ili ya

meaning: A child who dresses beyond his years is soon swept off his feet; pretension past one's size invites a fall.
literal: A child who has not yet grown ties a loincloth; the wind blows and carries him and the loincloth.
usage: A warning to a youngster who dresses or acts above his age and means.
igbo: Nwata erughi etoghi eto wara ogodo, ikuku kue o buru ya buru ogodo

meaning: A child too young to know better who goes looking for the thing that killed his father will be killed by that same thing.
literal: A child who has not grown up seeks what killed his father; what killed his father will kill him.
usage: A warning against prying into, or repeating, the very thing that destroyed one's family.
igbo: Nwata etoghi eto chọwa ihe gburu nna ya, ihe gburu nna ya egbuo ya

meaning: One who wraps himself in the cloth of a grown person before he has grown is carried off by the wind along with the cloth.
literal: A child not yet grown ties a wrapper; the wind carries him together with the wrapper.
usage: A warning against a small man taking on the dress and airs of a big one.
igbo: Nwata etoghị eto wara ọgọdọ, ikuku eburu ya bụrụ ọgọdọ

meaning: A child who walks into a house and finds none of his own age-mates announces that the house is empty, as though no one else were there.
literal: A child goes to a house and does not see his fellow child; he says there is nobody in that house.
usage: Said of someone who counts only his own kind and dismisses everyone else as nothing.
igbo: Nwata gaa n'ụlọ ahụghị nwata ibe ya, ọ sị enweghi onye nọ n'ụlọ ahụ

meaning: [uncertain] The line is too garbled to yield a reliable meaning; it seems to involve a child playing a game, being hit, and an unknown cause behind it.
literal: A child played igbe and threw mbọ at me; I played igbe and it hit him; it is not known; if there is something the land sent to him.
usage: Uncertain; the Igbo is corrupt and the saying cannot be used with confidence.
igbo: Nwata gbere igbe tụọ mụ mbọ m gbere igbe tụgwara ya, adịghị ama ama, o nwee ihe ala ziri ya

meaning: A child who gets a new bag is so delighted that he takes it to bed—new possessions bring out a child's pride and joy.
literal: A child got a new bag, it is pleasing him; he took it and slept.
usage: Said indulgently of a child showing off a new possession.
igbo: Nwata gotere akpa ọhụrụ na-anya ya were alaba ụra

meaning: If you tell an elder where you are going, the elder will tell you what to say—openness to guidance brings help.
literal: A child tells me where he is going, I tell him what he will say.
usage: Said to encourage a child to confide in elders and accept their counsel.
igbo: Nwata gwa m ebe ọ na-aga, m gwa ya ihe ọ ga-ekwu

meaning: A child sees a short person and thinks he has met his equal—inexperience judges by appearance and misses what truly separates people.
literal: A child sees a short person, it seems to him he has seen his peer.
usage: Used to chide a child who treats a short elder as an equal.
igbo: Nwata hụ onye mkpụmkpụ, ọ di ya ka ọ hụrụ ebiri ya

meaning: A child who has seen something will speak about it; children reveal what they witness.
literal: A child has seen, he has opened his mouth.
usage: A warning not to do or say things in front of children, who will report them.
igbo: Nwata hụwaa anya, o kwụwaa ọnụ

meaning: He leads a charmed life—danger does not touch him.
equivalent: He leads a charmed life.
literal: A child holds fire, holds knife; the fire did not burn him, the knife did not cut him.
usage: Said in wonder of someone who repeatedly escapes harm.
igbo: Nwata jide ọkụ jide mma, ọkụ ereghi ya, mma eghe ya

meaning: One who enjoys the catch does not know the labor of digging the ground that made it possible.
literal: A child who killed a squirrel in a trap does not know that digging the ground is what aches the body.
usage: Said of someone who takes the benefit without appreciating the effort behind it.
igbo: Nwata kwegburu ewi n'ọnya amaghị na igwu ala na ara ahụ

meaning: If you prepare yourself properly, you can take your place among elders.
literal: A child washes his hands, he eats with elders.
usage: Used to urge a child to be clean and ready so as to be included with adults.
igbo: Nwata kwọchaa aka o soro ndi okenye rie nri

meaning: A child who opens his mouth claims he can outtalk an elder—inexperience overreaches in speech.
literal: A child opens his mouth, he says that he will outtalk an elder in talk.
usage: A rebuke to a child who talks as if he can match his elders.
igbo: Nwata kwuwaa ọnụ ọ sị na ya agwagbụe okenye n'okwu

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is garbled; it appears to say that a child who fights and is beaten says the fight has killed him.
literal: A child fights, egboro egbo, he says this fight has killed himself.
usage: Uncertain; the line is corrupt and its use cannot be stated with confidence.
igbo: Nwata lụọ ọgụ egboro egbo ọ sị ọgụ nke a atọgbuo onwe ya

meaning: A child who stays close to elders does not chew his own kola and pepper—he shares in theirs.
literal: A child is near an elder, he does not chew his kola and chew pepper.
usage: Said to encourage children to keep the company of elders, from whom they will gain.
igbo: Nwata na-agba okenye nso, ya ataghị ọjị ya taa ose

meaning: A child who has never seen his mother says the market has not dispersed—inexperience speaks with false authority.
literal: A child has not seen his mother, he says the market has not dispersed.
usage: Said to dismiss a claim made by someone who lacks the experience to know better.
igbo: Nwata na-ahụbeghi nne ya sị ahịa agbasabeghi

meaning: As a child grows, the mother weeps—the child's growth brings sorrow along with joy.
literal: A child is growing up, his mother is crying.
usage: Said when a child's growing independence brings a parent pain or worry.
igbo: Nwata na-amụ elu nne ya na-amụ akwa

meaning: A child who grows to maturity becomes strong-hearted.
literal: A child is growing up to ten, his heart will be strong.
usage: Said of a child who is growing up and gaining courage or resilience.
igbo: Nwata na-amụ iri elu, obi ga-esi ya ike

meaning: There's no such thing as a free lunch—what you enjoy, you pay for.
equivalent: There's no such thing as a free lunch.
literal: A child is eating akara and chewing its money.
usage: Said when someone enjoys something without counting the cost, or as a reminder that pleasures have a price.
igbo: Nwata na-ata akara na ata ego ya

meaning: A child learns and matures as they grow; correction and instruction take root over time.
literal: A child is growing, his ears are being washed.
usage: Used to counsel patience with a growing child, since understanding comes with age.
igbo: Nwata na-eto, ntị ya ana-asa

meaning: Someone who has been badly hurt by one person may run from anyone who resembles them; past trauma makes people fearful.
equivalent: Once bitten, twice shy
literal: A child whose father a madman killed, when he sees a mechanic, he runs.
usage: Said to explain an apparently irrational fear that traces back to a painful experience.
igbo: Nwata onye ara gburu nna ya, ọ hụ mechanic ọ na-agba

meaning: Someone accepts something worthless while rejecting something valuable; they settle for less and spurn what is good.
literal: A child eats toad, he refuses meat.
usage: A rebuke to someone who embraces what is inferior and rejects what is better.
igbo: Nwata rie awọ ọ jụ anụ

meaning: When a person gets what they have been longing for, they are satisfied and rest easy.
literal: A child eats the thing he is staring at, he sleeps.
usage: Said when someone finally gets a deep desire and becomes calm and content.
igbo: Nwata rie ihe ọ na amụrụ anya ọ rahụo ụra

meaning: A child's words can come true, especially when spoken against a parent; a mother may indeed lose sleep because of her child.
literal: A child says that his mother will not sleep, she will not sleep.
usage: A warning that a child's pronouncement, or a child's trouble, can bring sleepless nights to a parent.
igbo: Nwata sị na nne ya agaghị arahụ ụra, agaghị arahụ ụra

meaning: If a child takes up the father's words or status, he must also take up the father's debts and duties.
literal: A child speaks the proverb his father spoke, let him also pay the debt his father has.
usage: A reminder that inheriting a parent's privileges means inheriting their obligations.
igbo: Nwata tụọ ilu nna ya tụrụ, ya kwụọkwa ụgwọ nna ya ji

meaning: [uncertain] If you cause trouble or boast of setting something ablaze, do not then run away from the consequences.
equivalent: You made your bed, now lie in it
literal: A child said he burned agbara with fire; he should not run.
usage: A rebuke to someone who starts trouble and then tries to escape the blame.
igbo: Nwata sị sue agbara ọkụ, ya agbakwala ọsọ

meaning: Certain things naturally belong to certain stages of life—children are clumsy, elders have grey hair—and should be accepted, not mocked.
literal: A child with clumsy feet and an elder with a grey head are known things.
usage: Said to remind people that age brings predictable changes and not to mock them.
igbo: Nwata ụkwụ nga nga na-aka okenye isi awọ ihe ama

meaning: [uncertain] Patience, not haste, is the way to finish a hot or delicate task; rushing only brings trouble.
literal: Slowly slowly will use to finish soup with oke.
usage: A counsel of patience when someone is rushing a delicate matter.
igbo: Nwayo nwayo ga eji aracha ofe ji oke

meaning: Patience is the way to accomplish a delicate or difficult task; rushing only brings harm.
equivalent: Slow and steady wins the race
literal: Slowly slowly is how one finishes soup that is hot.
usage: A counsel of patience when someone is rushing a delicate matter.
igbo: Nwayọ nwayọ ka eji aracha ofe dị ọkụ

meaning: [uncertain] A person cannot just sit at home and expect their crops or offspring to thrive; effort and going out are required.
literal: A man does not stay in his house and his seed germinates.
usage: Said to urge someone to get up and work rather than idly waiting for results.
igbo: Nwoke anaghị anọ be ya nọpịa mkpụrụ amụ

meaning: Men do the fighting and women are left to tell the story; the one who acts is not the one who spreads the news.
literal: A man finishes a fight, a woman has a story.
usage: A wry comment that women will talk about whatever men have done.
igbo: Nwoke lụchaa ọgụ, nwaanyị enwere akụkọ

meaning: [uncertain] A man who takes on women's roles will end up in the dance of spirits; stepping outside one's proper gender role brings consequences.
literal: A man-woman blows flute, dances the mgbala of the spirits.
usage: A mocking or warning remark about a man behaving like a woman.
igbo: Nwoke nwaanyị na-afụrụ ọja, na-awụ mgbala ndị mmụọ

meaning: A person should not race ahead of their peers; when you have finished your own part, you wait for your companion.
literal: A man has finished; he waits for his fellow.
usage: Used to urge patience and consideration for others who are still on the same journey.
igbo: Nwoke tochaa, o chere ibe ya

meaning: Love makes a person gladly bear the burden of the one they have chosen; people cherish their own spouse despite the cost.
literal: The frog's wife says that a husband is sweet; that is why she married her own and carries him on her back.
usage: Said when someone willingly puts up with hardship for a spouse or loved one, or to note that everyone values their own choice.
igbo: Nwunye awọ sị na di atọka ụtọ, ya jiri lụta nke ya kwọrọ ya n'azụ

meaning: Do not force a relationship on someone who does not reciprocate; if you visit one who never visits you, leave, and do not burden yourself with carrying them.
literal: He came to the house of one who has not come to him; let him return; let him not carry a hunchback on his back.
usage: Used to counsel someone against imposing on people who do not value them.
igbo: Ọ bịara be onye abịagbula ya, ọ lawa, mkpumkpu akwọkwala ya n'azụ

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo appears corrupt or truncated; it may concern a traveler and a home or sleep, but the sense cannot be fixed.
literal: He came on a journey and has sleep/home.
usage: Uncertain; the line is too corrupt to assign a clear use.
igbo: Ọ bịara ije nwe ụla

meaning: People ask questions and take action only after the harm is done; the chance to prevent it has already passed.
equivalent: Lock the stable door after the horse has bolted
literal: It is after the dust has been driven off that the chicken is asked where it went.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who investigates or reacts too late to stop a loss.
igbo: Ọ bụ a chụpụchaa ufu, a jụọ ọkụkọ ebe ọ gara

meaning: Others may arrange the main thing for you, but they cannot do your own part; you must take the final step yourself.
literal: Is it when a wife has been married for you that a mat will be spread for you?
usage: Used to tell someone not to expect others to do everything for them.
igbo: Ọ bụ a lụnye gi nwaanyị, akpọnye gi ute?

meaning: The very deity or thing a person worships and trusts can be what destroys them.
literal: It is the deity that people worship that kills them.
usage: A warning that one's devotion or trusted power may become one's ruin.
igbo: Ọ bụ alụsị ndi na-efe na egbu ha

meaning: Do things in the proper order; secure the main thing before the lesser accessory.
equivalent: Don't put the cart before the horse
literal: It is after buying land that one buys a mat.
usage: Used when someone attends to secondary things before the essential one.
igbo: Ọ bụ a zọta ala a zọwa ute

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled; it appears to speak of an animal with teeth climbing and chewing a bitter tree, but the intended proverb cannot be confirmed.
literal: It is an animal with teeth that climbs up and chews a tree that is bitter.
usage: Uncertain; likely a warning about being equipped for a hard task, but the text is too corrupt to say.
igbo: Ọ bụ anụ ji eze ari elu na-ama osisi na-elu ilu

meaning: A person's own chi—their personal god or guardian—can be the very power that destroys them.
literal: It is a person's chi that they worship that kills them.
usage: Used to warn against trusting one's own source of power or fortune without caution.
igbo: Ọ bụ chi onye na-efe na egbu ya

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is garbled, but it seems to reverse the point of asking after the chicken: it may mean taking the first step before the later event, yet the exact sense is unclear.
literal: It is first driving away the dust, before the chicken's bow is cut to enter the bush.
usage: Uncertain; the line is too corrupt to assign a clear use.
igbo: Ọ bụ eburu ụzọ achụpụ ufu, tupu atawa ọkụkọ ụta ịba n'ọhịa

meaning: You get out of a situation what you put into it; your harvest matches what you planted.
equivalent: You reap what you sow
literal: It is what a person has that sprouts in his farm.
usage: Used to tell someone that their results come from their own actions.
igbo: Ọ bụ ihe onye nwere na-epu n'ubi ya

meaning: Only the one who is present and visible receives recognition; the unseen are passed over.
equivalent: Out of sight, out of mind
literal: It is the head that was seen that put on a cap.
usage: Said when someone misses an opportunity or honor because they were not present.
igbo: Ọ bụ isi a hụrụ kwaa okpu

meaning: Certain actions bring their own damage; if you chew hard things, you should expect your teeth to break.
literal: It is chewing ụkwa that causes teeth to break.
usage: Used to warn that a risky or hard course will bring its own injury.
igbo: Ọ bụ itakọ ụkwa na-ebute ịjakọ eze

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is obscure; it seems to describe a bird or person claiming teeth after seeing another, possibly about imitation or baseless claim, but the sense cannot be confirmed.
literal: It is how the ọsa saw the akwụ that it says it keeps teeth.
usage: Uncertain; the line is too obscure to assign a clear use.
igbo: Ọ bụ ka ọsa hụrụ akwụ si edebe eze

meaning: Not everything that happens is about you; do not assume you are the center or cause of every event.
equivalent: The world doesn't revolve around you.
literal: Is it me that Aba is snoring for?
usage: A rebuke to someone who takes everything personally or assumes an event is aimed at them.
igbo: Ọ bụ m ka Aba na-amụrụ ọkpụ?

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is awkward and may be corrupted; it seems to say that only the tree which hears it is about to be felled stands still, perhaps because it cannot run, but the exact lesson is unclear.
literal: It is only the tree that heard that it is going to be killed that stood.
usage: Obscure; a speaker might use it of someone who stays put despite knowing danger, though the proverb's precise force is uncertain.
igbo: Ọ bụ naanị osisi nụrụ na-aga egbu ya kwụrụ

meaning: When there is something to gain, people are quick to notice and show interest, just as flies are alert when ogiri is being cooked.
literal: It is a woman cooking ogiri, but the fly's eyes are dry.
usage: Said when people suddenly gather or show interest because there is a benefit to be had.
igbo: Ọ bụ nwaanyị na-eshi ogiri ma ijiji anya kpọrọ

meaning: Children may share one mother, but each has a different personal destiny, so siblings can turn out very differently.
literal: It is one mother that gives birth, but it is not one chi that creates.
usage: Used to explain why brothers and sisters differ in character, fortune, or fate.
igbo: Ọ bụ ofu nne na-amụ mana ọ bụghị ofu chi na-eke

meaning: An insider who knows a place can lure an outsider into danger, like the house rat telling the bush rat that fish is in the trap.
literal: It is the rat in the house that told the one in the bush that fish is in the ngiga.
usage: A warning against trusting an insider's invitation without checking where it may lead.
igbo: Ọ bụ oke nọ na ụlọ gwara nke nọ na ọhịa na azụ dị na ngiga

meaning: A woman should not lean her whole weight on her husband; she should keep one hand for her own support.
literal: It is with one hand that a woman leans on her husband.
usage: Advice to a wife, or anyone, not to become completely dependent on a spouse.
igbo: Ọ bụ otu aka ha nwaanyi ka ọ na-atukwasị di ya

meaning: Being too gentle or accommodating invites others to take liberties with you.
literal: It is the dog's goodness that forces a hand into its mouth.
usage: A warning that excessive gentleness or friendliness can lead people to impose on you.
igbo: Ọ bụ ọma nkịta na-amanye ya aka n'ọnụ

meaning: Those who stay close to people and to important sources hear the news and secrets first.
literal: It is the person who is near people that hears the king's head.
usage: Used to explain how someone came by news or influence through being near the right people.
igbo: Ọ bụ onye nọ mmadu nso na anụ ishi eze

meaning: You must rely on your own effort and resources to reach your goal.
equivalent: God helps those who help themselves.
literal: It is this leg that I will use to reach Umuahia.
usage: An encouragement to self-reliance, reminding someone that they must make their own effort.
igbo: Ọ bụ ụkwụ a ka nama ji ga-eru Umuahia

meaning: Once the outcome is already before you, further evidence is unnecessary; do not demand proof when the thing is obvious.
literal: It is not after seeing the corpse of an antelope that one looks for its footprints.
usage: Used to dismiss a demand for proof when the result itself already settles the matter.
igbo: Ọ bụghị a hụchaa ozu ele, a na-achọ nzọ ụkwụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is unclear; it appears to say that fear is not what holds the tobacco in the gourd, perhaps meaning that people do some things by choice rather than from fear.
literal: It is not fear that rules tobacco in the hand of a gourd.
usage: Uncertain; perhaps used to say that an action is voluntary rather than forced.
igbo: Ọ bụghị egwu achị ụtaba n'aka agba

meaning: Something may taste bitter at first but turn sweet later; do not judge by the first impression.
literal: It is not as the bitter kola falls into the mouth that it is sweet.
usage: Used to encourage patience through an unpleasant beginning or to caution against judging by first taste.
igbo: Ọ bụghị ka aki ilụ na-ada n'ọnụ ka ọ na-atọ

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is fragmentary; it seems to warn that something is not as sweet as it tastes, so pleasant taste or appearance can deceive.
literal: It is not as the thing tasted says it is sweet.
usage: Uncertain; perhaps a warning not to be fooled by a sweet taste or pleasing appearance.
igbo: Ọ bụghị ka ihe nracha sị amị

meaning: Enjoying a benefit is not the same as paying for it; the one who enjoys may not be the one who settles the cost.
literal: It is not the mouth with which one eats wealth that one uses to pay for it.
usage: Used to remind someone that enjoying something does not discharge the obligation to pay.
igbo: Ọ bụghị ọnụ eji biri akụ ka eji akwụ ya

meaning: Punishment does not follow every mistake; it comes when the mistake is serious or crosses a line.
literal: It is not the day a child spilled oil that he is beaten, but the day he spilled ogiri akwụ.
usage: Used to explain why one fault is punished while another is overlooked, or to warn that not every error will be tolerated forever.
igbo: Ọ bụghị ụbochị nwata kwafuru mmanụ ka a na-eti ya ihe, kama ọ bụ ụbọchị ọkwafuru ogiri akwụ

meaning: If you fail to give the person in charge the correct facts, he will act on the wrong information and may end up mourning or blaming the wrong person.
literal: If one did not tell the head the name of the one who died, [he] will cry for the living one.
usage: A warning to pass word accurately to those who must act on it, especially in family or community matters.
igbo: Ọ bụrụ na agwaghị onye isi aha onye nwụrụnụ ya bee akwa onye dị ndụ

meaning: A skilled practitioner keeps working at his craft even when he is not in need; being satisfied does not make him idle.
literal: If the dibia is full, he goes to the bad bush; he will bring out roots.
usage: Used to praise a person's diligence or to explain why an expert keeps working when others expect him to rest.
igbo: Ọ bụrụ na dibịa rijuo afọ, ọ gaa n’ajọ ọhịa ga bụta mgbọrọgwụ

meaning: [uncertain] A large animal's urination cannot be matched by a chicken's; do not expect the same capacity from unequal beings.
literal: If a horse urinates urine abundantly, let the chicken urinate.
usage: A rebuke to someone demanding equal output from those who are not equals.
igbo: Ọ bụrụ na ịnyụ mamịrị efeka, ka ọkụkọ nyụọ

meaning: Forgiveness only has meaning because wrongdoing exists; where there is no offense, there is nothing to forgive.
literal: If wrongdoing were not, forgiveness would not be.
usage: A consolation or mild rebuke when someone is wronged, urging forgiveness because human error is unavoidable.
igbo: Ọ bụrụ na mmehie adịghị mgbaghara agaghị adị

meaning: [uncertain] The words are garbled; they may concern a father's path and the spirit of the firstborn, but the sense cannot be fixed.
literal: If it were his father's path, the spirit is the firstborn.
usage: Uncertain; not enough clear context to say when a speaker would use it.
igbo: O buru nnaya ụzọ mmụọ di ọkpara

meaning: [uncertain] Someone has dodged responsibility or slipped away from a matter, as Aaron is said to have clasped hands and left.
literal: It has now become Aaron who clasped hand and left.
usage: Uncertain; likely used to criticize someone who avoids responsibility.
igbo: Ọ bụzị Aaron gbara aka laa

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is garbled, but it seems to say someone looks for an excuse or weapon because meat cooked at night still gets eaten.
literal: It looks for something to strike hand, because meat that cooks at night is eaten.
usage: Uncertain; possibly a rebuke to someone hunting for a pretext.
igbo: Ọ chọ ihe kụọ aka, maka na anụ na-akpa n'abalị erika

meaning: [uncertain] One who seeks something great has seen the elephant's tusk; large ambitions require having seen large things.
literal: It seeks a big thing; it has seen the elephant's tusk.
usage: Uncertain; perhaps used of an ambitious person.
igbo: Ọ chọ ihe ukwu ahụla agba enyi

meaning: [uncertain] It speaks of seeking beauty or a knife and holding wealth or a handle; the exact sense is unclear, perhaps about wanting both beauty and wealth.
literal: It seeks beauty/knife to hold wealth/handle.
usage: Uncertain; not enough clear context to say when a speaker would use it.
igbo: Ọ chọ mma jide akụ

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled and the proverb's sense cannot be recovered; it mentions chasing a chick and running.
literal: It chased the chick that has a daughter; the chick then ran.
usage: Uncertain; not enough clear context to say when a speaker would use it.
igbo: Ọ chụ nwa ọkụkọ nwe ada, nwa ọkụkọ mwe mwe ọsọ

meaning: [uncertain] The words are unclear; they may concern brevity and the tongue, but no reliable sense can be given.
literal: It is short and does tongue.
usage: Uncertain; not enough clear context to say when a speaker would use it.
igbo: Ọ dị nkenke na-eme ire

meaning: The lowly ground supports even the mighty python; the humble can carry greatness.
literal: It is on the ground and carries a python.
usage: Used to praise humility or to note that the humble may support the powerful.
igbo: Ọ dị n'ala na-ebu eke

meaning: [uncertain] It is not good for a person to be among people and keep talking about spirits; perhaps a warning against strange or antisocial talk in company.
literal: It is not good that one stays with people and one is talking spirits spirits.
usage: Uncertain; likely a rebuke to someone who talks mysteriously or inappropriately among others.
igbo: Ọ dịghị mma a nọdị mmadụ mmadụ a na-ekwu mmụo mmụo

meaning: A stubborn or inexperienced person will learn from experience, like the tortoise discovering that hot water kills.
equivalent: Experience is the best teacher.
literal: It will know that hot water kills the tortoise.
usage: A warning to a stubborn person that reality will teach him what warnings did not.
igbo: Ọ ga-ama na mmiri ọku na-egbu mbe

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled or truncated and cannot be translated with confidence.
literal: It broke/snapped and drew.
usage: Uncertain; not enough clear context to say when a speaker would use it.
igbo: Ọ gbajuona dọrọ

meaning: Someone does a thing in plain view and then denies it, wiping his mouth as though he had said nothing; a barefaced denial after the deed.
literal: He blew the horn and is wiping his mouth.
usage: Flung at a person who loudly denies an act he was seen performing.
igbo: O gbu opi na-ehicha ọnụ

meaning: A person disowns in public what he did in secret, and even asks who did it.
literal: If he kills in the bush and comes out on the road, he asks who killed it.
usage: Said of a hypocrite who feigns ignorance of his own deed once witnesses appear.
igbo: O gbuo n’ọhịa ọ pụta n’ụzo na-ajụ onye gburunụ

meaning: Each person knows his own true state, however little others can see of it.
literal: He uses cloth to wash the body; he knows himself.
usage: Used to say that a person's own conscience knows the truth about him, whatever others think.
igbo: O ji akwa asa ahụ, mara onwe ya

meaning: [uncertain] A person is brought down by the very thing that was his own or was given to him.
literal: He used the yam of the child and it killed him, awayị [unclear].
usage: Turned to when someone is ruined by what he himself supplied or relied on.
igbo: O ji ji nwata egburu ya awayị

meaning: [uncertain] Someone is used as another's mouthpiece to talk him up, yet the good done for him is never to be mentioned.
literal: He uses me to make mouth; do not recount to me the thing I did for him.
usage: A complaint about a person who exploits you while ignoring the favours you showed him.
igbo: O ji m eme ọnụ, ihe m ji emere ya ọjị akọkwala m

meaning: Whoever holds the means decides who eats; the one with the knife and the yam names the beneficiary.
literal: He holds the knife, holding a piece of yam; whoever he gives it to eats.
usage: Remarked when power or resources are in one hand and favours are handed out at that person's will.
igbo: O ji mma, jiri ibe ji, onye ọ wanyere ya rie

meaning: Going about things gently and patiently does no harm to anyone; patience is the safe way.
literal: With gentleness one does not injure the body.
usage: Offered as counsel to someone rushing a task or a quarrel, urging calm and patience.
igbo: O ji nwayọọ adịghị emerụ ahụ

meaning: The one who holds the ọfọ of truth will come home with his name intact; an innocent person is not destroyed.
literal: He holds ọfọ; he will go home.
usage: Spoken to steady someone facing an accusation, assuring him that truth and a clean name carry him through.
igbo: O ji ọfọ ga-ala

meaning: [uncertain] One person's outcome is no rule for another; a case already settled elsewhere should not be forced on a different matter.
literal: He takes a case already judged as an example, saying the etito grew on the chicken's head like this — does the chicken's head then become bald?
usage: Raised against someone who cites another's case as if it must decide the present one.
igbo: O ji ụka ama atụ sị na etito toro ọkụkọ n'isi ha otu a, isi ọkụkọ ọ hazị aghaa?

meaning: [uncertain] A matter is closed by weight of the king's authority rather than by the parties' own agreement.
literal: He has used the king to make agreement.
usage: Said when a dispute is settled by invoking authority instead of by genuine consent.
igbo: O jirila eze kpee ekwere

meaning: He has seen it for himself; the matter is plain and cannot be argued away.
literal: He used his own eyes to see his own ears.
usage: Asserted when someone claims first-hand knowledge that no one can dispute.
igbo: O jirinụ anya ya hụ nti ya

meaning: He will not grant me even the smallest liberty, not even the little act that ends a favour already given.
literal: He did not allow me to drink water and throw away the cup.
usage: A complaint about a controlling or tight-fisted person who begrudges the least freedom.
igbo: O kweghi m ṅụrụ mmiri tọwa iko

meaning: He is speaking about a matter whose background he does not know — he does not even know whose death is being mourned.
literal: He does not know the person who died that is being wept for.
usage: A rebuke to someone who intrudes into an affair he has not followed.
igbo: Ọ maghi onye nwụrụ a na-ebe

meaning: [uncertain] Real enquiry starts from the ground up, from what is already known, before reaching after what is hidden.
literal: He knows how to ask; he began his hand at the foot of the ụgbọgụrụ, asking what grows on the anyụ [unclear].
usage: Used to praise a careful questioner, or to advise asking step by step from the obvious.
igbo: Ọ mara ajụ bidoro aka n'ụkwụ ụgbọgụrụ na-ajụ ihe na-ami anyụ

meaning: [uncertain] A person is bold and fluent where he has standing, but tongue-tied once he is on the ground with everyone else.
literal: He knows how to speak; let him speak up on the rafters — he does not know how to speak down on the ground.
usage: Mocking someone who talks big only in his own circle and falls silent elsewhere.
igbo: Ọ mara asụ, ya sụọ n'ikwe, ọ maghị asụ ya sụọ n'ala

meaning: When someone has done everything they can and their personal god still refuses, no one should blame or attack them.
equivalent: Man proposes, God disposes
literal: He did it, but chi did not agree; let no one shoot him.
usage: Used to console or defend someone whose sincere effort failed through no fault of their own.
igbo: O mewere ma chi ekweghi, onye ụta atagbụla ya

meaning: If you plant what goats eat, you have only yourself to blame when goats eat it; you set yourself up for the trouble.
equivalent: You reap what you sow
literal: He planted what the goat eats.
usage: Used to point out that someone has brought a misfortune on themselves by their own choice.
igbo: Ọ kwara ihe eghu na-ata

meaning: You cannot learn how to handle fire just by watching; some things must be learned through experience.
equivalent: Experience is the best teacher
literal: Is it that after seeing the way one learns fire?
usage: Used to say that observation or book knowledge is not enough for a practical skill.
igbo: Ọ na-abụ a hụchaa ụzọ a si mụta ọkụ?

meaning: It is an attempt to go back to how things were, to undo the past.
equivalent: turn back the clock
literal: It is turning the hand of the clock backward.
usage: Used when someone wishes to return to an earlier time or reverse a decision.
igbo: Ọ na-agbaghachị aka clock azụ

meaning: [uncertain] He is doing something futile, like digging a hole that cannot be used to cook cocoyam.
literal: He is digging a hole with which he does not cook cocoyam.
usage: Used to mock effort that cannot produce any useful result.
igbo: Ọ na-akọ oghere ji egheghi ede

meaning: [uncertain] He is behaving like a dog that a woman raised — pampered, dependent, and useless for real work.
literal: It is acting like a dog a woman reared.
usage: Used to criticize someone who is spoiled or too soft for serious responsibility.
igbo: Ọ na-eme ka nkịta nwaanyị zụrụ

meaning: [uncertain] It never falls where it can be picked up; it is lost beyond recovery.
literal: It does not fall where one will pick it up.
usage: Used to lament a loss that cannot be retrieved or a situation beyond repair.
igbo: Ọ naghị ada ebe a ga-atụtụta ya

meaning: He is still alive and has lived to see another day; while there is life, there is hope.
equivalent: While there is life, there is hope
literal: He is alive to see the moon.
usage: Used to console someone who has survived hardship or to express relief that life remains.
igbo: Ọ nọ na ndụ hụ onwa

meaning: [uncertain] Even the hidden pregnancy of a bat is known to the ground; the earth knows secrets people think are hidden.
literal: It is on the ground that knows the bat is pregnant.
usage: Used as a warning that hidden deeds will eventually be exposed.
igbo: Ọ nọ n'ala mara ụsụ dị ime

meaning: [uncertain] He is in the fire, yet the ụgụrụ comes out; someone escapes from a dangerous situation.
literal: It is in the fire but ụgụrụ comes out.
usage: Used to describe an unexpected escape from danger.
igbo: Ọ nọ n'okụ ma ụgụrụ apụta

meaning: [uncertain] He heard his brother's cry and ran — he fled instead of going to help.
literal: He heard the cry of a brother and ran.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who abandons a relative in trouble.
igbo: Ọ nụrụ ube nwanne agbala ọsọ

meaning: [uncertain] He cooked soup with a lamb and it turned red; something good was spoiled or a situation took a bad turn.
literal: He cooked soup with a lamb and it turned red.
usage: Used when a promising situation turns sour unexpectedly.
igbo: O tere ofe nwa atụrụ ji rawa agba

meaning: A small child who tries to climb too high will find it painful; do not attempt what is beyond your capacity.
equivalent: Don't bite off more than you can chew
literal: A small child climbing ten heights, it will pain him.
usage: Used to caution someone who is overreaching their strength or ability.
igbo: Obere nwa na-amụ iri elu, obi ga-esi ya ike

meaning: [uncertain] Every community that is perishing while laughing is not perishing for nothing; its laughter does not cancel the danger.
literal: Every town that is lost and is laughing does not get lost for nothing.
usage: Used to warn a community that ignores warning signs while heading for ruin.
igbo: Obodo ọbụla na-efu efu na-achị ọchị anaghị efufọ nnaa

meaning: If the small market is already like this, what will the main market be like? The bigger situation will be even more extreme.
literal: If the ọchanja is like this, how will the main market be?
usage: Used to emphasize that a larger version of the same thing will be even worse or more impressive.
igbo: Ọchanja dị otu a kedụ ka main market ga adị?

meaning: Laughter is not the same as happiness; a laughing face can hide a sad heart.
literal: Laughter is not sweetness.
usage: Used to caution someone against assuming that a cheerful face means a carefree heart.
igbo: Ọchị abụghị ụtọ

meaning: [uncertain] When an old native doctor performs a sacrifice, it is as though he has been handed over to the spirits; perhaps the expert's work puts him fully at the service of the spirit world.
literal: An old native doctor, when he sacrifices, it is like one took him and gave him into the hands of the spirits.
usage: Used to describe an expert who is utterly absorbed in a spiritual or ritual task.
igbo: Ochie dibịa chụa aja ọ dịka e weere ya nye ndị mmụọ n’aka

meaning: [uncertain] A chick that has a mother runs to her when chased; those with someone to protect them have a refuge.
literal: The chase of a chick that has a daughter, the chick that has mwemwe runs.
usage: Used to say that having a protector makes one bold or safe.
igbo: Ọchụ nwa ọkụkọ nwe ada, nwa ọkụkọ nwe mwemwe ọsọ

meaning: If one refuses to cooperate or bend, one will be forced to, or will suffer the consequences.
literal: If the tail refuses to agree, it drags on the ground.
usage: A warning to someone stubbornly refusing to go along with what is expected.
igbo: Ọdụ ghara ikwe, ọsụọ n'ala

meaning: You get what you pay for.
equivalent: You get what you pay for.
literal: The soup is good; it is money that killed it.
usage: Used to explain that quality or enjoyment comes from the money spent on it.
igbo: Ofe di mma bụ ego gburu ya

meaning: You can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink.
equivalent: You can lead a horse to water but you can't make it drink.
literal: If the soup is good and the meat is good, what makes the guest not eat to fullness?
usage: Used when someone fails to enjoy or take advantage of good things provided for them.
igbo: Ofe dịrị mma ụtara dịrị mma, kedụ ihe jizi onye ọbịa erijughi afọ

meaning: A person may not realize that even a close relative is a guest who deserves hospitality.
literal: Ofeke does not know that his brother is a guest.
usage: Used to remind someone to treat relatives with the courtesy due to guests.
igbo: Ofeke amaghị na nwanne ya bụ ọbịa

meaning: [uncertain] Ofeke does not know when the firewood was split; the ignorant or uninformed person is unaware of what has happened.
literal: Ofeke does not know when firewood was split.
usage: Used to describe someone who is out of touch or ill-informed.
igbo: Ofeke amaghị mgbe e kere nkụ ụkwa

meaning: [uncertain] Ofeke does not know the time the firewood was split; the ignorant person is unaware of common events.
literal: Ofeke does not know the time when firewood was split.
usage: Used to describe someone who is out of touch or ill-informed.
igbo: Ofeke amaghị oge e kere nkụ ụkwa

meaning: By the time a poor man learns to trap, the traps in the bush are finished; the opportunity is gone by the time one is ready.
literal: When Ofeke learns to trap, traps are finished in the bush.
usage: Used to lament that one has learned or prepared too late.
igbo: Ofeke mụta atụta atụ, atụ gwụ n'ọhịa

meaning: A foolish person uses his left hand to build his father's house; he does not take his own family's work seriously.
literal: Ofeke is using the left hand to build father's house.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who does a personal or family duty carelessly.
igbo: Ofeke na-eji aka ekpe arụ ụlọ nna aka

meaning: Rather than let the wine remain in the pot, let it remain in the stomach; better to consume than to waste.
literal: Ofeke said instead of wine remaining in the pot, let it remain in the stomach.
usage: Used to justify consuming something rather than saving or wasting it.
igbo: Ofeke sị kama mmanya ga adọ n'ite, ya dọrọ n'afọ

meaning: [uncertain] The ofo used for writing is washed with water; the sense is obscure, perhaps about truth or ritual cleansing.
literal: The ofo that is used to write is its washing water.
usage: Used in ritual or proverbial speech about ofo and truth; exact sense is unclear.
igbo: Ọfọ a na-ejiri ede bụ isita ya mmiri

meaning: [uncertain] It is ofo that writing uses to divide land; truth or ancestral authority is the basis for settling land matters.
literal: It is ofo that idide uses to divide land.
usage: Used in discussions of land disputes, invoking ofo as the standard of truth.
igbo: Ọfọ ka idide ji awa ala

meaning: [uncertain] The ofo that fills the bag has its bag open; the sense is obscure, perhaps about abundance or truth that cannot be contained.
literal: Ofo that fills a bag, its bag is open.
usage: Used in proverbial speech about ofo; exact sense is unclear.
igbo: Ọfọ nfọju akpa, akpa ya na eghe oghe

meaning: Some things cannot be done alone — a bundle needs a second hand to be tied. It takes another person's help to get certain jobs done.
literal: One hand does not tie a bundle.
usage: Said when someone is struggling alone with a job meant for two, or to urge a proud person to accept help.
igbo: Ofu aka anaghị eke ngwugwu

meaning: A burden that belongs to many cannot be settled by one person; no single person can carry the whole debt alone.
literal: One eye owes the head a debt.
usage: Said to persuade someone that the load they are carrying is too heavy for one person and should be shared.
igbo: Ofu anya ji ishi ụgwọ

meaning: When one person succeeds, the good fortune reaches the whole family; one member's blessing oils the rest.
literal: One finger produces oil, it reaches the others.
usage: Said in praise of a person whose success has lifted everyone around them.
igbo: Ofu mkpụrụ aka rụta mmanụ, o zue ndi ọzọ

meaning: No one, however small or lowly, is lost or overlooked among the rest; every single one counts.
literal: One palm kernel is not lost in the fire.
usage: Said to reassure someone that even the least member of a group still matters and will be accounted for.
igbo: Ofu mkpụrụ akwụ anaghị efu n'ọkụ

meaning: [uncertain] The one who was never there does not know how much is now known — even the leaves have stood up ears and heard it all.
literal: Ọganọhịa does not know that the leaf stands ear.
usage: A light rebuke to someone who has stayed away and now speaks as though nothing has changed.
igbo: Ọganọhịa amaghị na akwụkwọ kwụ ntị

meaning: Good looks and prosperity are all very well, but they are no substitute for real substance; you cannot use fine appearance to settle a matter that calls for weight.
literal: Ogazị is fine, but one does not use it to appease a spirit.
usage: Said to take someone down a peg when they lean on charm or wealth in a matter that demands substance.
igbo: Ogazị amaka mana ejighi ya agọ mmụọ

meaning: The poor do not let themselves dream of what they can never have; want is kept within the reach of one's means.
literal: The poor person does not dream rice.
usage: Said with resignation when someone urges the poor to dream beyond their means, or to explain why they do not.
igbo: Ogbenye adịghị arọ nrọ osikapa

meaning: One who lives by a weapon never lets it fall behind him; whoever depends on a thing keeps it always within reach and stays alert.
literal: The knife-killer does not let the knife go behind him.
usage: A warning to stay alert and keep whatever protects you close at hand.
igbo: Ogbu mma anaghị ekwe ka mma gaa ya n'azụ

meaning: [uncertain] Whoever would make music must first put himself in order — the flute player is the one who keeps wiping his mouth.
literal: The flute player is wiping his mouth.
usage: Said of a performer or craftsman who tends to himself before the work begins.
igbo: Ogbu ọja na-ehicha ọnụ

meaning: An in-law stands to a person as their own guardian spirit; they are to be treated with reverence and care, for they can bless or harm.
literal: A person's in-law is his chi.
usage: Said to counsel respect and caution in the way one deals with in-laws.
igbo: Ọgọ onye bụ chi ya

meaning: Good conduct is worth more than good looks: a woman may have no beauty to speak of, yet her good behaviour is what makes her worth having.
equivalent: Handsome is as handsome does
literal: Ogoli does not know beauty, but she has good conduct.
usage: Said when a wife is being chosen or spoken of, to praise character over appearance.
igbo: Ogoli amaghị mma, onwee ezi agwa

meaning: [uncertain] When a beautiful bride behaves badly, it is as though no wealth was spent to marry her — her looks cannot cover her conduct.
literal: Ogoli overflowing, it is like she was not married with wealth.
usage: Said in censure when a woman's behaviour shames the family that paid to marry her.
igbo: Ogoli kawa ọ dị ka ejighị akụ lụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] A beauty who knows her own worth carries herself like something newly made, as though she had been to God.
literal: The ogoli that knows the heart in it, it is like new, it is like she went to God.
usage: Said of a striking woman who carries herself with the air of one newly made.
igbo: Ogoli mara obi dị ya ọdịka ọhụrụ ọ dịka ọ gara na chukwu

meaning: Being tall is not the same as being grown; size is no proof of maturity.
literal: Tallness is not that my child has grown.
usage: A reminder to a parent or elder not to mistake a child's height for maturity.
igbo: Ogologo abụghị na nwa m etoola

meaning: There is a proper time and measure for everything; a long sermon belongs to the day's service, not to the evening one, when people are tired and must get home.
literal: A long sermon is not in the evening church.
usage: Said when a preacher or speaker goes on too long at an hour that calls for brevity.
igbo: Ogologo okwuchukwu adịghị n'ụka mgbede

meaning: A person keeps on good terms with the world by meeting each situation on its own terms, giving white its whiteness and black its blackness.
literal: Ogwumagala says that what he and the world use to be on good terms is that he brings its white and it is white, he takes its black and it goes.
usage: Said admiringly of a man who fits in at every gathering and quarrels with no one.
