igbo: Ogwumagala sị na ihe ya na ụwa jiri dịrị na mma, bụ na o weta ocha ya achaa, o nwete oji ya ejie

meaning: Trouble at home is no reason to throw away the good manners and dignity a father taught.
literal: Ogwumagala says that he will not, because fire burns in the hearth, forget the ways of the rich man that his father taught him.
usage: A reminder to someone in hard times not to let hardship strip him of his breeding.
igbo: Ogwumagala sị na ya agaghị eji maka na ọku n'agba n'ịkpa we chefuo ije ọgaranya nna ya kuziere ya

meaning: [uncertain] When a place gets ready to give what it has, the good thing should not be lost in the handling — the bush that shakes out its basket should not spill the mushrooms.
literal: The forest that washes its basket should not let the mushroom out.
usage: Recited where careful preparation is undone by carelessness in the doing.
igbo: Ọhịa na-asọ nkata ya epula ero

meaning: [uncertain] When the bush itself puts firewood in your hand, it has spared you the labour — a windfall saves the work.
literal: The bush that brought you firewood spared you work.
usage: Said of an easy gain that saves a person the toil he expected.
igbo: Ọhịa wọrọ gi nkụ, zeere gi olu

meaning: When you see how a fellow slave is buried, you know that your own day is coming — the end that takes another is waiting for you too.
literal: A slave who saw where they use mbazụ to bury his fellow slave knows that his own day will be just like that.
usage: A warning against gloating over another's misfortune, or sober counsel that no one escapes the common fate.
igbo: Ohu hụrụ ebe e ji mbazụ eli ohu ibe ya, mara na otu ahụ ka ụbọchị nke ya ga-adị

meaning: A traveller among other towns has no enemy — a stranger is received as a guest, and quarrels belong to one's own place.
literal: One who goes to towns has no enemy.
usage: Said to encourage or console someone setting out to live among strangers.
igbo: Oje mba enwe iro

meaning: [uncertain] A man marks out who he is by the cloth he puts on — people announce themselves by the insignia they wear.
literal: He uses the cloth of that leopard to know himself.
usage: Said of someone whose dress or bearing declares his standing among people.
igbo: Oji akwa aghụ ahụ mara onwe ya

meaning: That a man buries his father with wealth does not make him the one who killed him — outward show proves nothing.
literal: He uses wealth to bury his father; it is not the firstborn who killed him.
usage: Said to check anyone who reads a big funeral as proof of love, or of guilt.
igbo: Oji akụ kwaa nna ya, ọ bụghị ọkpara gburu ya

meaning: Whoever rushes eagerly into a fight does not understand that fighting means death.
literal: One who uses speed to enter a fight does not know that a fight is death.
usage: A caution to a hothead who is quick to pick a quarrel.
igbo: Oji ọsọ agbakwu ọgụ amaghi na ọgụ bu ọnwụ

meaning: Once a person is settled in among others, where he comes from becomes plain — the kola nut speaks of its origin as soon as it enters the house.
literal: When kola reaches the house, it says where it comes from.
usage: Said when a visitor's conduct makes his home and upbringing obvious.
igbo: Ọjị rue ụlọ o kwue ebe osi

meaning: [uncertain] She walks to her husband's children on her own two feet and then declares that they love her — the affection she boasts of is one she has to go and earn herself.
literal: She uses her feet to go, saying her husband's children love her.
usage: Said of a woman who mistakes her own effort for the goodwill of her husband's people.
igbo: Oji ụkwụ ya eje sị ụmụ di ya hụrụ ya n'anya

meaning: [uncertain] The rat must mind itself as it eats the diviner's bag and the diviner must mind himself as he deals with the rat — in a quarrel both sides stand in danger.
literal: The rat should watch out when it eats the diviner's bag, and the diviner should watch out and carry a big mouth.
usage: Reserved for a quarrel in which neither party is safe from the other.
igbo: Oke akpachala anya taa akpa dibịa ma dibịa akpachala anya bụọ oke ọnụ

meaning: A rat does not eat the food of a person who is awake — the watchful do not get robbed.
literal: A rat does not eat the thing of the person who is awake.
usage: Said to urge someone to keep watch over what is his.
igbo: Oke anaghị ata ihe onye mụ anya

meaning: [uncertain] The rat ate the diviner's bag without knowing, and the diviner struck the rat without knowing either — harm is done on both sides in ignorance.
literal: The rat did not know and ate the diviner's bag; the diviner did not know and seized the rat's teeth.
usage: Said of a quarrel in which both parties acted without understanding what they were doing.
igbo: Oke amaghị ama taa akpa dibịa, dibịa amaghị ama kpaa oke eze

meaning: It is too much thinking that left the sheep without horns — brooding and worry stunt a person.
literal: It is much thought that made the sheep have no horn.
usage: A chiding of someone who broods endlessly instead of acting.
igbo: Oke echiche mere atụrụ enweghi mpi

meaning: People make a public show of the smallest act so that everyone can see that all is well with them.
literal: The big dog says the thing it uses its raised leg to urinate for is so that everybody sees that its anus has not fallen.
usage: Said teasingly of someone who turns a private, ordinary act into a display meant to be noticed.
igbo: Oke nkịta sị ihe ya ji anyụ mamiri ewela ụkwụ elu bụ ka onye ọbụla hụ na ibi adaghị ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line is obscure and does not yield a settled sense; it concerns something large or of high rank (oke nkwụkwụ) refusing to let a woman do something to the body with the mouth.
literal: A big nkwụkwụ did not allow a woman to strike the body with the mouth.
usage: Recorded in proverb lists but its occasion of use cannot be recovered from this line.
igbo: Oke nkwụkwụ ekweghi nwanyị gba ahụ ọnụ

meaning: [uncertain] What is only a rat at home passes for a lizard out on the road — a person's standing depends on where he is standing.
literal: A rat in the bush, a lizard on the road.
usage: Said of someone whose worth looks larger or smaller depending on the ground he stands on.
igbo: Oke n'ọhịa ngwere n'ụzọ

meaning: When a great one falls, the whole community feels it and many gather around the event.
literal: If a big tree falls, the birds fill the forest.
usage: Said when a notable person dies or is brought down, to note how many are touched or drawn in.
igbo: Oke osisi daa, ụmụ nnụnụ eju ọhịa

meaning: Do not follow another person into what his nature fits and yours does not; you may not come out of it as he does.
literal: The rat followed the lizard and entered the water; when the lizard dries off, will the rat also dry?
usage: A warning to someone copying a risk that only the other person is built to survive.
igbo: Oke sooro ngwere maa mmiri, ọ kọchaa ngwere, ọ ga-akochakwa oke?

meaning: [uncertain] A short elder-and-soup line, probably about what an elder does not stoop to do, but the sense cannot be pinned down from the text as given.
literal: An elder does not brew/treat soup.
usage: Cited in collections of elder sayings; the exact occasion of use is not recoverable.
igbo: Okenye anaghị agwo ofe

meaning: Someone of standing does not sit indoors, unconcerned, while something that needs attending to is happening outside.
literal: An elder does not stay in the house while a goat gives birth in the pen.
usage: A rebuke to a person who remains aloof when he ought to be up and seeing to what is going on.
igbo: Okenye anaghị anọ n’ụlọ ewu mụọ n’ọgbụ

meaning: [uncertain] An elder does not quarrel with a child who shoves him off his seat; the matter belongs to the child's parents, whose place it is to call the child to order.
literal: An elder does not say a child knocked him off the seat; if the child's mother has not called him, his father should call him.
usage: A rebuke aimed at parents when their child behaves rudely toward an elder.
igbo: Okenye anaghị asị nwata kuliere ya n'oche, nne nwata akpọghị ya, nna ya akpọọ ya

meaning: Nothing done in secret is truly hidden: people may not see it, but the spirits do.
equivalent: What's done in the dark will come to light.
literal: An elder used the night to eat a rat; people did not see him, the spirits saw him.
usage: A caution to someone counting on darkness and secrecy for a deed he would not want known.
igbo: Okenye ji abalị eri oke, ma mmadụ ahụghị ya mmụọ hụrụ ya

meaning: When an elder takes kola in hand and speaks, even the spirits fall silent and listen — his word commands attention.
literal: An elder holds kola nut, clears his throat; the spirits prick up their ears.
usage: Used to add weight to an elder's words or to quiet a gathering as an elder rises to speak.
igbo: Okenye jide ọjị kwachaa akpịrị, ndị mmụọ ṅawa ntị

meaning: When an elder clears his throat, even the spirits stand alert to hear him — an elder's word carries authority.
literal: An elder clears his throat; the ears of the spirits stand up.
usage: Said to call for silence and respect when an elder is about to speak.
igbo: Okenye kwachaa akpịrị, ntị ekelie ndị mmụọ

meaning: An elder sees further than ordinary sight allows; his judgement is guided by something beyond two eyes.
literal: An elder has two eyes but it is with the third that he sees the road.
usage: Used to defer to an elder's counsel or to praise the deep sight that comes with age.
igbo: Okenye nwere anya abụọ mana nke atọ ka o ji ahụ ụzọ

meaning: [uncertain] Even an elder's small private act is spoken of as service to the spirits — his doings are read as carrying spiritual weight.
literal: If an elder blows (nyụọ ahụrụ), it is said that he is cracking palm kernels for the spirits.
usage: Obscure; cited of an elder whose ordinary private acts are given a spiritual reading.
igbo: Okenye nyụọ ahụrụ asị na ọ na-etiri ndi mmụọ akị

meaning: [uncertain] A fragment about a cockroach, a debt and a debtor; the sense does not come through cleanly enough to render.
literal: A big cockroach broke apart; the debtor ... killed its owner.
usage: Obscure; the setting in which a speaker would reach for it is not recoverable.
igbo: Okeọkpa kwaa, onye ụgwọ eche gbue onye ya

meaning: Some things may be circled round and round but never risen above; there are boundaries no amount of effort climbs over.
literal: It is in a circle that one dances around the pepper plant; one does not climb it.
usage: Said to someone pressing at a limit he cannot pass, or to note that a matter can only be approached one way.
igbo: Okirikiriri ka a na-agba ukwu ose anaghị arị ya elu

meaning: A person can stray past the bounds of good conduct without realising it; you must know where your limits lie.
literal: The youth does not know when he has passed through his in-law's compound.
usage: A mild rebuke to a young person who has overstepped without noticing.
igbo: Okokporo anaghị ama mgbe ọ gafere n'ama ọgọ ya

meaning: Setting everything in motion before the means are in hand ends in waste and ruin.
literal: The youth climbed a palm tree and set a pot on the fire; the palm tree yielded nothing, and the food in the pot burned.
usage: Said to someone who has started cooking, spending, or celebrating before the harvest is in.
igbo: Okokporo chiwe nkwụ, siwe ite, nkwụ agbafughi, nri dị n'ite eree ọkụ

meaning: A person's restless, agitated behaviour already announces what they are about to do.
literal: The youth is blowing the fire and shaking himself; it is known that wife-marrying has arrived.
usage: Teasing someone whose fidgeting has given away the plan they have not yet announced.
igbo: Okokporo na-afụ ọkụ na-ama ọsụ, amara na ịlụ nwaanyị eruala

meaning: [uncertain] A person finds grand excuses about the world outside while neglecting the small matters in his own house.
literal: The youth says the market has not filled up today — how many people are in his house?
usage: A retort to someone who blames outside conditions for his own inaction.
igbo: Okokporo sị ahịa ejughi eju taata, mmadụ ole nọ n'ụlọ ya

meaning: [uncertain] Someone keeps promising to do a thing today and tomorrow and never does it; talk is not the deed.
literal: The youth said he wants a wife today, wants a wife tomorrow; is it he and who that lives?
usage: A jab at someone who keeps announcing plans that never come to anything.
igbo: Okokporo sịrị chọọrọ ya nwaanyị taata, chọọrọ ya nwaanyị echi, ọ bụ ya na onye bi bu?

meaning: [uncertain] Whatever duty you leave behind in the morning is still waiting for you when you return.
literal: The youth asked for ash in the morning and went out; when he came back, ash was waiting for him.
usage: A reminder that an unfinished chore does not disappear while you are away.
igbo: Okokporo sọrọ ntụ ụtụtụ pụọ, ọ lọta ntụ na-eche ya

meaning: Unless a man makes his need loudly known, his own people will not move to help him.
literal: If Okoro has not done like a madman, his kinsmen will not marry a wife for him.
usage: Said to someone who suffers in silence and then wonders why no help comes.
igbo: Okoro emeghi ka onye ara, ụmụnna ya agaghị alụnye ya nwaanyị

meaning: [uncertain] A person claims to be seeking something while quietly ruling out every candidate that comes along.
literal: Okoro says he is looking for a wife, but not one who is pregnant.
usage: A mocking remark about someone whose conditions make every option impossible.
igbo: Okoro sị ya na-achọ nwaanyị ma ọ bụghị nke dị ime

meaning: [uncertain] The wording is corrupt and the point cannot be recovered; the line seems to belong to a funeral context and turns on the closed mouths of the dead.
literal: The akụ hook, eating and eating; look at how the mouth of the dead is.
usage: Obscure and no longer reliably used; recorded only in funerary settings.
igbo: Ọkpa akụ eri eri lekwanụ ka ọnụ dị ndị nwụrụ anwụ

meaning: Recovering what is lost takes the right instrument, not force; match the means to the task.
literal: It is a hook that is used to seek what has fallen into water.
usage: Said when a task needs the proper tool or approach rather than brute effort.
igbo: Ọkpa ka e ji achọ ihe danyere na mmiri

meaning: [uncertain] Each creature has its own way of taking what it is given; do not prescribe your way to another.
literal: A dog's bone does not taste the way the chicken gave it to it to chew.
usage: A rebuke to someone who insists that others do things exactly his way.
igbo: Ọkpụkpụ nkịta na-atalịghị ka ọkụkọ sị nye ya ka ya tapịa

meaning: [uncertain] A near-duplicate of the dog-and-bone saying, with the wording disordered; the point is that each creature takes its portion in its own way.
literal: The bone gave the dog to chew as the chicken gave it to it to chew it.
usage: Used in the same way as the dog-and-bone saying about differing ways of doing things.
igbo: Ọkpụkpụ nyịrị nkịta ịta ka ọkụkọ sị nye ya ka ya tapịa

meaning: [uncertain] What is aimed at a person by name does not harm him; the fire lit for a child warms rather than burns.
literal: A fire that has been counted for a child does not burn him.
usage: A reassurance that harm intended for a particular person will not reach them.
igbo: Ọkụ a gụnyere nwata anaghị ere ya

meaning: [uncertain] Each force keeps to its own element; the line is garbled and its exact point is not recoverable.
literal: Fire does not wash; water kills the toad's child.
usage: Obscure; a speaker would use it of things that each act only within their own domain.
igbo: Ọkụ anaghị asa mmiri agbagbu nwa awọ

meaning: [uncertain] A variant of the preceding line, also disordered; it seems to say that each force acts only where it belongs.
literal: Fire does not blow; water kills the toad.
usage: Obscure; reserved for talk of forces that keep to their own element.
igbo: Ọkụ anaghị efe mmiri egbu awọ

meaning: [uncertain] A fire that falls on tinder behaves as though it has drunk water — a small beginning can grow into an unstoppable blaze.
literal: Fire falls on ibube, it is like it drank anyụ.
usage: A warning that a small spark or small trouble can spread quickly if it is not checked.
igbo: Ọkụ daa ibube, ọdị ka ọnyụrụ anyụ

meaning: A fowl does not forget the person who plucked its tail feathers in the rainy season — people remember those who wronged them.
literal: The fowl does not forget the person who pulled its tail in the rainy season.
usage: A warning that a wronged person will remember the harm done to them.
igbo: Ọkụkọ anaghị echefu onye foro ya ọdụ na udu mmiri

meaning: [uncertain] A fowl does not use both legs to scratch for something; it must stand on one leg to scratch with the other — one cannot do everything at once.
literal: The fowl does not use two legs to scratch a thing.
usage: Used to caution someone against trying to do a task with both hands or legs at once.
igbo: Ọkụkọ anaghị eji ụkwụ abụọ abọ ihe

meaning: A hen with chicks does not sleep up high — responsibility keeps one grounded and cautious.
literal: A fowl that has chicks does not sleep on top.
usage: Used to remind a parent or leader that dependents require them to avoid reckless risks.
igbo: Ọkụkọ chị ụmụ anaghị arahụ n'elu

meaning: [uncertain] A fowl living in another person's compound eats goat droppings — a dependent or guest must accept what is available.
literal: The fowl that is at someone's place ụbịam eats goat dung.
usage: Used to tell a guest or dependent to accept the conditions they find.
igbo: Ọkụkọ dị be onye ụbịam na-eri nsi ewu

meaning: When you are in a place whose ways you do not know, stay cautious and ready to leave.
literal: A fowl goes to a place it does not know the ground, it stood with one leg.
usage: A caution to a stranger or newcomer to be watchful in unfamiliar surroundings.
igbo: Ọkụkọ gaa ebe ọ na-amaghị ala, o jiri ofu ụkwụ kwụrụ

meaning: [uncertain] A fowl that escaped the knife is killed by something else in the pot — one danger may be exchanged for another.
literal: The fowl left the knife; killed it in ọrọgọrọ pot neck.
usage: Used when someone escapes one trouble only to fall into another.
igbo: Ọkụkọ hapụrụ mma gburu ya na-ọrọgọrọ ite olu

meaning: If a hen stops clucking, what will she use to raise her chicks? — a parent or leader must keep guiding and providing.
literal: The fowl stops kwọm kwọm, with what does it raise children?
usage: Used to urge a caretaker not to abandon the duty of guiding dependents.
igbo: Ọkụkọ kwụsị kwọm kwọm, o jiri gịnị zụo ụmụ?

meaning: [uncertain] A fowl does not sleep because its stomach has rejected food — hunger or need keeps one awake and active.
literal: The fowl slept; it was not because the stomach rejected it.
usage: Used to say that need, not comfort, keeps a person moving.
igbo: Ọkụkọ lakpụrụ ụra abụghi n'afọ jụrụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] The fowl that wine will kill has not seen the half before madness sets in — drink can lead to ruin.
literal: The fowl of wine that kills has not seen ufu; madness is becoming.
usage: A warning about the destructive effects of drink.
igbo: Ọkụkọ mmanya na-egbu ahụbeghi ufu ara na-aghọ

meaning: Even a deaf chicken hears when it is in the soup pot — people ignore warnings until disaster strikes.
literal: The fowl with hard ears hears something in the soup pot.
usage: A rebuke to someone who will not listen until it is too late.
igbo: Ọkụkọ ntị ike na-anụ ihe n'ite ofe

meaning: [uncertain] When a fowl drinks ahụrụ, the ground denies it a race — some actions cost one speed or freedom.
literal: The fowl drinks ahụrụ, the ground refuses it a race.
usage: A warning that a certain indulgence will hamper you when you need to escape.
igbo: Ọkụkọ nyụọ ahụrụ, ala jụwa ya ọsọ

meaning: When a fowl reaches a place whose ground it does not know, it stands on one leg — be cautious in unfamiliar surroundings.
literal: A fowl reaches a place it does not know, it stood with one leg.
usage: A caution to a newcomer to be watchful and ready to leave.
igbo: Ọkụkọ ruo ebe ọ na-amaghị, o jiri ofu ụkwụ kwụrụ

meaning: [uncertain] The fowl says that even if the ekwe is played it will not listen, because it has no teeth — one may refuse advice because they cannot benefit from it.
literal: The fowl says, if the ekwe is played, it says it will not listen, because it has no teeth.
usage: Used to mock someone who rejects a message because it offers them no advantage.
igbo: Ọkụkọ sị akụọ ekwe ọjị na ya agaghị ege ntị maka na ya enweghi eze

meaning: The chicken says the reason it knows it is king is that it is carried on the head into town — being carried to market is mistaken for honor.
literal: The fowl says the thing that made it know it is king is that it is carried on the head and enters town.
usage: A warning against mistaking being used or taken somewhere for respect and status.
igbo: Ọkụkọ sị ihe mere ya jiri mara na ya bụ eze, bụ na ana-ebu ya n'isi aba obodo

meaning: One must stay alert even while doing something ordinary, because danger can come from an unexpected direction.
literal: The chicken says the reason it drinks water with eyes looking up is because of what kills it and comes from above.
usage: Used to explain why someone keeps watching for danger even in a safe-seeming moment.
igbo: Ọkụkọ sị ihe ya ji anụ mmiri eleli anya elu bụ maka ihe na-egbu ya na esi n'elu

meaning: You must do the work before you can enjoy the reward.
equivalent: No pain, no gain.
literal: The chicken says that it will scratch the ground before it swallows.
usage: Used to urge someone to put in effort before expecting the benefit.
igbo: Ọkụkọ sị na ya ga atụgbu tupu ya eloo

meaning: When someone cries out, it is not always to escape their situation but to make their suffering known.
literal: The chicken says, its crying is not so that the thing that owns it should leave it, but it is so that above and below hear its voice.
usage: Used when someone raises an alarm or complains aloud, to say they want their plight witnessed.
igbo: Ọkụkọ sị, ya na-ebe abụghị ka ihe ji ya hapụ ya, kama ọ bụ ka elu na ala nụrụ olu ya

meaning: [uncertain] A person's actions can cost them their voice or standing; the one who scratches the ground is the one whose voice fails.
literal: The chicken scratched the ground, its voice denied it.
usage: Used as a warning that taking on a task may bring a personal loss.
igbo: Ọkụkọ tụhie ala, olu agọọ ya

meaning: If you are honest with what you find and look to the rightful owner, you will receive your due share.
literal: The chicken that picked one akwụ seed and looked up, it will be given its own portion.
usage: Used to encourage honesty and contentment when one finds something.
igbo: Ọkụkọ tụọrọ ofu mkpụrụ akwụ lewe anya n'elu, aga ebunye ya ogbe ya

meaning: Always have a backup plan, because the main source you rely on may be taken away.
equivalent: Don't put all your eggs in one basket.
literal: Ọkwa told its children to plant yam and also plant roots, because when the yam owner digs up his yam, they will use the roots to live.
usage: Used to advise someone to prepare an alternative source of support.
igbo: Ọkwa sịrị ụmụ ya ha tụrụ ji ha tụrụkwa mgbọrọgwụ, maka onye nwe ji gwuru ji ya ka ha were mgbọrọgwụ biri

meaning: [uncertain] A hidden obstacle close behind can trip a person and bring them down.
literal: The hook behind my foot that scrapes the ground, it hooked me.
usage: Used to lament that a hidden or close source caused one's downfall.
igbo: Ọkwọ m n'azụ ụkwụ m na-akpụ n'ala, ya kwọtuo m

meaning: [uncertain] A matter that is straight should be answered straight; plain speech deserves a plain reply.
literal: A word that is standing standing, let the mouth be put standing standing.
usage: Used to urge someone to answer directly and not evade.
igbo: Okwu dị kwụrụ kwụrụ, e dewe ọnu kwụrụ kwụrụ

meaning: [uncertain] A matter that is decided does not simply disappear; tomorrow it will be spoken of again.
literal: A matter that has been decided does not break kolanut; tomorrow it will be spoken again.
usage: Used to warn that a hasty decision or unresolved issue will come up again.
igbo: Okwu e kpebiri na-awaghị ọjị, echi a ga ekwugharị ya

meaning: Faith gives one the boldness to do what seems beyond one's ability.
equivalent: Faith can move mountains.
literal: It is faith that the kid goat uses to jump over its mother.
usage: Used to encourage someone to trust and attempt a difficult thing.
igbo: Okwukwe ka nwa ewu ji amago nne ya

meaning: The one who plants may not be the one who enjoys the harvest.
equivalent: One sows, another reaps.
literal: The ọkwụrụ does not grow tall for the one who planted it.
usage: Used to console or lament that the benefit of one's labor may go to others.
igbo: Ọkwụrụ anaghị aka onye kụrụ ya ogologo

meaning: What is the point of doing what is already natural or inevitable?
literal: What is the benefit of the awaị that drank water?
usage: Used to dismiss an action as pointless because it is something one would do anyway.
igbo: Olee uru awaị tara mmiri?

meaning: [uncertain] Ritual roles and consequences are not interchangeable; what belongs to one rite does not belong to another.
literal: The doer of nshi does aja; the hand of nshi does not reach the mouth, the hand of aja enters his mouth.
usage: Used to caution against mixing up distinct duties or traditions.
igbo: Ome nshi eme aja, aka nshi abaghị ọnụ, aka aja abaa ya ọnụ

meaning: The person who hides a secret is not the one who should reveal it.
equivalent: Loose lips sink ships.
literal: The mouth used to bury wealth is not the mouth used to dig it up.
usage: Used to caution someone against revealing what they were entrusted with.
igbo: Ọnu eji biri akụ abụghị ọnụ eji akwụ ya

meaning: If someone had any sense, they would have noticed the obvious danger.
literal: If it had a nose, it would smell smoke.
usage: Used to mock someone who fails to notice what is plainly before them.
igbo: O nwee imi ọ ga akpọ anwụrụ

meaning: You cannot make progress by turning your back on a task; success comes from facing it.
literal: There is no place you use your back to go.
usage: Used to urge someone to face a challenge instead of retreating from it.
igbo: Onweghi ebe i ji-azụ aga

meaning: There is no treatment that can fully cure a mad person; some forms of folly cannot be corrected.
literal: There is nothing one uses to treat a mad person that cures him even a little.
usage: Said when someone's foolish behavior seems beyond correction or advice.
igbo: Onweghi ihe agwọrọ onye ara gwọta ya ntakwu

meaning: No one admits that his own mother's cooking is bad; people are partial to what is theirs.
equivalent: Every cook praises his own broth.
literal: There is no one who will say the soup his mother cooked is not sweet.
usage: Said when people defend their own family, work, or side without objectivity.
igbo: Onweghi onye ga-asi ofe nne ya tere adịghị ụtọ

meaning: No one can tell what a person who has been held down will do once released—whether he will fight or run.
literal: There is no one who knows the heart of a person held on the ground; if you leave him, whether he will fight or run.
usage: Used to warn against assuming how a suppressed or quiet person will act when freed.
igbo: Onweghi onye ma obi onye eji n'ala, a hapụ ya ọ ga-alụ ọgụ ka ọ ga-agba ọsọ

meaning: There is more than one way to reach the same goal; no single route is the only sacred one.
equivalent: All roads lead to Rome.
literal: There is no road one uses to go to Onitsha that is sacred.
usage: Said when someone insists that only one method or path is acceptable.
igbo: Onweghi uzo e si gawa Onicha ọ di nsọ

meaning: Even the most unlikely creature can join the dance; no one is so incapable that they have nothing to contribute.
literal: Is there a dance that a pig does not dance?
usage: Said to include someone unexpectedly or to chide those who think another person cannot take part.
igbo: Onwekwara egwu ezi na-agaghị agba?

meaning: Things that go by the same name are not necessarily the same; individuals differ in quality.
literal: There is something different between one gun and another gun.
usage: Said when comparing two people or things that seem alike but are not equal.
igbo: Onwere ihe di iche egbe na egbe

meaning: There is a reason for everything; nothing is done without a cause.
equivalent: Everything happens for a reason.
literal: There is something that made the cocoyam cut into pieces.
usage: Said when someone asks why something is done a certain way or when a seemingly odd action has a hidden purpose.
igbo: Onwere ihe mere ede jiri bee nwịị

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb seems to say that when death has not finished with one creature, it turns to consume what is closest to it; the exact sense is unclear.
literal: The death that did not kill utu, it eats the thing that created the head.
usage: Uncertain; likely used about death's persistence or an unfinished calamity.
igbo: Ọnwụ egbuchughi utu, o rie ihe kere isi

meaning: When someone is doomed, they ignore the warning signs that could save them.
equivalent: Whom the gods would destroy, they first make mad.
literal: The death that will kill a puppy does not let it smell the smell of faeces.
usage: Said of someone heading for trouble who ignores every warning.
igbo: Ọnwụ ga-egbu nwa nkịta anaghị ekwe ya nụ usi nshị

meaning: Death does not spare anyone; after it takes the strong man, it drags away the weakling too.
equivalent: Death is the great leveler.
literal: Death killed a hero, then took a fool and dragged him.
usage: Said when death or misfortune strikes both the mighty and the lowly.
igbo: Ọnwụ gburu dike, nwete ofeke ọ dọrie ya

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb's sense is unclear; it appears to speak of death counting or choosing among the young shoots of the banana and their response.
literal: Death counted the child of the banana, it answered otukwuru and vomited.
usage: Uncertain; the image is obscure and the line may be corrupt.
igbo: Ọnwụ gụwa nwa unere, ọ zaa otukwuru ọ mịa

meaning: [uncertain] It is a disgrace for someone meant for a great purpose to be brought down by something small; the exact proverb is unclear.
literal: The person with whom a cow will be used, it is not good to hear that a rat bit him.
usage: Uncertain; likely said when a great person is undone by a petty cause.
igbo: Onye a ga-eji ehi kwa adịghị mma ịnụ na ọ bụ oke tagburu ya

meaning: Being deceived is as damaging as being shot; a trick can wound just as badly.
literal: A person who is deceived is like one who is shot.
usage: Said to console or warn someone who has been tricked, stressing the seriousness of deceit.
igbo: Onye a ghọgburu ka a gbara

meaning: When others reject you, do not reject yourself; keep your own worth.
literal: The person who is rejected does not reject himself.
usage: Said to encourage someone who has been turned down or excluded to keep self-respect.
igbo: Onye a jụrụ anaghị ajụ onwe ya

meaning: A person and his personal god share one fate, so an insult aimed at a man strikes his chi too — you cannot attack someone without touching what guards him.
literal: The person whose mouth is scraped, it is his chi that is scraped.
usage: Said to console or defend someone who is being mocked or slandered, pointing out that the attack falls on his guardian spirit as well.
igbo: Onye a kọrọ ọnụ bụ chi ya ka akọrọ

meaning: When you are invited, take your full share without shyness — the host will not resent a guest who eats eagerly.
literal: The person invited to a meal, if he washes two hands, will the owner of the food then frown at him?
usage: Said to a hesitant guest at a meal or gathering, urging him to eat and join in freely.
igbo: Onye a kpọrọ oku nri ọ kwụọ aka abụọ, onye nwe nri ọ ga-aghụzi ahụ

meaning: A man goes after what he wants with whatever means he has; if he lacks the proper whip, he still has his medicine.
literal: The person chasing cattle and calling out — if he does not hold his cowhide whip, he holds his medicine.
usage: Said in praise of someone improvising cleverly when the usual tool or means is missing.
igbo: Onye a na-achụ ehi na-akpọku, ma o jighi ọgbụ ya, o jiri ọgwụ ya

meaning: The man who is publicly defended gets to rejoice, but the one who actually did the stealing never admits it.
literal: The person for whom a case is pleaded is rejoicing; the person who stole, has he agreed?
usage: Said when a case ends with celebration for the accused while the real wrongdoing goes unacknowledged.
igbo: Onye a na-agbara ama ọ na-aṅụrị, onye zuru oshi okwetela?

meaning: A person who stays comfortable and well fed while his neighbour suffers will soon be summoned into trouble of his own.
literal: The person whose neighbour's ailment is being treated is praising his stomach; the spirits are calling him into the bad bush.
usage: A warning to someone who is untroubled by, or even enjoying, a neighbour's misfortune.
igbo: Onye a na-agwọ ibi ya na-eto afọ, ndị mmụọ na-akpọ ya oku n'ajọ ọhịa

meaning: A person who does not answer a call has something in hand — his silence is business, not rudeness.
literal: The person being called has a thing he is doing.
usage: Offered as an excuse for someone who failed to answer or turn up, reminding listeners that he was occupied.
igbo: Onye a na-akpọ nwere ihe ọ na-eme

meaning: Someone who was never invited but sneaks a share for himself will not announce it to the host.
literal: The person not invited who secretly killed a chick, will he tell the one who invited him?
usage: Said of someone who has quietly taken an unearned benefit and keeps quiet about it.
igbo: Onye a na-akpọghị oku zogbue nwa ọkụkọ, o kwue onye kpọrọ ya nụ

meaning: In any rivalry a person is really measuring himself against himself; the true opponent is his own self.
literal: The person one is competing with, it is himself he is competing with.
usage: Said to encourage someone who is fixated on a rival, turning his attention back to his own effort.
igbo: Onye a na-azọ na-azọ onwe ya

meaning: [uncertain] The saying seems to warn that a person who is already being stared at and judged should not be shamed further before onlookers — it is not right to daub ash on his face while people watch.
literal: The person who is being watched and watched, it is not good to smear pot-ash on the face.
usage: Used as a caution against humiliating or disgracing someone in front of others.
igbo: Onye a na-ekiri ekiri adịghị mma ite ntụ ihu

meaning: When people tell you to keep holding it just the way you hold it, take that as proof that what you have is good.
literal: The person one told to hold as he holds, let him know that the thing he holds is fine.
usage: Said to reassure or praise someone whose own way of doing things has been endorsed by others.
igbo: Onye a sị jide ka o ji, ya mara na nke o ji amaka

meaning: Telling a person a proverb and then having to explain it means every effort spent on him was wasted.
literal: The person for whom a proverb was told and explained to him, the money with which his mother was married is lost.
usage: A sharp rebuke to a dull or inattentive listener who failed to grasp the point of a proverb.
igbo: Onye a tụọrọ ilu kọwaara ya, ego e ji lụ nne ya lara n'iyi

meaning: One whose own stomach is satisfied knows nothing of another person's hardship.
literal: The person whose stomach is washing does not know the bad bush.
usage: Said as a reproach to someone who is comfortable and therefore unsympathetic to those in need.
igbo: Onye afọ na-asa amaghị ajọ ohịa

meaning: A deceitful person cannot hide himself completely; some part of him always shows.
literal: The deceitful person buried himself, one of his hands is showing.
usage: Said when a liar's or schemer's hidden handiwork begins to surface despite his cover.
igbo: Onye aghụghọ lie onwe ya, ofu aka ya na-apụta

meaning: The cunning deserve their own kind — only a trickster is fit to handle a trickster.
literal: Let a deceitful person die; let a deceitful person bury him.
usage: Said when a schemer is finally outplayed by someone just as cunning, or when crooks are set to deal with crooks.
igbo: Onye aghụghọ nwụọ, onye aghụghọ e lie ya

meaning: [uncertain] The saying seems to describe someone who had no part in a solemn matter — absent when the burial was done — yet goes strutting about on his own two legs as if he were involved.
literal: The person who was not where the corpse was buried is walking on two legs.
usage: Said as a jab at someone who claims a share in an event he did not attend or help with.
igbo: Onye anọghi ebe a liri ozu na-esi n'ukwu abọ

meaning: Someone who has been hurt once becomes afraid of things that resemble the hurt, even when they are harmless.
equivalent: Once bitten, twice shy.
literal: The person a bee stung is afraid of a swarm of flies.
usage: Said to explain why someone shrinks from something harmless after a bad experience.
igbo: Onye aṅụ gbara na-atụ okporokporo ijiji ụjọ

meaning: A person who has experienced something good recognizes its signs and can sense where it comes from.
literal: The person who has tasted palm wine, the palm tree is coming.
usage: Said of an experienced person who can tell what is coming by its signs.
igbo: Onye aṅụla ngwọ na nkwụ na-abia

meaning: [uncertain] Death is inevitable and touches one's peers; if one person is not taken, another of the same age is lost.
literal: A person should not die; his peer is lost.
usage: Said as a reflection or consolation when a death reminds people of mortality.
igbo: Onye anwụla ibe ya e fụla

meaning: [uncertain] A fool ignores the danger behind him until it is too late; he has nothing to say to the person with a knife until his head is demanded.
literal: The mad person says there is nothing he will tell the person holding a knife following behind him, until the time he wants his head.
usage: Said of someone who dismisses a threat until it becomes fatal.
igbo: Onye ara sị onweghị ihe ya ga-agwa onye ji mma aga ya n'azụ, tutu rue mgbe ya chọrọ ishi ya achọ

meaning: A foolish person claims to understand what he is doing, while what is really being done to him is hidden from him.
literal: The mad person says he knows what he is doing, but what is happening to him is what he does not know.
usage: Used to expose someone who is confident in his actions but blind to the consequences being arranged around him.
igbo: Onye ara sị ya ma ihe ya na-eme, mana ihe na-eme ya ka ya na-amaghị

meaning: It is better to beg than to steal.
equivalent: Better to beg than to steal.
literal: A beggar is better than a thief.
usage: Said to steer someone away from theft toward honest need.
igbo: Onye arịrịọ ka onye oshi mma (Onye ayịyọ ka onye ori mma)

meaning: People who have plenty at hand should not resort to poor substitutes.
literal: A person who lives at the side of the river does not use spit to wash hands.
usage: Said to rebuke someone who ignores available resources and makes do with something inadequate.
igbo: Onye bi na agiga oshimiri anaghi eji asụ akwọ aka

meaning: Anyone who rises to act has a destination or purpose in mind.
literal: A person who stood up has a place he is going.
usage: Said when someone questions another's departure or action, to note that every movement has a reason.
igbo: Onye biliri ọtọ nwere ebe ọ na-aga

meaning: Live and let live.
equivalent: Live and let live.
literal: A person who lives, his fellow lives.
usage: Said to counsel tolerance and peaceful coexistence with others.
igbo: Onye biri ibe ya biri

meaning: Someone already carrying a heavy responsibility cannot also be expected to shoulder petty burdens.
literal: A person carrying an elephant on the head does not use a leg to carry a mat.
usage: Said to excuse someone from minor tasks because of a larger burden.
igbo: Onye bu enyi n'isi anaghi eji ọkpa akpa nte

meaning: People follow whoever carries what they want.
literal: The person carrying igu, goats follow him.
usage: Said when people gather around someone because of what he has or can give.
igbo: Onye bu igu ka ewu na-eso

meaning: Do not try to outrun your own destiny or limits; the one who does destroys himself in the race.
literal: The person who carried his chi ahead, he killed himself in the race.
usage: Said as a warning against overreaching or trying to force a destiny faster than it allows.
igbo: Onye buru chi ya ụzọ ọ gbagbuo onwe ya n'ọsọ

meaning: A person with bad luck suffers misfortune even when doing ordinary things in the wrong season.
literal: The person of bad chi who goes to fetch firewood in the dry season, rain washes his body.
usage: Said to console or describe someone whose misfortunes come even in unlikely circumstances.
igbo: Onye chi ọjọọ gaa nkụ n'ọkọchị, mmiri na-asa ya ahụ

meaning: A person with bad luck meets misfortune even in small, ordinary matters.
literal: The person of bad chi, water enters his teeth.
usage: Said when someone suffers a petty misfortune that seems to confirm his bad luck.
igbo: Onye chi ọjọọ, mmiri na-afanye ya n’eze

meaning: A painful experience teaches caution; one who is burned learns to put the dangerous thing away.
equivalent: A burnt child dreads the fire.
literal: The person who kindled fire and burned his hand, he will hang it on the wall.
usage: Said when someone avoids a thing after being hurt by it.
igbo: Onye chị ọkụ aracha aka, ọ ga-ekonye ya n'uko

meaning: The desire to run a race keeps a person awake; a strong goal disturbs sleep.
literal: The one who wants to run says it is keeping him awake.
usage: Said of someone whose eagerness or ambition will not let him rest.
igbo: Onye chọrọ ịgba ọsọ sị na-arọrọ ya anya

meaning: [uncertain] A person who pushes himself forward and is not welcomed then blames others for rejecting him.
literal: The one who forced himself into the vehicle says the vehicle refused him.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who intrudes and then plays the victim.
igbo: Onye chụọ onwe ya na ụgbọ, o sị ụgbọ ghara ya

meaning: If you enable someone to handle something dangerous, you must also help him face the consequences.
literal: The one who helped a child hold a knife will also give him water with which he will wash his hands.
usage: A warning that helping someone do a risky thing makes you responsible for the aftermath.
igbo: Onye dinyere nwata nwude nkapia (nkakwụ), ga-ekunye ya mmiri o ji ga-akwọ aka

meaning: People are pleased when they are treated the same as everyone else.
literal: The one for whom it was done as it was done for his fellow, his heart is glad.
usage: Used to argue for fairness or to explain why equal treatment satisfies people.
igbo: Onye emere ka emere ibe ya obi a dị ya mma

meaning: Let sleeping dogs lie.
equivalent: Let sleeping dogs lie.
literal: Let no one touch a leopard cub's tail, whether it is alive or dead.
usage: A warning not to provoke a powerful person or meddle with danger even when it seems harmless or dead.
igbo: Onye emetụkwala nwa agụ aka n'ọdụ, ma ọ dị ndụ ma ọ nwụrụ anwụ

meaning: [uncertain] A man who follows a woman's invitation may walk into grave or supernatural danger.
literal: The one whose female friend told him to come is hearing the footsteps of spirits.
usage: A warning against letting a woman's summons or infatuation lead one into ruin.
igbo: Onye enyi ya nwaanyị sị ya ga-abịa na-anụ nzọ ukwu ndị mmụọ

meaning: Look before you leap.
equivalent: Look before you leap.
literal: The one who will swallow an udara seed should also know how hard it is.
usage: A warning to weigh the difficulty of an action before undertaking it.
igbo: Onye ga elo mkpụrụ ụdara marakwa ka ike ya ha

meaning: If you are going to be blamed anyway, you might as well get the full benefit.
equivalent: As well be hanged for a sheep as a lamb.
literal: The one who will eat frog, let him eat the fat one, so that it will not be that he is called frog thief and he answers.
usage: Said to urge someone to make the most of a risky choice once the risk is unavoidable.
igbo: Onye ga-eri awọ, ya rie nke mara abụba, ka ọ ga-abụ akpọọ ya ori awọ ya za

meaning: A guest who rejects the seat offered to him, and even wants the seat the host is sitting on, is impossible to please.
equivalent: Beggars can't be choosers.
literal: The person who went to another's house, when they said to give him a chair, he also refused the one the other was sitting on.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who is not satisfied with what is offered and demands more.
igbo: Onye gara be awọ sị bunye ya oche, ọ jụkwara nke awọ nọ na ya

meaning: If you give away your own mat for others to use, you are the one left sleeping on the bare floor; self-sacrifice can leave you with nothing.
literal: The person who spread his mat, he lies on the ground.
usage: A warning against giving away your own comfort or resources to the point of personal loss.
igbo: Onye gbakaa ute ya, o dina n'ala

meaning: A person who can kill the healer trying to cure him is capable of anything, especially against those who harm him.
literal: The person who killed the dibia that was treating him with medicine, those who are poisoning him, have they not died?
usage: Said of someone who repays kindness with harm, warning that such a person is dangerous.
igbo: Onye gburu dibịa na agwọrọ ya ogwụ, ndị na-eme ya nshi ọnwụchala?

meaning: [uncertain] The wording is garbled; it appears to contrast someone cutting achara with someone killing a person, but the point cannot be reliably recovered.
literal: The one who cuts achara, the one who kills a person, do not call his fellow 'onye ikoli'.
usage: Unclear because the text is corrupt; not safe to use.
igbo: Onye gbuwe achara onye gbuwe onye akpọla ibe ya onye ikoli

meaning: A person with new power or equipment rushes into a situation where he should not, acting without judgment.
equivalent: Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
literal: The person who got a new gun is going hunting in the bedroom of a person whose belly is big.
usage: Used to caution someone who, having acquired new power or tools, acts rashly in the wrong place.
igbo: Onye gotere egbe ọhụrụ na-aga mgbaru n'ụlo akwa onye afo toro

meaning: Do not tolerate a present nuisance just because you might benefit from it later, since you do not know who will actually reap that benefit.
literal: The person who saw where a chicken is defecating, let him chase it away, because he does not know who will eat its egg.
usage: Used to advise someone to stop a nuisance now rather than endure it for a future gain that may go to someone else.
igbo: Onye hụrụ ebe ọkụkọ na-abọ nshị, ya chụpụ ya, maka amaghị onye ga-ata ọkpa ya

meaning: The person you help or train may become arrogant and forget you.
equivalent: Set a beggar on horseback, and he'll ride to the devil.
literal: The person you trained has become proud of himself.
usage: Said with bitterness when someone you helped rises and turns against you or acts superior.
igbo: Onye ị zụrụ tooro onwe ya

meaning: Do not lift yourself up on a child's back: once the strain starts to hurt, you will be the one to let the child drop.
literal: The one who holds a child's thing and raises his hand up, when the hand aches him with pain, he brings it down.
usage: A warning to an adult who leans on a child or a dependent to gain an advantage.
igbo: Onye ji ihe nwata welie aka elu, aka gbuwe ya mgbu, o wetuo ya

meaning: Whoever has people and land has himself — a person's true substance is the people who belong to him, not what he holds alone.
literal: The one who holds people and land holds himself.
usage: Said in praise of a person whose standing rests on the community he keeps around him.
igbo: Onye ji mmadụ na ala ji onwe ya

meaning: To bait your trap with a friend is to ask a question whose answer you already know: you will surely lose the friend.
literal: The one who used a friend to set a trap, what does he want to know?
usage: A rebuke to someone ready to sacrifice a friend for his own ends.
igbo: Onye jiri enyi kwe onya, ọ chọrọ imata gịnị?

meaning: A person is greater than his personal god — human effort and character count for more than destiny.
literal: A person is greater than his chi (personal god).
usage: Said to encourage someone not to blame fate for what effort and character can decide.
igbo: Onye ka mmadụ ka chi ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt as recorded; it appears to involve someone gathering firewood and a lizard's creeping trouble coming upon him — a small errand bringing an unexpected nuisance.
literal: The one who gathered firewood; the lizard's affliction came upon him, it crept.
usage: Cannot be reliably used as recorded; the line is garbled.
igbo: Onye kpata nkụ ahụhụ ngwere biara ya ọrịrị

meaning: If you call your basket the finest there is, the neighbours will end up using it to sweep grass — boasting about what you own gets it treated as rubbish.
literal: The one who called his basket nkịrịka, the neighbours used it to sweep grass.
usage: A caution to someone who brags about the quality of his possessions.
igbo: Onye kpọọ nkata ya nkịrịka, agbatobia ewere ya kpoo ahịhịa

meaning: If you announce that your barn is well stocked, the children will use it to scoop ashes — making a show of your store invites others to treat it as nothing.
literal: The one who called his barn nkpọkọrọ, the children used it to scoop ashes.
usage: Said to cut down a person showing off his wealth or harvest.
igbo: Onye kpọọ ọba ya nkpọkọrọ,ụmụaka ewere ya kpoo ntụ

meaning: Whoever accepts what the assembly has decided gets home early — falling in with the word of the group saves a man time and trouble.
literal: The one who agreed with what the otu said, he goes home in good time.
usage: Said to urge someone to accept the decision of the elders or age grade rather than fight it.
igbo: Onye kwe n'ihe otu kwuru, a laa n'oge

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt or truncated; it seems to concern the one who pays what he owes being his own master.
literal: The one who paid the price he holds, he has its owner.
usage: Not usable as recorded; the line is damaged.
igbo: Onye kwụo ụgwo o ji o nwere onye ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line is unclear; it appears to mock the man who boasts he has finished the harvest standing upright, since he ends up stooped to the ground digging out the last tail of the yam.
literal: The one who stood up straight and dug out yams, he crouched to the ground and dug out its tail.
usage: A warning against declaring a task finished before it truly is.
igbo: Onye kwuru ọtọ gwujie ji, o tukwuru ala gwupụta ọdụ ya

meaning: [uncertain] The wording is difficult; it appears to say that looking a corpse full in the face brings a person to weep himself to death — courting grief draws it in.
literal: The one who looked a corpse in the face, he killed himself with weeping.
usage: A caution against dwelling on a painful loss.
igbo: Onye lewe ozu anya n'ihu o begbue onwe ya n'akwa

meaning: The person who wrecks his own life turns round and blames his personal god — what spoils a man's world is his own doing, not fate.
equivalent: A bad workman blames his tools.
literal: The one who ruined his world blames his chi.
usage: A reproach to someone who will not own his failures.
igbo: Onye lobie ụwa ya bo chi ya

meaning: Let the one who knows how to shoot aim at the roof beam, and the one who does not keep to the ground — each should act within what he can do.
literal: The one who knows how to shoot, let him shoot at the rafter; the one who does not know how to shoot, let him shoot at the ground.
usage: Said to tell a person to match his undertaking to his ability.
igbo: Onye mara asụ, ya sụọ n'ikwe, onye amaghị asụ, ya sụọ n'ala

meaning: [uncertain] The line is partly unclear; it appears to say that whoever behaves like a rat will be chased off like one — act beneath your dignity and you will be treated as vermin.
literal: The one who behaved like a rat, buusu chased him away.
usage: A rebuke to someone whose behaviour invites contempt.
igbo: Onye mee ka oke, buusu chụọ ya ọsọ

meaning: [uncertain] The line is obscure; it seems to say that one whose father was shot through the head now wears a brass pot for a cap — a costly lesson teaches a man to shield himself.
literal: The one whom a bullet struck his father's head, he uses a brass pot to make a cap.
usage: Said of someone who has grown cautious after a hard lesson.
igbo: Onye mgbọ tụpuru nna ya isi na eji ite ọla eme okpu

meaning: A person who merely joins you in a task may begin to claim the same ability as the one you are pursuing.
literal: The person I and he together chase mgbada, says leg is like leg of ele.
usage: Used to check someone who boasts of equality with those they only accompany.
igbo: Onye mụ na ya so achụ mgbada, si ụkwụ di ka ụkwụ ele

meaning: Cursing and beating one's chest openly shows enemies where one's life is vulnerable.
literal: The person who is cursing beats hand on chest, is showing the spirits where his life is.
usage: A warning against boastful cursing or exposing one's weak points.
igbo: Onye na-aba mba eti aka n'obi na-egosi ndi mmụọ ebe ndụ ya di

meaning: If you do not know where a trouble began, you cannot know where it spared you.
literal: The person who does not know where water started and overflowed him, does not know where it avoided him.
usage: Said to urge someone to trace the root of a problem.
igbo: Onye na-amaghị ebe mmiri bidoro mawa ya, anaghị ama ebe o zere ya

meaning: [uncertain] Someone who does not know what was done to win a girlfriend says, 'Just talk to her and she will go.'
literal: The person who does not know what was done to get a female friend says 'tell her words she leaves'.
usage: Used to dismiss naive advice from someone who ignores the effort involved.
igbo: Onye na-amaghị ihe e mere were nwete enyi nwaanyị na-asi "gwa ya okwu ọ laa"

meaning: Not knowing someone can make one address them disrespectfully.
literal: The person who does not know people calls him 'this person'.
usage: Said to excuse or note disrespect born of unfamiliarity.
igbo: Onye na-amaghị mmadu na-akpọ ya onye a

meaning: [uncertain] One who has never known sickness should watch how a sick monkey is tended, to learn what illness means.
literal: The person who does not know sickness, when a monkey is sick, let him look at the atani with which fire was blown on it.
usage: Used to tell someone not to judge what they have not experienced.
igbo: Onye na-amaghị ọria enwe rịarịa, ya lee anya atani jiri fụrụ ya ọkụ

meaning: If you are not close to where things are done, you will not get quick results.
literal: The person who is not staying near fire, his yam is not cooking quickly.
usage: Advising someone to stay involved and attentive if they want results.
igbo: Onye na-anoghị n'akụkụ ọku, ji ya anaghi eghe ngwa ngwa

meaning: [uncertain] One who was absent when the corpse was buried later tries to claim a part in it.
literal: The person who was not there when they buried the corpse is speaking from his two legs.
usage: Used to dismiss someone who claims a role in what they did not attend.
igbo: Onye na-anoghị ya mgbe eliri ozu na-esi n'ụkwụ abọ ya

meaning: If you do not attend to your own affairs, someone else will do it for you.
literal: The person who does not clean his mouth, egret cleaned it for him.
usage: A warning against neglect or meddling in what should be one's own responsibility.
igbo: Onye na-arachaghị onụ ya, ụgụrụ arachaara ya

meaning: One who fights others' battles, especially for spirits, ends up suffering for it.
literal: The person who fights for the spirits, his head becomes aja aja.
usage: A warning against taking up fights that are not one's own.
igbo: Onye na-egboro ndị mmụọ ọgu, isi ya na-abụ aja aja

meaning: If you have no wealth, at least keep a good tongue.
literal: The person who does not have wealth, let him hold a good tongue.
usage: Advising good conduct and respectful speech when one lacks means.
igbo: Onye na-ejighi akụ o jide ire oma

meaning: If you do not gather your own, your basket will gather it for you.
literal: The person who does not gather, his ọgọdọ gathered for him.
usage: A rebuke for laziness or neglect that lets others take what is yours.
igbo: Onye na-ekoteghi, ọgọdọ ya ekotere ya

meaning: If you cannot speak as the community does, you will be sent back to your father's compound in shame.
literal: The person who does not speak like the community, they carry him to his father's compound.
usage: A warning to learn to speak up and fit in at public gatherings.
igbo: Onye na-ekwughi ka ọha, e bufee ya ama nna ya

meaning: Unless you make a fuss, your people will not act on your behalf.
equivalent: The squeaky wheel gets the grease.
literal: The person who does not do like a mad person, his kinsmen will not marry a wife for him.
usage: Said to urge someone to speak up and press for what they need.
igbo: Onye na-emeghị ka onye ara, ụmụnna ya agaghị alụnye ya nwaanyị

meaning: [uncertain] One who cooks for the leader kills the mkpọrọhihi when the food is done.
literal: The person who cooks food for the head/leader kills mkpọrọhihi when it cooks.
usage: Used of a servant who gains small advantages from serving the powerful.
igbo: Onye na-esiri onye ishi nri na-egbu mkpọrọhihi ma o siwe

meaning: A person who boasts and exposes himself is showing his enemies where he can be struck.
literal: The person who is beating a hand on the chest is showing the spirits where his life is.
usage: A warning against boasting or revealing your weak point before people who may harm you.
igbo: Onye na-eti aka n’obi, na-egosi ndị mmụo ebe ndụ ya dị

meaning: A person surrounded by enemies must always be on guard.
literal: The person whom enemies have surrounded is guarding his life always.
usage: A warning to stay vigilant when you have many enemies.
igbo: Onye ndị iro gbara gburugburu na-eche ndụ ya nche mgbe niile

meaning: Patience brings good things.
equivalent: Good things come to those who wait.
literal: The person of patience eats the ukpo fish.
usage: An encouragement to endure because the reward will come in time.
igbo: Onye ndidi na-eri azụ ukpo

meaning: Travel and experience teach more than old age alone.
equivalent: Travel broadens the mind.
literal: A traveler is more beautiful than a grey-haired person.
usage: Used to encourage travel or to say that experience is worth more than age.
igbo: Onye njem ka onye isi awọ mma

meaning: [uncertain] The saying seems to concern a child inheriting a parent's bad conduct and acting with reckless boldness, but the Igbo is unclear.
literal: The person whose father lay with a thief uses his foot to break a bullet/thorn.
usage: Probably a warning about bad family influence, but the exact situation is unclear.
igbo: Onye nna ya dinyere ohi na-eji ukwu agbawa mgbo

meaning: Living close to others makes you aware of your own faults.
literal: The person who is near people smells the hiss/odour of his teeth.
usage: A reminder that being among people teaches you about your own shortcomings.
igbo: Onye nọ mmadụ nsụ na-anụ ushi eze ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line is too short and ambiguous to interpret confidently; it may concern staying at home versus going out.
literal: The person who stayed in his house, does he enter?
usage: Unclear; the proverb is fragmentary and its exact use is uncertain.
igbo: Onye nọrọ be ya, ọ na-aba

meaning: People will talk about you even where you are not; gossip follows everyone.
literal: The person stayed where he is; where he is not, they are counting him.
usage: A consolation or warning that people will mention you in your absence.
igbo: Onye nọrọ ebe ọnọ, ebe ọ na-anọghị ana-agụ ya

meaning: Having a relative in a high place spares you from hard or dangerous tasks.
equivalent: It's not what you know, it's who you know.
literal: The person whose sibling lives in the palace does not go to spirit firewood.
usage: Used to note the advantages of family connections and patronage.
igbo: Onye nwanne ya bi n'alaeze anaghị aga okụ mmụọ

meaning: A person whose relative is incompetent makes a trivial complaint to cover the shame.
literal: The person whose sibling does not know how to dance is complaining of lack of eyelashes.
usage: A mocking rebuke of someone who finds irrelevant excuses for a relative's failure.
igbo: Onye nwanne ya na-amaghị agba egwu na-akọ ụkọ nku anya

meaning: The person responsible for a problem must bear it himself.
literal: The owner of a corpse carries it on his head.
usage: A reminder that responsibility cannot be shifted to someone else.
igbo: Onye nwe ozu na-ebu ya n'isi

meaning: [uncertain] The saying seems to describe a coward who is bold only against something harmless, but the sense is not fully certain.
literal: The person who has fear is plucking a dried chicken.
usage: Likely used to mock someone who acts brave only against harmless things.
igbo: Onye nwere efe na-ayọ okuko akpụ

meaning: [uncertain] It seems to urge a man to keep an enlarged photo of his girlfriend because marriage will change her, but the exact sense is unclear.
literal: The person who has a girlfriend, take her photo and enlarge it; when he marries the woman, will he carve her?
usage: A humorous warning to appreciate a girlfriend's beauty before marriage changes it.
igbo: Onye nwere enyi nwaanyị see ya photo mee ya enlarge, ọ lụzie nwaanyị ọ ga akpụ ya akpụ

meaning: A person who has someone to turn to does not go hungry or despair.
literal: The person who has someone to run to does not beat hand on stomach.
usage: Used to value support networks and the security of having someone to help.
igbo: Onye nwere onye ịgba anaghị eti aka n'afọ

meaning: A fool does not realize that his sister will marry out and leave the family.
literal: The foolish person does not know that his mother's daughter is a visitor.
usage: A warning against taking a sister for granted or mistreating her.
igbo: Onye nzuzu amaghị na ada nne ya bu obịa

meaning: [uncertain] Intelligence and skill are greater than brute strength; the one who can handle fire with a bare hand surpasses the leopard.
equivalent: Brain over brawn
literal: The person who surpasses the leopard is the one who holds a hand in fire.
usage: Used to praise cleverness or strategy over raw power.
igbo: Onye ọ ka agụ na-aka ejido aka n'ọkụ

meaning: [uncertain] Someone who benefits from another person's misfortune will not let the opportunity go to waste.
literal: The person who finds it good to eat the meat a motor killed does not allow its meat to leave and rot in the bush.
usage: Said of opportunists who exploit a disaster for personal gain.
igbo: Onye ọ na-adi mma iri anụ motor kụgburu, anaghị ekwe ka anụ ya pụọ na iro korota

meaning: Anyone may hold the ọfọ staff, but the ọfọ recognizes the one who truly owns it; authority or innocence cannot be faked.
literal: Every person holds ọfọ, but ọfọ knows the person holding it.
usage: Used to warn that a symbol of authority or innocence only works for the rightful person.
igbo: Onye ọbụla ji ọfọ mana ọfọ ma onye ji ya

meaning: [uncertain] When a pursued person flees to his maternal kin, he has run every race he can run; there is no further refuge.
equivalent: At the end of one's tether
literal: The person whom running caught up with, if he runs to his mother's kin, he has finished all the running he will run.
usage: Said when someone has exhausted every escape or excuse.
igbo: Onye ọsọ chụkatara o gbalaa ikwunne ya, agbachaala ihe niile ọ ga-agba n’ọsọ

meaning: [uncertain] Envy or hot anger can lead a hardworking person down the path of death.
literal: A hot-hearted person carries the one who worked the land to the road of death.
usage: A warning that jealousy can destroy the person who has labored and prospered.
igbo: Onye obi ọkụ na ebu onye arụrụ ala ụzọ anwụ

meaning: Among people who lack ability, someone with even a little ability stands out as a leader.
equivalent: In the land of the blind, the one-eyed man is king.
literal: A one-eyed person becomes king in the land of blind people.
usage: Said when someone is admired or takes charge only because others are less capable.
igbo: Onye otu anya na-abụ eze n'ala ndị ishi

meaning: [uncertain] Replacing something useful with something useless leaves the original need unmet; a foolish trade does not solve the problem.
literal: The person who sold his dog and hired a monkey, the thing ntukwu is still in his house.
usage: A rebuke for a foolish replacement that leaves the real trouble in place.
igbo: Onye rere nkịta ya goro enwe, ihe ntukwu ka nọkwa n’ụlọ ya

meaning: Do everything that belongs to an opportunity while it is there, because the same chance will not come twice.
equivalent: Opportunity knocks but once.
literal: The person who eats kola nut, also gather firewood, because one does not eat kola nut a second time.
usage: Used to urge someone to finish all related tasks at the one time they have.
igbo: Onye rịrị ọjị, kparachaa nkụ, maka anaghi arị ọjị ugboro abụọ

meaning: If you work the land, the land will not run away from you; it remains yours.
literal: The person who works the land, the land refuses him running.
usage: Said to encourage farming or owning land, since land is a dependable inheritance.
igbo: Onye rụọ ala, ala jụwa ya ọsọ

meaning: Taste is personal; what one person calls sweet, another may not, so each speaks for himself.
equivalent: To each his own.
literal: The person who says that a thing is sweet, let him say how it is sweet to him.
usage: Said when people disagree about what is good or pleasing.
igbo: Onye sị na ihe na-atọ ụtọ, okwue ihe ọ na-atọ ka ya

meaning: [uncertain] Someone who denies a small wrongdoing should not be trusted with something more serious; hypocrisy hides greater appetite.
literal: The person who says he does not eat rat, do not use teeth to share children to him.
usage: A warning against trusting a person who loudly denies a small vice.
igbo: Onye sị ya anaghị eri oke, ejila eze ekere ya ụmụaka

meaning: If you attack me for a fault, I will answer by attacking a fault of yours; people who mock others' flaws expose their own.
equivalent: People who live in glass houses shouldn't throw stones.
literal: The person who bit me on the head that was unwashed of hair, I bite him on the buttocks that are unwashed of excrement.
usage: A retort to someone who criticizes you while having a worse flaw.
igbo: Onye taa m arụ n'ishi asọghị ntutu, m taa ya n'ike asọghị nshi

meaning: Consuming the seed meant for planting puts you in debt to future hunger; do not destroy the source of tomorrow's food.
equivalent: Kill the goose that lays the golden eggs.
literal: The person who ate the seed yam has begun to owe debt.
usage: A warning against using up resources that are needed to produce future wealth.
igbo: Onye tara mkpụrụ amụ ebila ji ibi ụgwọ

meaning: [uncertain] If you wake up late, you may have to flee even from a chicken, because you do not know what happened in the night; ignorance of a situation leaves you at a disadvantage.
literal: The person who wakes from sleep in the morning, if a chicken chases him and he runs, because he does not know whether the chicken crowed at night.
usage: Said of someone who avoids a fight or danger because he lacks full knowledge of it.
igbo: Onye teta ura n'ụtụtụ ọkụkọ chụwa ọsọ ya gbawa, maka ọ maghị ma ọkụkọ o puru eze n'abalị

meaning: [uncertain] If you throw away the hard shell when preparing palm nuts, you will lack the materials for things like seats later; do not discard what seems useless now.
equivalent: Waste not, want not.
literal: The person who plucked palm nuts and threw away the stone, chair and ụbịam will no longer exist.
usage: A warning against wasting or discarding materials that will be needed later.
igbo: Onye tịchara akị tụfue okwute, oche na ụbịam agaghịzi adị

meaning: People enjoy what someone else's hard work cracked open, and no one bothers to ask who that someone was.
literal: Who cracked the palm kernel that the chicken used to gather?
usage: Thrown pointedly at someone taking credit for a result, to make people remember who did the original work.
igbo: Onye tiri akị ọkụkọ jiri gbakọọ?

meaning: Whoever honours the great man will find that the great man's hand reaches back to help him.
literal: Whoever praises the king, the king reaches him a hand.
usage: Said to encourage respect and courtesy toward those in authority, or wryly, that praise of the powerful does not go unrewarded.
igbo: Onye too eze,eze eruo ya aka

meaning: Whoever repeats his father's proverbs also pays his father's debts — a heritage comes bundled with its obligations.
literal: Whoever throws the proverb his father threw also pays the debt his father owed.
usage: Said when someone claims the honour of a family name, to remind him he has inherited its burdens too.
igbo: Onye tụọ ilu nna ya tụrụ ya kwụkwaa ụgwọ nna ya ji

meaning: A reckless act does not choose its victim — the stone flung up in the market may come down on your own mother's head.
literal: Whoever tossed a stone up in the market, let him also remember that there is a falling on his mother's head.
usage: A warning to someone acting rashly, that the harm he sets loose can land on his own people.
igbo: Onye tụrụliri okwute elu n'ahia, ya chetakwa na o nwere ịda nne ya n'isi

meaning: [uncertain] A man whose month's debt keeps slipping past him is told that money will, over time, be enough to cover it; the line is corrupt, with English mixed into the Igbo, so the sense cannot be fixed.
literal: The person whose debt of the month escapes him, it is now money over time that will be enough for him.
usage: Cannot be placed with confidence; the line is corrupt and only its talk of debt and time survives.
igbo: Onye ụgwọ onwa ya na-ezuoro ya, ọ bụzi ego over time ga-ezuru ya

meaning: A man afraid of a fight pretends he was about to do something else anyway — the coward always has his excuse ready.
literal: Whoever fears a fight is like one on whom water was poured; he says he was already preparing to bathe.
usage: A mocking rebuke to someone inventing a reason to slip out of a confrontation.
igbo: Onye ụjọ ọgu ka a wụrụ mmiri, ọ sị ya na-akwadobu ịsa ahụ

meaning: The crooked means a man swears by will be the crooked means that destroys him.
equivalent: He who lives by the sword dies by the sword.
literal: Whoever took a bent thing to swear an oath, the oath killed him with a bent thing.
usage: A warning to someone trying to win by trickery, that the very trick will be what ruins him.
igbo: Onye were ngọngọ ṅụa iyi, iyi were ngọngọ gbuo ya

meaning: The man who volunteers his own head as the anvil is not among those invited to share the nuts he cracked.
literal: Whoever brought his head so that the white man's palm kernel be cracked on it will not be joined in eating that kernel.
usage: A warning against offering yourself up to be used, since the one who pays the price is rarely among those who enjoy the gain.
igbo: Onye wetara isi ya ka e were kụwa akị oyibo, agaghị eso ata akị ahụ

meaning: A person at peace with his own god needs no diviner to tell him his fortune.
literal: Whoever he and his chi are on good terms does not go to the diviner's house.
usage: Said of someone who is at ease with himself and needs no one else to read his fate for him.
igbo: Onye ya na chi ya dị na mma anaghị eje be dibịa

meaning: Dealing with dangerous powers calls for distance and caution.
equivalent: He who sups with the devil should have a long spoon.
literal: Whoever eats with the spirits uses a long spoon.
usage: A caution to anyone keeping company with dangerous or dubious people to hold them at arm's length.
igbo: Onye ya na ndi mmụọ na-erikọ nri na-eji ogologo ngazi

meaning: [uncertain] Probably something like: whoever answers back also gets called out, so words cut both ways; the line is very short and fragmentary and its sense cannot be fixed.
literal: Whoever answered back, he called.
usage: Cannot be placed confidently; the line is too short and fragmentary to say when it would be used.
igbo: Onye zakọọ, o kpoo

meaning: A man set on shooting his own brother has nowhere good to aim — every shot wounds his own flesh.
literal: Whoever has prepared to shoot his brother, where will he shoot him?
usage: A rebuke to someone bent on harming a relative, pointing out that the hurt lands on his own blood.
igbo: Onye zuru ịgba nwanne ya, kedu ebe ọ ga akụ ya?

meaning: A meal is sweeter when it is someone else who does the inviting and the paying.
literal: A feast is good if it is another person who called one to it.
usage: Said lightly in accepting hospitality, or wryly of a man who always eats at other people's expense.
igbo: Oriri dị mma ma onye ozo kpọọ ya

meaning: [uncertain] The line names the ọsa and uze birds and something climbing a palm tree, but it is garbled and truncated and no clear sense can be recovered.
literal: Ọsa has no agwụ, uze has no akwụ; and it is their ... that is climbing up the palm tree.
usage: Cannot be given; the line is corrupt and its occasion is lost.
igbo: Ọsa enwe agwụ, uze enwe akwụ, m ọgu ha abụrụ na-elu nkwụ

meaning: Something sharp and hot is what makes spoiled meat go down — a rotten matter is only tolerable when a harsh thing is used to cover it.
literal: It is pepper that one uses to eat rotten meat.
usage: Said when someone's sharp tongue or bluster is being used to make a rotten matter pass as fit.
igbo: Ose ka e ji eri anụ ure

meaning: A warning is not the blow itself: the tree that was told it would be cut down is the one still standing, so being told of danger is what keeps a person on his feet.
literal: It is the tree that was told it is going to be cut that stood.
usage: Said to put heart back into someone who has been warned or threatened.
igbo: Osisi ka a gwara na-aga egbu ọ kwụrụ

meaning: [uncertain] Trouble reaches a person through the place and company he keeps — the tree standing where the dove nests is the one the knife finds.
literal: The tree that is in the dove's nest is eating the knife's blade.
usage: A pointed remark about someone caught up in trouble that began with his neighbours.
igbo: Osisi nọ na akwa nduru na-eri ube mma

meaning: A warning is not the blow itself: the tree that was told it would be cut down is the one still standing, so being told of danger is what keeps a person on his feet.
literal: It is the tree that was told it is going to be cut that stood.
usage: Said to put heart back into someone who has been warned or threatened.
igbo: Oshishi ka a gwara na-aga egbu ọ kwụrụ

meaning: No one grows tired when it is his own life he is running for; the struggle to stay alive never runs out of strength.
literal: The race for life does not grow tired.
usage: Said of someone fighting hard for his own survival, as a comment rather than a rebuke.
igbo: Ọsọ ndụ anaghị agwụ ike

meaning: A woman does not run with her breasts swinging loose for nothing; when she flees like that, the danger must be grave.
literal: The race a woman runs leaving her breast behind is not a small race.
usage: Offered in defence of a person who fled or acted in panic, insisting the danger was real.
igbo: Ọsọ nwaanyị na-agba hapụ ara ya aka abụghị obere ọsọ

meaning: Better the wine inside you than spilt on the ground — take and enjoy what is yours while you still can.
literal: Ọtawaraiko said that instead of the palm wine dripping into the pot, let it drip into the stomach.
usage: Said to urge a person to take and enjoy what is set before him before it is lost.
igbo: Ọtawaraiko si kama mmanya ga adọ n'ite, ya dọrọ n’afọ

meaning: [uncertain] A hand made for real work is not spent on playthings — the one who beats the great gong does not beat a palm frond.
literal: The beater of the gong does not beat the palm frond.
usage: Said when someone is asked to save his strength for matters that deserve it.
igbo: Oti ọkpọ anaghị eti ogbe akwụ

meaning: One person, however able, cannot do everything by himself — a single tooth cannot chew; the work of many needs many.
literal: One tooth does not chew.
usage: Said when a whole task is being left to one person, or when a leader is expected to decide without counsel.
igbo: Otu eze anaghị ata atụ

meaning: What one person does touches everybody — one finger dipped in palm oil leaves every finger oily, and no man's deed stays his own.
literal: If one finger touches palm oil, it stains the others.
usage: Invoked when one person's act brings consequences on his family, age-group or community.
igbo: Otu mkpụrụ aka rụta mmanụ o zue ndị ọzọ

meaning: A single person cannot answer or speak for the whole community; the business of the many must be answered by the many.
literal: One person does not answer nnamọha (the summons of the whole town).
usage: Said when the business of a whole community is being left to one person to answer for.
igbo: Otu onye anaghị aza nnamọha

meaning: The many can finish whatever one man provides, but one man cannot finish what the many provide — one person's store is small beside the community's.
literal: If one person cooks for the public, the public will eat it all up; but if the public cooks for one person, he will not eat it all.
usage: Said when one person is expected to feed or carry a whole gathering.
igbo: Otu onye siere ọha, ọha ga-ericha, mana ọha siere otu onye, ọ gaghị erichanwu

meaning: Boasting about what you will do when sorrow comes ends in your own mouth — the loud promise turns back on the one who made it.
literal: Oturukpokpo said that if his mother died he would use his mouth to pull down every tree in their town; his mother died, and the pulling-down landed on his mouth.
usage: Used to deflate someone boasting about what he will do when the moment comes.
igbo: Oturukpokpo sị nne ya nwụọ ya jiri ọnụ ya tụtuo osisi niile dị n'obodo ha, nne ya nwụọ etuto too ya n'ọnụ

meaning: Once a word or message has left you it cannot be called back — it has gone up like smoke to the sky, and everyone knows it.
literal: The message that was sent has smoked and reached the sky.
usage: Said when a secret has spread or a word has gone out that can no longer be recalled.
igbo: Ozi eziri anwụrụ oku erugo eluigwe

meaning: Whatever a person turns out to be, it is his home and family that must own and carry it — the corpse that dances is carried to its father's compound.
literal: If a corpse dances nkịtị, it is carried off to its father's compound.
usage: Said when a family must own and carry the conduct of one of their own.
igbo: Ozu gbaa nkịtị, e bufee ya ama nna ya

meaning: A kindness done where it cannot be heard or returned is not lost — if the sky did not hear it, the ground did.
literal: Greet the person whose ears are shut; the above did not hear, the below heard.
usage: Said as encouragement to show courtesy and kindness where it cannot be acknowledged or repaid.
igbo: Sị kelee onye ntị chiri, elu anụghị, ala anụ

meaning: What matters is the thing wrapped, not the wrapping — the outside of a person or a matter tells you nothing about its worth.
equivalent: Don't judge a book by its cover.
literal: It is the hand that tied the bundle, but the thing is inside the bundle.
usage: Said when someone is being sized up or waved away on appearance, to turn attention back to what is really inside.
igbo: Sọ aka kere ngwugwu ma ihe di ngwugwu n'ime

meaning: What is happening today is only the old days come round again; there is nothing new in it.
equivalent: There is nothing new under the sun.
literal: Today is long ago.
usage: Offered when a fresh trouble or fashion is treated as unheard-of, to say it has all happened before.
igbo: Taa bụ gboo

meaning: [uncertain] the sense cannot be recovered with confidence from this wording; it turns on cracking a palm kernel from Nsugbe, apparently treating some matter as a small, contemptible task.
literal: Cracked for me the palm kernel of Nsugbe.
