usage: Kept as a set phrase in storytelling or a taunt about a matter being no more than cracking a nut.
igbo: Tiwaara m akị Nsugbe

meaning: A small thing is thrown to someone and then they are left alone to face a far bigger fight — the help was a throw-away, not support.
literal: Threw a dog a bone in the yard, and left it to fight with the spirits.
usage: A rebuke for the one who hands over a token and then steps back while another takes the brunt.
igbo: Tụpụrụ nkịta ọkpụkpụ n'ezi, hapụrụ ya na ndị mmuọ ọgụ

meaning: A bone is tossed to a puppy and it is left to fight the spirits on its own — a favour that only makes a small creature a target.
literal: Threw a puppy a bone so that the fight should be between it and the spirits.
usage: Said of someone set up to carry the blame or the beating after being handed a trifle.
igbo: Tụpụrụ nwa nkịta ọkpụkpụ ka ọgụ bụrụ nke ya na ndị mmuọ

meaning: [uncertain] a day of reckoning comes when what was taken is brought to light and the guilty one is named.
literal: The day the hand will seize the ezeka, the vulture should tell again who stole it.
usage: Reached for as a warning to someone who believes an old wrong has been forgotten.
igbo: Ụbọchị aka ga-akpara ezeka udele ọ kọọ onye chiri ya ọzọ

meaning: The day a great man is born, his match is born with him — no one stands alone above all others.
literal: The day a hero was born in the land, his peer was born too.
usage: Dropped to cool a boastful man, or to console one who feels outmatched.
igbo: Ụbọchị amụrụ dike na mba ka amụrụ ibe ya

meaning: On the very day one sets out to hunt, the game takes to the treetops — when the need is greatest, everything goes contrary.
literal: The day I was hunting, the duiker was climbing up.
usage: Said with a wry shrug when a plan meets an absurd, unexpected obstacle.
igbo: Ụbọchị m na-achụ nta, mgbada na-ari elu

meaning: [uncertain] hunting is for the day of hunting — a thing must be done in its own season, when the moment is given.
literal: The day of hunting is when hunting should be done.
usage: Used to press someone who keeps putting off what can only be done now.
igbo: Ụbọchị nta ka achụọ n'owere nchi

meaning: The day a thief buries his father, everyone he robbed turns up to claim back their things — a man's past finds him when he is least able to bear it.
literal: The day a thief will weep for his father, those whose things were lost arrive for the taking-back.
usage: A warning to anyone who thinks an old wrong will stay buried.
igbo: Ụbọchị onye oshi ga-akwa nna ya, ndi ihe ha furu abịa mgbaru

meaning: Each person's mind is a load only he carries — another's thoughts can never be seen or shouldered for him.
literal: Mind is a bag; each person carries his own.
usage: Said when people expect to know exactly what someone else is thinking, or when one must decide alone.
igbo: Uche bụ akpa onye ọbụla nya nke ya

meaning: Thoughts and worries keep coming and never finish.
literal: Thoughts come and come, it does not die out.
usage: Voiced as a sigh when one trouble has barely passed and another is already forming.
igbo: Uche na-abịa abịa o bighi ebi

meaning: No one thinks his own thinking is bad — a man is never the judge who condemns his own plan.
literal: A person's mind is not bad to him.
usage: Said of someone defending a scheme everyone else can see through.
igbo: Uche onye adị ya njọ

meaning: [uncertain] the thing did what had been allotted to it — each does exactly the part marked out for it.
literal: Ụchịcha did the thing that a share was set aside for.
usage: Said when someone finally acts true to his known nature or role.
igbo: Ụchịcha mere ihe e boro oke

meaning: [uncertain] the credit for what a person gets goes to his head — his wit and destiny — even when it was the feet that did the walking.
literal: The udara fruit that a person's head saved from the foot.
usage: Used where the one who takes the praise for a thing did none of the labour.
igbo: Ụdara onye ishi zọtara n'ukwu

meaning: The one who is punished protests that others who did the same are left alone — the complaint of being singled out while the rest go free.
literal: Udara says that it is only it that bore the child that is being slapped on the mouth.
usage: Thrown out when one person is picked on for what a whole group did, or when one child is punished among many.
igbo: Ụdara si na ọ bụ sọsọ ya mụtara nwa a na-apịwa ọnụ?

meaning: The rain that soaks me will fall on others too — trouble comes to everyone in turn, so no one should mock another's misfortune.
literal: The vulture says that rain is falling and has killed it; the one that reaches a person, will it not be known?
usage: Said to steady someone in trouble, or to warn those gloating over another's bad luck.
igbo: Udele sị na mmiri na-ezo amagbuo ya, nke na-eru onye ka ọ ga ama?

meaning: [uncertain] When the elders are gone, the young lose restraint and treat what was once held in awe as nothing.
literal: The vulture says the elders have died so that the young should not eat it and call it a paltry thing.
usage: A lament for the passing of the old people and the discipline they kept.
igbo: Udele sị ndị okenye anwụchala ka umụazị ghara iri ya kpọọ ya nkịrịka egbe

meaning: [uncertain] A creature of courage does not bring forth a timid child — bravery runs in the line.
literal: Ufu does not give birth to a child of fear.
usage: Said in praise of a bold child whose parent was bold before them.
igbo: Ufu anaghị amụ nwa ụjọ

meaning: [uncertain] Something has silently swallowed up my husband's other wife — ruin comes on a rival quietly and without warning.
literal: Ugboguru has swallowed, swallowed my husband's wife.
usage: A jeering remark about a rival who has been quietly taken out of the way.
igbo: Ụgbọgụrụ mịaram mịara nwunye di m

meaning: [uncertain] It is not a sickness as such, but once it takes hold it acts like one — a small thing turns grave if it is left to settle.
literal: Ughere is not sickness; if it becomes aguo.
usage: A caution that a small trouble ignored will grow into a real affliction.
igbo: Ughere abụghị ọrịa, ọ bụrụ agụọ

meaning: The eagle has taken its perch on the kola tree — the finest has arrived and the honoured place is his.
literal: The eagle has perched on top of the kola tree.
usage: Said in praise when a person of great worth arrives or takes the seat of honour.
igbo: Ugo eberela n’elu ọjị

meaning: A well-formed eagle does not scratch about for scraps — a person of worth does not stoop to petty scrambling.
literal: The eagle that is fine does not scratch about.
usage: A rebuke to someone of standing who is scrabbling for what is beneath them.
igbo: Ugo chara acha anaghị echu echu

meaning: If the eagle eats a toad, its beauty is spoiled — what a person stoops to for gain costs them their dignity.
literal: The eagle eats a toad, its beauty spoils.
usage: A warning to someone about to debase themselves for gain.
igbo: Ugo rie awọ, mma ya arụọ

meaning: [uncertain] What is still budding does not rot — a thing kept growing and tended stays sound.
literal: The ugwo is sprouting; it does not rot.
usage: Said of a thing or a person kept active and cared for, to note that it does not decay.
igbo: Ụgwọ na-ama ebu, ọ naghị ere ure

meaning: Respect is an exchange: the courtesy a woman shows her mates is the respect she gets back from them.
equivalent: Respect is a two-way street.
literal: Honour is the greetings a woman uses to greet her fellow women.
usage: Said to the haughty or the rude, to remind them that respect must be given before it is received.
igbo: Ugwu bụ nkwanye nkwanye nwaanyị ji atọ ibe ya

meaning: [uncertain] When famine teaches, even the old woman learns a new trick — hard times force everyone to learn what they never knew.
literal: Ugwu learns the breaking of a leg; the old woman learns arikata akwuru.
usage: Said when hardship pushes people to learn things they never expected to.
igbo: Ugwu mụta mgbaji ukwu, agadi nwaanyị amụta arikata akwụrụ

meaning: A woman's honour is her husband — her standing in the world is bound up with the man she married.
literal: A woman's honour is her husband.
usage: Said of a married woman's standing, to show how closely it rests on her marriage.
igbo: Ugwu nwaanyi bụ di ya

meaning: Fear cannot grip you once it is you who goes first — meeting dread head-on strips it of its power.
literal: Fear does not frighten the belly if it leads the way.
usage: A spur to someone hanging back: go first, and the fear will not hold you.
igbo: Ụjọ anaghị atụ afọ ma ya bute ụzọ

meaning: A crowded gathering is settled by one head — it takes a leader for many voices to come to one agreement.
literal: An assembly crowded together: it is with the head that it is agreed.
usage: Said when a crowd cannot agree, to point to the one head that must settle it.
igbo: Ụka akparakpa, isi ka eji ekwe ya

meaning: A human being who falls into trouble has his fellow human beings to come for him, while a wild animal caught in the same trap has only the tree it is tied to — people survive by standing with one another.
literal: If a trap catches a wild animal, it goes to the foot of a tree; if it catches a person, it goes to that person's fellow human being.
usage: Said to someone in trouble to remind him that he is not alone, because he has his own people to stand for him.
igbo: Ụkọ kọwa anụ ọhịa ọ gaa n'ukwu osisi, ọ kọwa mmadụ, ọ gakwuru mmadụ ibe ya

meaning: Whoever joins a company that is doomed perishes along with it.
literal: The ụkpala entered the flock of chickens; it entered the land of the spirits.
usage: A warning to someone drifting into the company of people whose fate is already sealed.
igbo: Ụkpala bara n'ikpo ọkụkọ bara n'ala ndi mmụọ

meaning: Stubbornness, the refusal to take advice, is what kills a man.
literal: The hard-eared ụkpala rests in the belly of a bird.
usage: A rebuke to someone who waves off advice and is walking into ruin.
igbo: Ụkpala ntị ike na-ezu ike n'afọ nnụnụ

meaning: [uncertain] Whoever shuts his ears to warning is the one who is killed.
literal: Ụkpala, okpoko killed it; its ears were shut.
usage: A warning to someone who will not listen to those warning him.
igbo: Ụkpala okpoko gburu ntị chiri ya

meaning: [uncertain] The one harming you gives the harm an innocent name — the burning brand tells the man it scorches that he is only sweating oil.
literal: The burning ụkpala waited and said to him that he is spitting out oil.
usage: Said against someone who makes light of the very harm he is doing.
igbo: Ụkpala ọkụ na-ere chere sị ya na-asụpụta mmanụ

meaning: [uncertain] Even a thing held in your own hand can still struggle free of your grasp.
literal: The ụkwa held in the hand, it is running.
usage: A caution to someone who thinks that what he holds is already safely his.
igbo: Ụkwa a chị n'aka ọ na-agba

meaning: What a man waits and longs for arrives empty and disappoints him.
literal: The ụkwa that is being waited for has no seeds.
usage: Said with disappointment when a long-awaited thing turns out to be worth nothing.
igbo: Ụkwa a na-eche, mkpụrụ adịghị ya

meaning: A thing that comes on the very day it is needed has not come late — good fortune is a matter of timing.
literal: The ụkwa that fell on the day the mouths to be fed are counted did not fall out of season.
usage: Said in wonder or thanks when help arrives at exactly the moment it is needed.
igbo: Ụkwa dara ụbọchị a na-agụ afọ, adaghị n'oge

meaning: Good fortune that lands on the day of the feast has landed exactly when it was wanted — such timing is providence, not lateness.
literal: The ụkwa that fell on the day of the feast did not fall out of season.
usage: Said when something good arrives at precisely the moment it is wanted.
igbo: Ụkwa dara ụbọchị oriri, adaghị n'oge

meaning: [uncertain] Good things fall into the hands of those who do not know how to look after them.
literal: The ụkwa falls for those who do not know how to see.
usage: Said with envy or a shrug when a good thing lands with someone who does not value it.
igbo: Ụkwa na-adara ndị na-amaghị esi ahụ

meaning: If your legs can carry you clear of a leopard, the bushbuck is already yours — what saved you from the greater danger will win you the lesser.
literal: The legs that stopped a leopard, the bushbuck came owing them a debt.
usage: Said to hearten someone who has already survived something hard as he faces an easier test.
igbo: Ụkwụ jie agụ mgbada bịara ya ụgwọ

meaning: What has fallen into the water must be groped for with your own feet — recovering anything takes your own effort, not another's.
literal: It is the feet that are used to look for what has fallen into water.
usage: A spur to someone who wants a lost thing back but will not stir himself.
igbo: Ụkwụ ka e ji achọ ihe danyere na mmiri

meaning: [uncertain] A leg with a blemish on it is no leg to show off naked — a person should not bare the part of himself that shames him.
literal: The leg that has ọgọdọ on it is not good to be shown naked.
usage: A caution to someone who is about to expose a weakness of his own.
igbo: Ukwu na-ama ọgọdọ adịghị mma ịgba ọtọ

meaning: A man may move softly and say nothing, but there are watchful eyes that see where he goes.
literal: The feet go wam wam, the eyes go zam zam and see it.
usage: A warning to someone who believes his quiet, secret moves go unseen.
igbo: Ụkwụ na-ga wam wam, anya na-aga zam zam na-ahụ ya

meaning: A parent's rough handling of a child is not meant to destroy the child — the hen treads on her chicks and none of them dies.
literal: The hen's foot that stepped on its child does not kill it.
usage: Said to a child who resents a parent's correction, or in defence of a parent's firmness.
igbo: Ụkwụ ọkụkọ zọrọ nwa ya anaghị egbu ya

meaning: You can trace a matter back to the person who brought it; whoever introduces something must answer for it.
literal: The leg of the person who brought it is what is used to follow him.
usage: Said when a matter is traced back to its source or when holding the introducer responsible.
igbo: Ụkwụ onye wetara ka eji eso ya

meaning: Haste causes trouble; it is better to finish your journey patiently than to rush.
equivalent: Haste makes waste.
literal: Ulili says that the person who has walked his journey should jump/run, because of what haste has done.
usage: A warning to slow down and not rush into action.
igbo: Ulili si onye jekata ije ya tụọ nkwa ọsọ, maka ihe ọsọ eme mee

meaning: When the main house falls, the fence cannot remain standing; a person's fall affects those attached to him.
literal: A house does not fall and leave its fence.
usage: Said when one person's misfortune spreads to the family or community.
igbo: Ụlọ anaghị ada hapụ uko

meaning: [uncertain] The line seems to say that it is the people of the land who enable one to escape the land; even in flight, one depends on community.
literal: It is Umeala that ome uses to run away from the land.
usage: Said when reminding someone that even in escape or trouble, they rely on their people.
igbo: Umeala ka ome ji ji agbapu ala

meaning: Do not let a gathering or crowd lead you into something shameful or disastrous.
literal: You should not gather so that you eat vulture.
usage: A warning against bad company or following a crowd into disgrace.
igbo: Unu agbakọọla ka unu ha eri udele

meaning: Sleep does no harm to the eyes; rest is not damaging.
literal: Sleep does not spoil the eye.
usage: Said to urge someone to rest without guilt or to reassure that sleep is harmless.
igbo: Ụra anaghị emebi anya

meaning: Even sleep, if it goes on too long, becomes death; overindulgence destroys.
literal: Sleep that agrees to a week has become death.
usage: A warning against laziness or overindulging in rest.
igbo: Ụra kwere izu abụrụla ọnwụ

meaning: If sleep is sweet, people will talk about it; good things naturally earn praise.
literal: If sleep is sweet, it is talked about.
usage: Said when something good becomes known and praised on its own.
igbo: Ụra tọwa ụtọ, ekwowa ya ekwowa

meaning: Nothing can stop the sun from making its journey; no obstacle can halt what must happen.
literal: Urukpu does not take away the sun's journey.
usage: Said when a force or person cannot block an inevitable course of events.
igbo: Urukpu anaghị anapụ anyanwụ ije

meaning: [uncertain] It is better to flee and endure hardship than to be killed or captured.
literal: Ururu said it was better for it to run in the forest with the hunter than for its head to boil in a pot.
usage: Said when choosing survival through flight over certain death.
igbo: Ururu sị ọ kaara ya mma n'ọchị chịrị ọsọ ya na dinta gbara n'ime ọhịa kama isi ya ga-agbọ n'ite

meaning: The bat says that if it is ugly, it goes about at night; people hide their flaws in darkness or secrecy.
literal: The bat says that if it is ugly, it uses the night to go.
usage: Said teasingly of someone hiding a shameful or unattractive side.
igbo: Ụsụ si ya ma na ya jọrọ njọ wee jiri abalị aga

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt; its sense cannot be reliably recovered.
literal: The bow shot elekentịọba; it ate palm-kernel ọgụ.
usage: Not usable in its current form; the line needs repair before it can be cited.
igbo: Ụta gbatara elekentịọba ya rie ọgu mkpụrụ akụ

meaning: A child may kill a vulture with a bow, but an elder carved the bow; the young succeed through the tools and wisdom of their elders.
literal: The bow with which a child killed a vulture is an elder who carved it.
usage: Said to remind a boastful youth to credit the elders who equipped them.
igbo: Ụta nwata jiri gbagbuo udele bụ okenye pịara ya

meaning: A good thing does not fall on barren or sandy ground; valuable things do not come to an unready or unworthy place.
literal: The ụtara does not fall on ground that has gathered sand.
usage: Said when a good thing does not land where it would be wasted.
igbo: Ụtara anaghị ada n'ala gbara aka aja

meaning: When the ụtara and the soup are both good, the meal becomes a feast; when everything is right, it is a celebration.
literal: If the ụtara is good and the soup is good, we are at a feast.
usage: Said when things come together well and people are enjoying themselves.
igbo: Ụtara dịrị mma ofe dịrị mma, anyị nọ na oriri oriri

meaning: The world is like a market: when you have finished your business in it, you go home. Life is temporary, and each person must do their part and then depart.
literal: The world is a market; whoever finishes buying it should go home.
usage: Said at funerals or when urging contentment and readiness to leave a completed task or life itself.
igbo: Ụwa bụ ahịa, onye zụchaa ya laa

meaning: [uncertain] A blacksmith who does not know how to forge an ogene is told to look at the gun's tail/butt; the saying seems to advise learning by observing a related model, but the exact point is obscure.
literal: A blacksmith who does not know how to forge an ogene, let him look at the tail of a gun/hawk.
usage: Used when someone lacks a skill and is being told to study an example, though the proverb's application is uncertain.
igbo: Ụzụ na-amaghị akpụ ogene, ya lee egbe anya n'ọdụ

meaning: Stop a bad intrusion or habit early, before it becomes established and hard to remove.
equivalent: Nip it in the bud.
literal: Remove the monkey's hand from the soup before it becomes a person's hand.
usage: A warning to correct a small offense or encroachment before it grows into a serious one.
igbo: Wepụ aka enwe n’ofe tupu ọ ghọọ aka mmadụ

meaning: Speak carefully and tactfully; use your tongue to test the situation rather than letting it get you into trouble.
equivalent: Think before you speak.
literal: Use your tongue to count your teeth in your mouth.
usage: A caution against careless or disrespectful speech.
igbo: Were ire gị gụọ eze gị ọnụ

meaning: Be patient; if you wait, things will be ready in their own time.
equivalent: Good things come to those who wait.
literal: Take it slowly so that the soup that is boiling cooks food for you.
usage: A reminder to be patient and not rush a process.
igbo: Were nwayọ ka ofe rọrọ arọ zuoro gi nri

meaning: [uncertain] Whether the rope ties the goat or the goat ties the rope, they are all one thing — the two are bound together and the distinction is meaningless.
equivalent: Six of one, half a dozen of the other.
literal: Use a rope to tie a goat and use a goat to tie a rope, they are all one thing.
usage: Said when two ways of doing something amount to the same thing, or when parties in a bond share one fate.
igbo: Were ọgbụ kedo ewu na were ewu kedo n'ọgbụ, fa ncha bụ ofu ife afụ

meaning: May it go well for the man and also go well for the woman — a blessing for shared well-being, especially in marriage.
literal: Let it be good for the man, and let it also be good for the woman.
usage: A blessing offered over a couple or a shared undertaking.
igbo: Ya diri nwoke mma dịrịkwa nwaanyị mma

meaning: [uncertain] The event has become a byword — a story people tell as a lesson or warning.
literal: Then it became a church, became a proverb.
usage: Said when a happening turns into a cautionary tale or common saying.
igbo: Ya wee bụrụ ụka bụrụ ilu

meaning: [uncertain] If you use someone else to do a dirty or intimate task, the consequence still attaches to you; the exact Igbo wording is obscure.
literal: Whoever holds a servant/slave to lick his hand, will it not remain on him above?
usage: A warning that delegating a shameful act does not remove its stain.
igbo: Onye ji ohuhu aracha aka ya, og’afali ya n’elu?

meaning: Your words do not satisfy me; I need something tangible, not just talk or promises.
equivalent: Fine words butter no parsnips.
literal: The thing you said did not fill my stomach.
usage: A rebuke to someone whose promises or words are empty and unsatisfying.
igbo: Ihe i kwuru ejughi m afọ

meaning: [uncertain] However far the play goes, one still goes to the farm with a hoe in hand — work must not be neglected for amusement.
equivalent: Business before pleasure.
literal: Where the play reaches, but when one is going to the farm, one holds a hoe in hand.
usage: A reminder to put work before play.
igbo: Ebe ejije eteka mana ka ana aga n'ubi ka ji na aka

meaning: Do not ask an interested party for a fair answer; they will give the answer that benefits them.
equivalent: Don't ask a barber whether you need a haircut.
literal: You are asking a dog about faeces; is it you who will eat it?
usage: A warning against seeking advice from someone with a personal stake in the matter.
igbo: ina aju nkita na nsi obu gi ga eriya

meaning: If you pry into old matters or someone's private affairs, you will uncover something unpleasant.
equivalent: Let sleeping dogs lie.
literal: If you wash an old woman's cloth, excrement comes out.
usage: A warning not to dig into old people's affairs or long-buried matters.
igbo: asawa akwa agadi nwayi, agasputa nsi

meaning: [uncertain] One eye owes six people — one person or resource is burdened by many claims; the proverb likely warns against overcommitment or shows the burden of serving many.
literal: One eye owes six people.
usage: Used to describe a situation where one person or thing is responsible for too many people.
igbo: otu anya ji onye isii ugwo

meaning: Wherever the runner reaches, the walker will also reach — speed does not change the final destination, so there is no need to rush.
literal: Because of where the runner reached, that is where the walker will reach.
usage: A consolation to someone moving slowly, or a warning against pointless haste.
igbo: maka ebe onye oso ruru ka onye ije ga eru

meaning: [uncertain] An old woman does not dance the vigorous ọma-agba to show herself off — age itself sets the limit on what one puts on display.
literal: An old woman does not boast and dance ọma agba.
usage: Thrown at an elder who still dresses or carries on like a young person, to shame her back into her station.
igbo: agadi nwayi anaghi akanka na-egwu oma agba

meaning: Even the one whose job is loud and public must still see to his own small, unglamorous needs.
literal: The horn-blower is wiping [his] nose.
usage: Said of someone doing a grand task who still has to handle its humble side, or to a proud person who thinks ordinary chores are beneath him.
igbo: ogbu opi na eficha imi

meaning: [uncertain] A fragment of a song-line: the meat must be carried on the cow's own back — what is asked for is expected to come from the very one being asked.
literal: Bring meat, bring meat, carry [it] also on the cow's body.
usage: Said when someone is pressed to supply the very thing only they can supply.
igbo: Beta anu, beta anu bukwonu n'aru efi

meaning: [uncertain] Corrupt line; the sense cannot be recovered with confidence, though it appears to warn against carelessly throwing away something and then lacking it.
literal: Not holding the akpata, throw away the aba; it will [be] for him.
usage: Cannot be pinned down — the line as written is corrupt.
igbo: Ejiro akpata atufue aba oganyara

meaning: The person who is being carried never feels how long the road is.
literal: Because a child carried on the back does not know that the road is far.
usage: Said to remind a cushioned person that the ease they enjoy was borne on someone else's legs.
igbo: maka na nwata akwo n'azu amagi n'uzo di anya

meaning: What a powerful protector puts into your hands will not destroy you; being sent by the strong is itself a shield.
literal: Because the fire which a leopard gave a child in hand does not burn him to death.
usage: Said to steady someone handed a hard or risky task by a powerful person.
igbo: maka na oku agu nyere nwata n'aka anagi eregbu ya

meaning: Whoever sells ogiri must put up with the flies that the trade brings with it.
literal: Because the woman who sells ogiri, and the flies' eyes are dry.
usage: Said to someone complaining about the nuisance that comes attached to the work they chose.
igbo: maka na nwanyi n'ere ogiri ma Ijiji anya kporo

meaning: [uncertain] A plant growing beside its fellows grows as its fate allows — what you become is shaped by the company you keep.
literal: When ụkpaka grows with its fellow, it grows into destiny.
usage: Offered as a quiet caution about the companions a young person is keeping.
igbo: Ukpaka gba na ibe ya gba, o gba na akaraka

meaning: [uncertain] When things are scattered about, one lands at the toad's feet — a general windfall reaches even the least likely taker.
literal: The akụ scattered and fell to the frog.
usage: Said when a share of something being distributed ends up with an unlikely person.
igbo: Aku fesia odalu awo

meaning: It is the patient one who gets to eat the fish — waiting is what brings the reward.
equivalent: All things come to those who wait.
literal: The person of patience is [the one who] eats the ukpo fish.
usage: Said to encourage someone who is tired of waiting for a good thing to come round.
igbo: Onye ndidi na eli azu ukpo

meaning: A crowd is power — people standing together are strong.
equivalent: United we stand, divided we fall.
literal: A multitude is strength.
usage: Said when urging a family or town to settle its quarrel and act as one.
igbo: igwe-ibu-ike

meaning: [uncertain] Once a child has eaten a toad she turns her nose up at meat — a taste spoiled on something base loses its relish for the good thing.
literal: Do you know that [if] a child eats a toad, it refuses meat.
usage: Said of a person who has taken to something coarse and now scorns what is better.
igbo: I makwa na nwata rie awo oju anu

meaning: [uncertain] Whether it is struck once or struck twice, the kernel comes out only on that same beam — it is steady work in the same place that yields.
literal: Strike first once on the ogwe, strike second once on the ogwe, it is only on the ogwe that the akụ is cracked.
usage: Said to keep someone at the task they have already begun instead of starting afresh elsewhere.
igbo: Agbaa mbu otu na ogwe, agbaa abou otu n ogwe, obu so ogwe ka an apiri aku

meaning: All the lizards sprawl the same way, so nobody can tell which of them is carrying a belly — hidden burdens do not show in a person's look.
literal: All lizards lie flat, one does not know the one whose belly is pregnant.
usage: Said when people are being judged by appearance alone, or to excuse someone whose trouble is not visible.
igbo: Ngwere nile makpu mapku, amaghi nke afo n alu

meaning: If the head throws away the udara it has already plucked, where will it pluck another? Do not cast off the good thing you already have.
equivalent: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
literal: If the head throws away the udara it picked up with the foot, where will it pluck again?
usage: Said to someone on the point of discarding a good thing that is already in their hand.
igbo: Onye isi tufue udara ozotara n ukwu, kedu ebe oga atuta ozo

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is too garbled to recover a reliable sense; it appears to compare something to madness eating a vulture, but the trailing words are unclear.
literal: Ezue like madness eats vulture, atotue Nigiga.
usage: Not usable with confidence; likely a corrupted line.
igbo: Ezue ka ara eri udele atotue Nigiga

meaning: A person's real worth is known only when they are put to the test.
equivalent: The proof of the pudding is in the eating.
literal: When omara omara is put [to the test], when ofeke is put, he puts his head into the bush.
usage: Used when a boastful person is exposed once real competence is required.
igbo: Aturoro omara omara, aturoro ofeke ofenye isi no ohia

meaning: Water is indispensable to fish; a basic need without which life cannot go on.
equivalent: Water is life.
literal: Water is life of fish.
usage: Used to stress that something is a vital necessity, not a luxury.
igbo: miri bu ndu azu

meaning: Steady, repeated effort is what accomplishes the task.
equivalent: Constant dripping wears away a stone.
literal: It is round and round that grinds pepper.
usage: Encourages persistence when a task is slow.
igbo: okirikiri ka na agba ukwu ose

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled; it seems to say something about how events befell the toad's child and it failed to climb odudu, but the sense is not recoverable.
literal: As it came, as it came happened to the child of toad, it did not climb odudu.
usage: Not reliable; likely a corrupted proverb.
igbo: ka abia ka abia mere na nwa awo epughi odudu

meaning: If you follow another into an undertaking, you share in the outcome that befalls them.
literal: The rat followed the lizard and drank water; if the lizard dries, will the rat also dry?
usage: Warns that imitating another's action means sharing the consequence.
igbo: oke soro ngwere maa miri, okoo ngwere, oga akokwanu oke

meaning: If you treat an unworthy person with too much respect or indulgence, they will take liberties and harm you.
equivalent: Give him an inch and he'll take a mile.
literal: If a dog is called sacred, it tears cloth.
usage: A warning against pampering or over-respecting someone who will abuse it.
igbo: Akpokete nkita nso, otakaa akwa

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo say that a person's strength or bravery is known in a certain challenging situation; the exact phrase is unclear.
literal: The Igbo say that it is okwonu nberede that one uses to know a strong person.
usage: Used when someone's courage or ability only shows under pressure.
igbo: Ndi igbo si na okwonu nberede k'eji ama dike

meaning: When a younger or newer person appears, the older one is cast aside.
equivalent: Out with the old, in with the new.
literal: If one hears of a maiden, one drives away an old woman.
usage: Said when someone is discarded in favor of a younger or newer option.
igbo: O anuta agbogho achupu agadi

meaning: When resources are shared out, even the lowliest gets a portion, so there is no cause for complaint.
equivalent: A rising tide lifts all boats.
literal: There is no problem because when wealth is scattered, it falls to the toad.
usage: Used to reassure that a fair sharing will reach everyone.
igbo: nsogbu adiro makana aku fesia odalu awo

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled; no reliable sense can be recovered.
literal: I am throwing ikpu ikwu ekwu; will it kill itself?
usage: Not reliable; likely corrupt text.
igbo: Ana m atu ikpu ikwu ekwu, O ya ga ebi onwe ya?

meaning: A small amount of something harmful can ruin great strength or a good thing.
equivalent: One bad apple spoils the barrel.
literal: Small poison is spoiling strength.
usage: A warning that a small bad influence can destroy something much larger.
igbo: Obele nsi n'e mebi ike

meaning: Speak in public only if you know how to speak well; otherwise keep your words to yourself.
equivalent: Better to remain silent and be thought a fool than to speak and remove all doubt.
literal: If you know how to speak, speak at the ikwe; if you do not know how to speak, speak on your thigh.
usage: A caution against exposing one's ignorance in public.
igbo: imara asu, suo na ikwe; ma i maro asu i suo na apata gi

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled and mixes languages; it appears to be a monkey addressing its child about a head and a sheep in the belly, but the sense is not recoverable.
literal: Monkey says to child that when you [unclear] head is like sheep in belly.
usage: Not usable with confidence; likely a corrupted or pidgin line.
igbo: monkey si nwa ke oga i dutatra ishi wu kahi ovu na afo

meaning: A person does not compete with or prey on what is part of them; one does not chase one's own tail.
literal: A dog does not run after its tail.
usage: Used to caution someone against struggling against their own people or pursuing what is already theirs.
igbo: nkita anaghi agbala odu ya oso

meaning: [uncertain] A dog that has been washed no longer tolerates the stink — once a person has tasted better conditions, the squalor he once lived with becomes unbearable to him.
literal: The dog has gone to bathe; it does not smell the smell of excrement.
usage: Said of someone who, having bettered his lot, now turns up his nose at the very conditions he came out of.
igbo: nkita gala i wu onaghi anu ishi nshi

meaning: Look at an old woman's toothless mouth and you would swear she never nursed at her mother's breast — nothing in how a person looks today tells you what that person once was.
literal: It is said that one looks an old woman in the mouth; it is like she never used it to suck breast.
usage: Used to check anyone who judges people by their present appearance, since the shrivelled old woman was once a baby at the breast.
igbo: Asi na anaele agadi nwanyi anya n'onu odika ojighi ya we nua ara!

meaning: A frog does not hop about in broad daylight for nothing — nobody acts without a reason, so when someone behaves strangely, look for what lies behind it.
literal: A frog does not run in the daytime for nothing.
usage: Said when odd behaviour raises suspicion and the speaker wants to insist that there is something behind it.
igbo: Awo adighi agba oso ehihe n'efu

meaning: A child carried on someone's back has no idea that walking tires the body — those who never bear the burden cannot understand the strain of it.
literal: A child carried on the back does not know that walking takes the body.
usage: Used to brush aside or shame someone who talks lightly about hardship he has never had to carry.
igbo: Nwata akwo n'azu amaghi na ije nara ahu

meaning: One only ever walks round and round the pepper plant and never climbs it — a matter is hovered over, talked around, and never reached.
equivalent: to beat about the bush
literal: It is round and round that one runs at the foot of the pepper plant; it does not climb it up.
usage: Said of a speaker who keeps circling a subject without ever coming to the point of it.
igbo: okirikiri ka ana agba ukwu ose adighi ari ya elu

meaning: [uncertain] Only two words survive here, 'Ngbede, you agreed', and no proverb can be reliably read from them; the line is truncated and its sense cannot be recovered.
literal: Ngbede, you agreed.
usage: Cannot be determined from so short a fragment.
igbo: ngbede ikwere

meaning: [uncertain] Having a proverb explained to you costs as much as the money that was spent on your mother — wisdom is not passed on cheaply to the dull.
literal: The person a proverb is told to and explained to — the money used to hear his mother has gone into nothing.
usage: Said in reproach of someone so slow that every hint must be spelled out for him.
igbo: onye atru ilu kowaa ego eji nu nne ya lara niyi

meaning: Every person scratches where he is standing — each one looks first to his own place and his own people.
literal: Where a person is, that is where he is scratching.
usage: Said when someone is accused of favouring his own side, or to justify seeing to one's own first.
igbo: ebe onye no ka ona awachi

meaning: [uncertain] A fowl with no place of its own should not pick a fight, for when it is driven off, where will it drink? — do not start trouble when you have nowhere to run.
literal: A fowl that has no place and starts a fight; when it is chased away, where will it drink?
usage: A warning to someone picking a quarrel while having no allies and no refuge to fall back on.
igbo: okuko ebeghi ebe nyua ogu akpana obee ole ka o ga anyu

meaning: [uncertain] The one who says he cannot see still comes when he is called, and the one who says he cannot hear still answers — people plead blindness and deafness only when it suits them.
literal: Ọfụrụ said it did not see; call it. It heard and said it had no ear.
usage: Used to expose someone who claims ignorance of what he plainly perceives.
igbo: ofuru si na ya afughi anya kpoo ya onuru si ya anughi nti chie ya

meaning: With a piece of yam in your hand you can settle a case with the spirits — matters are settled only when you come with something in hand.
literal: One holds a piece of yam in hand, one uses it to settle words with the spirits.
usage: Said when a dispute is to be settled or a favour sought, to point out that nothing is done for the empty-handed.
igbo: E jide ibe ji n’aka e were sawa ndị mmụọ okwu

meaning: [uncertain] The bag has been woven and the maiden killed, and no one tears it apart in the market — what is done cannot be undone.
equivalent: What's done is done
literal: A bag was woven and used to kill a maiden; it does not tear in the afa.
usage: Said to close a matter that cannot be reversed and to stop people grieving over what is finished.
igbo: A kpaa akpa were gbuo nwaada, ọ naghị awa n’afa.

meaning: Saliva gathered in the mouth turns to foam — small things collected together amount to something more than each of them alone.
literal: One gathers saliva in the mouth, it foams.
usage: Used to urge people to pool their small contributions, or to remark how many mouths together make a great noise.
igbo: A nyụkọọ amịrị ọnụ ọ gbọọ ụfụfụ.

meaning: A child who sits close to an elder may get no kola nut, but he will get a piece of dried meat — those who stay near their elders never go away empty-handed.
literal: A child who sat close to an elder did not get a piece of kola nut; he got meat that is dried.
usage: Said to encourage the young to keep close to their elders, since there is always something to be gained from their company.
igbo: Nwatakịrị nọdebere okenye nso enwetaghị ibegiri ọjị, o nweta anụ kpọrọ nkụ.

meaning: [uncertain] Even if a marriage does not turn out well, it is still good to have made a friend — a union that fails is not wasted if goodwill is kept.
literal: Eating does not do a young woman, because if marriage is not good, it is good to make a friend.
usage: Said where a courtship or alliance has broken down, as consolation that friendship can outlast a failed arrangement.
igbo: Iri anaghị eme nwagbọghọ n’ihi na ọ bụrụ na ọ dịghị mma ọlụlụ, ọ dịnụ mma ime enyi.

meaning: An incompetent person, unable to do the real work, turns his attention to something irrelevant.
literal: The blacksmith who does not know how to forge an ogene looked at the gun's tail.
usage: Used to mock someone who, lacking skill, focuses on the wrong thing instead of the task at hand.
igbo: Ụzụ amaghị akpụ ogene lere egbe anya n’ọdụ.

meaning: Praise a rare and splendid thing when you meet it, because you will not meet it every day.
literal: The person who saw an eagle, praise it, because one does not see an eagle every day.
usage: Used to nudge someone to give credit where it is due — to honour an exceptional person while they are still around to hear it.
igbo: Onye hụrụ ugo jaa ya mma n’ihi na a naghị ahụ ugo kwa daa.

meaning: Anyone who has never had to carry a burden does not know how much it hurts.
literal: A child carried on the back does not know that walking is pain.
usage: A gentle rebuke to someone who makes light of a hardship they have never had to endure themselves.
igbo: Nwa a kwọ n’azụ amaghị na ije dị ụfụ.

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt and its point cannot be recovered with confidence; it appears to describe an old woman and a place scorched by fire.
literal: Old woman saw where the ịkpa burned, dried-scorched.
usage: Not usable as recorded; a speaker would not reach for this line in its present form.
igbo: Agadi nwaanyị hụ ebe ịkpa gbara ọkụ amịrị akpawa.

meaning: [uncertain] When a hand accomplishes something beyond human strength — plucking the vulture's tooth — it is the spirits, not the hand, that deserve the credit.
literal: The hand that plucked the vulture's tooth, let it say the spirits crowned it king.
usage: Said of someone whose feat is so far past the ordinary that people ascribe it to a power greater than themselves.
igbo: Aka kpara eze udele o kwuo ndị mmụọ chiri ya eze.

meaning: A sheep dressed in a leopard's skin is not a leopard; it is only dreaming its own death.
literal: The sheep that is dreaming while it wears a leopard's skin, it is a dream of its death.
usage: A warning to anyone who puts on a strength or a status that is not theirs, inviting ruin.
igbo: Atụrụ na-arọ nrọ ebe o yi akpụkpọ agụ bụ nrọ ọnwụ ya.

meaning: Nothing falls to the ground without touching sand — no happening is without a cause or a consequence.
literal: The ụtara does not fall to the ground without touching sand.
usage: Invoked when an event is being dismissed as mere chance, to insist that everything leaves a trace.
igbo: Ụtara anaghị ada n’ala ghara imetụ aja.

meaning: [uncertain] Do not walk into a house simply because you caught a glimpse of something; a sight from outside is not reason enough.
literal: One does not enter a house because one saw akanya (atanyi).
usage: Not reliable as recorded; the transcriber's own doubt in the text makes the saying unsafe to lean on.
igbo: A naghị aba ụlọ maka na a hụrụ akanya (atanyi)

meaning: A good tongue is what carries a person through thorny places.
literal: It is a good tongue that the snail uses to go into the thorn.
usage: A compliment for someone whose well-chosen, good-natured words bring them safely through a hostile situation.
igbo: Ọ bụ ire ọma ka ejula ji aga n’ogwu.

meaning: Taking responsibility for others also means facing the dangers that threaten them; every charge brings its own trouble.
literal: The hen that ruled the chicks also ruled the hawk.
usage: Used to warn that anyone who takes charge of dependents must also be ready to confront the threats against them.
igbo: Ọkụkọ chịrị ụmụ ọ chịrị ekwurekwu.

meaning: [uncertain] A bachelor who suddenly says a wife should be found for him today or tomorrow should ask who he has been living with all this time; you cannot claim you cannot do without what you have long done without.
literal: The bachelor said that a wife should be found for him today, tomorrow; is it he and who that have been living since long ago?
usage: Used to mock someone who suddenly insists he cannot manage without something he has managed without until now.
igbo: Okokporo sị ka a chọwara ya nwaanyị nke taa, nke echi, ọ bụ ya na onye bibu kemgbe?

meaning: [uncertain] The misfortune that caught someone on the outward journey will not catch us on the return; may we be spared the same fate.
literal: The person it happened to on the journey, it will not reach us on the return.
usage: Used as a hopeful or consoling remark when setting out or returning, that another's misfortune will not be repeated on us.
igbo: Onye ọ nyịrị n’ojije, ọ gaghị anyị n’ọlịla.

meaning: When people act together, they can overcome even the strongest opponent.
equivalent: There is strength in numbers.
literal: If they gather counsel together, they kill a strong man.
usage: Used to urge a group to unite against a common enemy or challenge.
igbo: A gbakọọ izu ọnụ, e gbuo dike.

meaning: A woman needs wisdom and good character to win a husband; beauty alone is not enough.
literal: Wisdom is what a woman uses; character is what a husband uses to marry her.
usage: Used to advise a woman that a good marriage is secured by wisdom and good conduct.
igbo: Uche ji nwaanyị àgà ji di na-alụ ya.

meaning: [uncertain] The reason a man with one wife does not take a second is the same reason a bachelor has none — lack of means; do not take on more than you can support.
literal: What made a man with one wife not take two made a bachelor not have the one he has.
usage: Used to rebuke someone who wants more than he can afford, or to explain why a man has no wife.
igbo: Ihe mere onye ji otu nwaanyị ejila abụọ mere okokporo ojighị nwee nke o ji.

meaning: It is a person's constant hurrying and restlessness that lands him in pain.
literal: The ewi says that the thing that made it have pain is because things are always in a hurry.
usage: Said to someone who is forever rushing about and then complains of the trouble it brings.
igbo: Ewi sị na ihe kpatara o ji enwe ụfụ bụ maka na ihe ọsọ na-eme mgbe ọbụla.

meaning: Do not throw away today what you will need tomorrow.
equivalent: Waste not, want not.
literal: If a child chews the palm kernel and throws away the shell, when hunger bites him he will go looking for it.
usage: A rebuke thrown at someone who has carelessly discarded something he will soon need.
igbo: Nwata tichaa akị tufuo mkpume, agụụ gụwa ya ọ chọwa ya.

meaning: Whoever neglects the very thing that makes him what he is will be at the mercy of others in every season.
literal: If the lizard does not do the thing it became a lizard for, the ụmụazị will eat it in the dry season and in the rainy season.
usage: A rebuke to someone who fails to do what his nature and position demand, then complains of endless trouble.
igbo: Ngwere emeghị ihe o jiri bụrụ ngwere, ụmụazị erie ya ọkọchị na udummiri.

meaning: [uncertain] Whoever keeps waiting for others to bring what is needed is left putting an empty pot on the fire.
literal: A woman who waits for her husband to bring, and he brings at whatever time, keeps setting the pot of ọkpọọ on the fire.
usage: Said of someone who waits on others to provide instead of acting, and so never gets anything cooked.
igbo: Nwaanyị na-eche ka di weta di weta mgbe ọbụla, na-esinye ite ọkpọọ n’ọkụ.

meaning: One who tells others what her husband did to her will just as readily tell others what she did to her husband.
literal: The woman who tells what her husband did to her also tells people what she did to her husband.
usage: A remark about a wife, or anyone, who complains about her spouse to the world and so exposes herself too.
igbo: Nwaanyị na-akọ ihe di ya mere ya, ọ na-akọkwara ndị mmadụ ihe o mere di ya.

meaning: Human effort on its own cannot bring success; without one's chi (personal god) on your side, the work will not prosper.
equivalent: Man proposes, God disposes.
literal: A person's work is not accomplished if his chi does not agree.
usage: A consolation to someone whose hard work is not yielding anything, or a caution against boasting over one's own strength.
igbo: A naghị akarụ onye ọrụ ma ọ bụrụ na chi ejighị.

meaning: A small thing done for one's own comfort is easily mistaken for devoted service to one's master.
literal: The lamb licks its own tail and says it is licking the heart of its owner.
usage: Said of a follower who dresses up his own self-serving little act as loyalty to the one he serves.
igbo: Nwa atụrụ na-anyụle ọdụ ya ọ sị na ọ na-anyụle obi onye nwe ya.

meaning: [uncertain] One does not take on a thing's nature or place merely by falling into it; such things do not come about by accident.
literal: It is not by falling from above that one becomes ete mmiri.
usage: Said when someone assumes that a position or nature came to another by mere accident.
igbo: Ọ bụghị a dachaa elu a bụwa ete mmiri.

meaning: [uncertain] Whoever accepts what is offered should also be ready for what comes along with it.
literal: The one who accepted the ude as it came should not also join in dancing the abịa.
usage: A reminder to someone taking something on that its obligations travel with it.
igbo: Onye kwere ude n’abịa esorola gbaa abịa.

meaning: [uncertain] You may say a creature cannot run, and still it gets where it is going; do not judge ability by looks.
literal: The snake is at the palm kernel; one would say it does not know how to run.
usage: Said when someone underrates another's ability because of how he looks or moves.
igbo: Agwọ na-eze akụ, a sị na ọ maghị agba ọsọ.

meaning: A thing can still be present and visible while all its substance has already been used up.
literal: The chicken is in the bush, but its meat is finished.
usage: Said of someone or something still around but no longer of any use.
igbo: Ọkụkọ nọ n’ọhịa mana anụ ya agwụla.

meaning: [uncertain] What one creature does is felt by the other that shares its space; one cannot move without touching the other.
literal: Brother frog stretches out its leg, that brother nkapị may lower its mouth.
usage: Said when one person's action at once disturbs another who shares the same home or water.
igbo: Nwanne awọ gbatịa ya ụkwụ ka nwanne nkapị bebilata ya ọnụ.

meaning: Do not behave in the way that earns you the very name you resent.
literal: Whoever does not want to be called a slave should not behave like a slave.
usage: A rebuke to someone who complains about a name his own conduct has earned him.
igbo: Onye achọghị ka a kpọọ ya ohu emekwala ka ohu.

meaning: Only a full, decisive effort defeats an opponent; a light touch against him is no victory.
literal: A mere scratch given to an enemy is not a victory.
usage: Said to urge someone on who has made only a token move against an opponent.
igbo: Nkịtị a gbara onye iro abụghị mmeri

meaning: People fret over what they lack while the little they do have is being cut away from them.
literal: The monkey says its tail has not grown long, and the hunter takes a knife and is cutting down the one that is there.
usage: A warning to someone who complains about what he lacks while losing what he still has.
igbo: Ọ kwa enwe na-ekwu na ọdụ ya etoghị ogologo, dinta were mma na-achabirikwa nke dị adị.

meaning: [uncertain] A small pleasure can be snatched away from an old woman and the theft dressed up as concern for everybody else.
literal: If you see an old woman eating a chicken's wing, you take it from her, because she will catch a cough and spread it to the people.
usage: Thrown at people who dress up their own meanness as concern for the public good.
igbo: Ị hụ agadi nwaanyị ka ọ na-eri akpala ọkụkọ, ị napụ ya maka na o bute ụkwara o zuo ọha.

meaning: Stay long enough among a people and the stranger is no longer a stranger.
literal: When the lizard has stayed long in the farm, it becomes an aghụ (a bigger lizard).
usage: Said of a newcomer who has lived among a people long enough to be counted as one of them.
igbo: Ngwere nọkarịa n’ubi ọ ghọrọ aghụ.

meaning: Put a thing off and the day carries it away from you; the moment will not wait.
equivalent: Time and tide wait for no man.
literal: The morning did not act quickly; the afternoon overtook it.
usage: A nudge to someone still putting off what the day is not going to wait for.
igbo: Ụtụtụ emeghị ngwa ngwa, ehihie eburu ya ụzọ

meaning: [uncertain] Do not celebrate or count on a thing before the condition it hangs on has come to pass.
literal: A person should not ... unless the white man has come back.
usage: A caution to someone already rejoicing over an outcome that has not yet been settled.
igbo: Onye ańụla nga ma ọ bụrụ na oyibo alaghị.

meaning: What a person can reach is fixed by what they have to reach with.
literal: A short hand did not allow the tortoise to bring down the thing that is up in the roof shelf.
usage: Said to explain why a person cannot do what others are asking of them.
igbo: Aka mkpụmkpụ ekweghị mbe weta ihe dị n’uko.

meaning: [uncertain] You cannot tell the truth of a message from the messenger's nodding head or outward show.
literal: One does not use faith placed on the lizard's head to know the one who was sent on the errand.
usage: A warning not to take the messenger's manner as proof that the message is genuine.
igbo: E jighị okwukwe n’isi ngwere ama nke e ziri ozi.

meaning: The moment a debtor comes by anything, he is reminded of what he owes.
literal: The hen cackled, and thought was thought for the one who holds a debt.
usage: Said when a person's new gain is already spoken for by what he owes.
igbo: Ọkụkọ kwaa akwa uche echewe onye ji ụgwọ.

meaning: [uncertain] Chase a sweetness and you can end up lying down where you never meant to stay.
literal: One followed the sweetness of agbọ and slept at the foot of the adụ.
usage: A caution against running after a pleasure that will leave you stranded.
igbo: E sowe ụtọ agbọnọ a rahụ n’ukwu adụ.

meaning: [uncertain] Even after a thing has been lent out, the one who lent it still has a say in it.
literal: It is the one who lent a person nchiche ụkwa who told him to cut it.
usage: Said of a lender who still feels entitled to direct what he has lent out.
igbo: Ọ bụ onye bunyere onye nchiche ụkwa sịrị ya sibe ya.

meaning: [uncertain] The person being treated most gently is often the one who cries the loudest.
literal: The one who is being treated with gentleness is the one weeping and weeping.
usage: A rebuke to someone complaining although he is the one being favoured.
igbo: Onye a na-eme omume omume na-ebe obube obube.

meaning: The offender can be killed or buried, but the anger and the grudge outlive him.
literal: Kill it, still anger; bury it, still resentment.
usage: Said when a quarrel is thought finished because the offender is gone, though the bitterness stays.
igbo: E gbuo ma iwe, e lie ma ọnụma.

meaning: [uncertain] Whatever is demanded of a poor man comes out of him only with pain.
literal: One marked the poor man's tribute, one marked a fist.
usage: Said of how hard it is to exact anything from a person who has nothing.
igbo: A kaa ụtụ ogbenye akaa ọkpọ.

meaning: What looks like someone's smile may be nothing but the face they put on for what they are getting.
literal: If you want the dog's laughter, give it yam that is hot.
usage: Said when a person's delight is plainly tied to what they are getting out of you.
igbo: Ị chọwa ọchị nkịta i nye ya ji dị ọkụ.

meaning: A young man never knows when he has stepped onto his in-laws' ground, so he must carry himself well everywhere.
literal: The young man does not know when he has passed the compound ground of his in-laws.
usage: A reminder to behave well anywhere, since you never know whose ground you are standing on.
igbo: Okokporo anaghị ama mgbe ọ gafere ama ọgọ ya.

meaning: [uncertain] The sounds of the living in the household — the clapping, the noise of people — are what tell the spirits that life is still there.
literal: When hands are clapped in the obi, the spirits are shown where life is.
usage: Said when the noise of a living, gathered household is understood to reach the ancestors.
igbo: A kụkata aka n’obi e gosi ndị mmụọ ebe ndụ dị.

meaning: [uncertain] The line appears garbled, but it seems to say that it is while the knife is already at hand that people start praising how long the little creature's life has been — flattery offered to someone whose fate is already settled.
literal: It is while following the knife; the life of a nwamkpi is praised as long.
usage: Said when someone is being flattered or praised just as harm is about to be done to them.
igbo: Ọ bụ a na-eso mma, ndụ nwamkpi a na-eto ogologo.

meaning: Someone may keep his own hands clean while quietly pointing another at the harm — the one who does not strike can still be the one who directs the blow.
literal: The eagle does not carry off chickens, but it shows the kite where the chicken is.
usage: Used to expose a person who arranges another's wrongdoing while claiming innocence of it.
igbo: Ugo anaghị ebu ọkụkọ mana ọ na-egosi egbe ebe ọkụkọ nọ.

meaning: The wrongdoer pleads that he was not around when the rule was made — the guilty claim absence or ignorance once the offence is named.
literal: The rat says that it was not in the house when the law against stealing was made.
usage: A rebuke for someone who dodges blame by pretending he never heard the rule he broke.
igbo: Oke sị na ọ nọghị n’ụlọ mgbe a mara iwu ohi.

meaning: What is made out of a thing is pleasing to that thing — a person takes delight in what matches his own nature, however foul it is to others.
literal: The water used in cooking a snake tastes of snake to the snake.
usage: Said when a person's appetite for something unsavoury reveals what he is made of.
igbo: Mmiri e jiri sie agwọ na-atọ agwọ agwọ.

meaning: [uncertain] Those who grow up side by side in the same place end up falling out over sharing what is between them; closeness breeds rivalry rather than harmony.
literal: When palm tree and palm tree grow together, they refuse together the igu.
usage: Said when people raised or planted together begin quarrelling over space or shares.
igbo: Nkwụ na nkwụ tokọọ, ha ajụkọọ igu.

meaning: The hidden power is never caught with its mouth wide open — the doer of secret deeds keeps his face covered, so you cannot catch him in the act.
literal: One does not see a spirit with its mouth opened wide.
usage: Said when someone does wrong out of sight and cannot be pinned down openly.
igbo: A naghị ahụ mmụo ghewe ọnụ oghe.

meaning: No settlement is without the thing that nibbles at it — every community has someone or something gnawing away at its peace.
literal: There is no town where the thing that chews does not exist.
usage: A consolation and a warning when people complain that their own town is the only one with a troublemaker in it.
igbo: O nweghị obodo ihe na-ata akwụ adịghị.

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt and the key word okukoro is unclear; it seems to say that keeping a close eye on the small creature does not stop the monkey from finishing off the store in the barn — watching the lesser thief does not save the harvest.
literal: If one follows okukoro with the eye, the monkey is not used up in the barn.
usage: Said when guarding against one small threat leaves the greater one free to plunder.
igbo: E sowe okukoro anya enwe ji agwụ n’ọba.

meaning: The dog barks and says it is fighting to save the little bird's life, and its master's life as well — troublemakers always dress their mischief up as protection of others.
literal: The dog that is barking says it is fighting for the life of the ekperima, and is also fighting for the life of its owner.
usage: Used to expose someone whose noisy aggression is excused as being done for other people's safety.
igbo: Nkịta na-agbọ ụja sị na ọ na-azọ ndụ ekperima, na-azọkwuazị ndụ onye nwe ya.

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo here is unclear; the image seems to be of something of no use to the knife yet sitting on top — a thing that has no part in the work pressing itself forward above those who do.
literal: A thing that was not for the knife's good, why did it climb up on top?
usage: Said of an idler or outsider who puts himself above those doing the actual work.
igbo: Ihe adịghịrị adụ mma kpatara o jiri mịa n’elu.

meaning: The one whose personal god is bright shines like the sun — a person favoured by his chi is radiantly, visibly blessed.
literal: The one whose chi is bright shines like the sun.
usage: Said in praise or in acknowledgement of someone whose good fortune shows plainly on him.
igbo: Onye chi ya wọrọ ọcha na-acha ka anyarị

meaning: The deity whose shrine was swept with a hen's egg knows that the hen's legs and head are inside that egg — whoever receives a piece of a matter already knows the whole of it, so nothing can be hidden from him.
literal: The deity for whom a hen's egg was used to sweep the shrine knows that the hen's legs and its head are in that egg.
usage: A warning to anyone hoping to deceive someone who is already part of the matter.
igbo: Arụsị e jiri akwa ọkụkọ chụọrọ aja mara na ụkwụ ọkụkọ na isi ya dị n’akwa ahụ.

meaning: It is the child who knows nothing who has the boundary of the land shown to him twice — the inexperienced must be told a thing over and over before it stays.
literal: It is the child who does not know that one shows the boundary of the land twice.
usage: Said patiently, or with mild reproach, when instruction has to be repeated for a beginner.
igbo: Ọ bụ nwata amaghị ihe ka a na-egosi oke ala ugboro abụọ.

meaning: The wife says her case with her husband is not one for people to judge — but if the spirits judged it instead, would it go any better for her? Refusing human judgement is no guarantee of a kinder verdict.
literal: The woman says her case with her husband is not one that people will judge — if the spirits judged them, would it be better for her?
usage: A rebuke to someone who dodges the judgement of his own community, imagining another court will favour him.
igbo: Nwaanyị sị na ikpe ya na di ya abụghị nke mmadụ ga-ekpe, ndị mmụo kpeere ha ọ ga-akara ya mma?

meaning: Whoever has decided to kill a dog first gives it a bad name — the excuse is manufactured to fit the harm already intended.
equivalent: Give a dog a bad name and hang him.
literal: Whoever wants to kill a dog, he gives it a bad name.
usage: Said when someone's reputation is being blackened simply to justify doing him harm.
igbo: Onye chọọ igbu nkịta o nye ya aha ọjọọ.

meaning: [uncertain] A person can be caught up in something, enjoying it and going along with it, without realizing that it is dangerous or has spiritual consequences.
literal: The person for whom one blows the ụsụrụga is dancing; he does not know that ụsụrụgada is the dance of the spirits.
usage: A warning that people may join in a practice or pleasure whose true nature and danger they fail to see.
igbo: Onye a na-afụrụ ụsụrụga ọ na-agba amaghị na ụsụrụgada bụ egwu ndị mmụọ.

meaning: When a community punishes wrongdoing, it begins with the chief offender or ringleader.
literal: If one is killing the animals that offended the land, one will first kill the nwamkpi.
usage: Said to urge that in dealing with a group's offense, the leader or chief culprit should be dealt with first.
igbo: Ọ bụrụ na a na-egbu anụ ndị merụrụ ala, a ga-ebu ụzọ gbuo nwamkpi.

meaning: An incomplete sacrifice—one missing its essential part—will be exposed in divination; a task done by half measures will be found out.
literal: If a sacrifice is offered, but its okoro is not offered, it will be revealed in divination.
usage: A warning that cutting corners in an important matter cannot stay hidden.
igbo: A gbaa aja, a gbaghị okoro ya, ọ wachikwa n’afa.

meaning: A deity that cares for many children receives many offerings; the one who carries many responsibilities also receives many rewards.
literal: A deity that rules children eats many baskets of yams.
usage: Said of a person with many dependents or clients, acknowledging both the burden and the benefits.
igbo: Arụsị chị ụmụ na-eri ọtụtụ akpara ji.

meaning: [uncertain] Using one's mouth greedily to chase sacrifices leads to ruin; greed for offerings destroys a person.
literal: If one carries the mouth pursuing sacrifice, it keeps falling and dying.
usage: A warning against greed or using one's position to demand gifts.
igbo: E buru ọnụ na-achụ aja, ọ na-ada ọnwụ ọnwụ.

meaning: [uncertain] A small act of respect or kindness can satisfy someone as deeply as a full meal.
literal: It is when a little is poured out in honor that it is like it has filled the stomach.
usage: Said to encourage small gestures of respect, noting how much they can mean.
igbo: Ọ bụ a kwanyere ụtara ugwu ọ dị ka o juru afọ.

meaning: The purpose of gathering for moonlight play is for people to see and meet one another, because the moon shines on everyone's compound alike; community gatherings bind everyone together.
literal: The thing with which one goes out for moonlight play is that people may see one another, because there is no person whose compound the moon does not shine on.
usage: Said to encourage community gatherings and to remind people that no one is excluded from the common light.
igbo: Ihe e ji apụ egwu ọnwa bụ ka a hụkọrịta n’ihi na o nweghị onye ọnwa anaghị eti be ya.

meaning: It is not by leaving the child at home that one goes looking for someone to watch over him; the help you need is already at hand.
literal: It is not that one abandoned a child in the house and goes to look for someone who will look at him.
usage: A rebuke to someone neglecting what is right in front of them while seeking help elsewhere.
igbo: Ọ bụghị a hapụrụ nwata ụlọ a chọwa onye ga-eledo ya anya.

meaning: [uncertain] A person with a new weapon or tool wants to use it on a big target; new power is tested against the strong.
literal: The person who bought a new gun uses it to go and shoot an adult.
usage: Said when someone with newly acquired power or wealth seeks a bold or dangerous target to prove himself.
igbo: Onye zụrụ egbe ọhụrụ na-eji ya aga akwa onye toro afọ.

meaning: A child—especially a daughter—is walking straight into danger or trouble.
literal: My daughter, my daughter, is falling into fire.
usage: A lament or warning when a child is repeating a mother's mistakes or heading toward ruin.
igbo: Ada m, ada m, na-adabanye n’ọkụ.

meaning: Mud does not recognize a visitor; trouble does not spare strangers or discriminate.
equivalent: The rain falls on the just and the unjust.
literal: Mud does not know a visitor.
usage: A consolation or observation when a visitor suffers the same hardship as the locals.
igbo: Apịtị amaghị onye ọbịa.

meaning: [uncertain] The proverb is obscure and possibly garbled; it appears to concern arriving or timing and the toad's tail, but the sense is not clear.
literal: It is when one arrives, when one arrives, that the toad does not use its tail to leave.
usage: Uncertain; the saying is not clearly understandable in this form.
igbo: Ọ bụ ka a bịa, ka a bịa, ka awọ ejighị puo ọdụ.

meaning: If the small duiker jumps, the big elephant will break it; a small person should not provoke a powerful one.
literal: If the mgbada jumps, let the big elephant break it.
usage: A warning to someone overstepping their limits against a stronger opponent.
igbo: Mgbada nyụọ ka enyi ukwu awaa ya.

meaning: A white-haired elder does not throw stones; maturity restrains a person from petty retaliation.
literal: The white-haired person does not throw stones.
usage: A rebuke to an elder or anyone acting childishly, reminding them that dignity should restrain them.
igbo: Onye isi nkwọcha anaghị atụ okwute.

meaning: [uncertain] If yams are crammed too tightly into the medicine, they become spoiled yams; overdoing something ruins it.
literal: If one packs yams too much into the medicine, it becomes ji awaị.
usage: A warning against excess or overdoing a good thing.
igbo: A bachanyekarịa ji n’ọgwụ, ọ ghọọ ji awaị.

meaning: People cannot hide their faults from those who know them well; you cannot deceive your own household.
literal: One does not sell a chicken with a broken leg in the house.
usage: A warning to someone trying to put on a false front before family or close neighbours.
igbo: A naghị ere ọkụkọ ọkpa gbajiri n’ụlọ.

meaning: Respect is what earns a woman recognition among her peers.
literal: Respect is the regard a woman uses to know her fellow.
usage: Said to urge a woman to conduct herself with dignity so her equals will accept her.
igbo: Ugwu bụ nkwanye nkwanye nwaanyị ji amụta ibe ya.

meaning: Whoever uses another person's resources to exalt himself will eventually be brought low.
equivalent: Pride goes before a fall.
literal: Whoever uses a child's thing to raise his hand high, the hand reaches him and he lowers it.
usage: A rebuke to someone boasting on the strength of what is not theirs.
igbo: Onye ji ihe nwata wellie aka elu, aka rowe ya o wetuo ya.

meaning: Everyone may make a claim or a noise, but the one with the real mark of distinction stands apart.
literal: All animals blow the horn, but the one with the horn is different.
usage: Used to point out the person who is genuinely set apart in a crowd.
igbo: Anụ niile na-afụ opi mana nke nkapị na-apụ iche.

meaning: What gives one creature pleasure is its own sweetness in life; enjoyment is personal.
literal: The cat says that that touch is the sweetness of life.
usage: Said when someone's source of joy seems odd to others.
igbo: Nwamba sị na mmetụta ahụ bụ ụtọ ndụ.

meaning: It is the insider who reveals the secrets of the house to outsiders.
literal: It is the rat in the house that told the rat in the bush that the bundle of ogiri is near the fire.
usage: A rebuke to someone who leaks family or community matters to strangers.
igbo: Ọ bụ oke nọ n’ụlọ gwara oke nọ n’ọhịa na ngwugwu ogiri dị n’anya ọkụ.

meaning: A hidden wrongdoing will sooner or later be exposed.
equivalent: Murder will out.
literal: The snake and what it swallowed have become stretched out.
usage: Said when a secret misdeed is beginning to show.
igbo: Agwọ na ihe o loro atọgbọrọla.

meaning: No matter how high one rises, one can still fall.
equivalent: The higher they fly, the harder they fall.
literal: The eagle flew and fell into a pit.
usage: A warning against arrogance and false security.
igbo: Akụ fechaa ọ daara awọ.

meaning: Hunger is not a sickness; it is simply hunger and can be satisfied.
literal: Hunger is not a disease; if it is hunger.
usage: Said to console or encourage someone who is hungry to eat and take heart.
igbo: Ughere abụghị ọrịa ọ bụrụ agụụ.

meaning: [uncertain] It is shameful to eat while a child cries for food and is not given any.
literal: A child is crying and not given akịilu; those who chewed ata, what does their face look like?
usage: A rebuke to those who eat without sharing with a hungry child.
igbo: Nwata na-ebe akwa na-enyeghị ya akịilu ndị tara ata kedụ otu ihu dị ha.

meaning: [uncertain] When a hero's corpse is carried past the place of his exploits, the honour of his deeds makes the burden light.
literal: If they carry the corpse of a strong man and pass through where he exerted strength, it becomes light in the hand.
usage: Said in praise of a person whose good deeds are remembered after death.
igbo: E buru ozu dike gazuo ebe ọ kpara ike o rekaa n’abọ.

meaning: A burden or trouble that belongs to someone else has landed on me.
literal: Igwurube carrying its load has come to me.
usage: Said when one is saddled with an unwanted responsibility.
igbo: Igwurube buru uru ya abịarala m.

meaning: [uncertain] When hunger and sickness have come, death no longer seems as dreadful or as distant as a king's cap.
literal: Hunger comes, sickness comes, death is no longer to a person like the king's cap.
usage: Said of a situation so hard that death loses its terror.
igbo: Agụụ bịa, ọrịa bịa, ọnwụ adịzịa onye ụbịam ka okpu eze.

meaning: A person who does not know those above him cannot know those below him.
literal: He who does not know who surpasses him does not know whom he surpasses.
usage: A rebuke to someone who lacks humility and self-knowledge.
igbo: Onye amaghị onye karịrị ya anaghị ama onye ọ karịrị.

meaning: [uncertain] When the community has completed a work, it becomes a custom in the home.
literal: When the community has finished work, it becomes the custom of this house.
usage: Said when a family adopts a practice because the wider community does it.
igbo: Mba mekarịa arụ, ọ bụrụ omenaala be a.

meaning: Work is finished a stage at a time, not all on one day: what is cut today is split into firewood another day, so no one should expect the whole task at once.
literal: It is not the day a tree was cut that it is split into firewood.
usage: Said to steady someone who is impatient for a long job to be done.
igbo: Ọ bụghị ụbọchị e gbuturu osisi ka a na-akpa ya nkụ.

meaning: A thing is only taken for what it is when it is done in its full, customary way; drop the finishing touch and it counts for nothing.
literal: When a lizard has finished excreting, if it does not add white chalk to it, it does not look like lizard's dung.
usage: A nudge to someone who has stopped just short of finishing a job properly.
igbo: Ngwere nyụchaa nsị ọ nyụnyeghị ya nzu ọ naghị adị ka nsị ngwere.

meaning: [uncertain] Discipline is not for every small mishap; the child is beaten for the day's deed that truly calls for it, not for the day he merely spilled the oil.
literal: It is not the day a small child spilled palm oil that he is beaten, but rather the day he spilled oguru akwụ [unclear].
usage: Said when sparing a child punishment over a trifle and reserving it for a real offence.
igbo: Ọ bụghị ụbọchị nwatakirị kwafuru mmanụ ka a na-eti ya ihe kama ọ bụ ụbọchị ọ kwafuru oguru akwụ.

meaning: A person so dull that a proverb must be explained to him before he takes the point is a fool — the bride price paid for his mother was money thrown away.
literal: Anybody to whom a proverb is told and explained knows that the money used to marry his mother was wasted.
usage: A cutting remark about someone who cannot take a hint and must have everything spelled out.
igbo: onye ọbụla a tụọrọ ilu kọwaara ya mara na ego e jiri lụta nne ya lara n’iyi.

meaning: If a learner has mastered a little, he should press on until he has mastered the whole of it; do not stop at the first step.
literal: If a small child learns the bird's cry, let him strive and learn its flight as well.
usage: Encouragement to a learner to keep going until the whole skill is his.
igbo: nwatakịrị mụta akwa nnụnụ, ọ gbaa mbọ mụtakwuo ufe ya.

meaning: An elder's experience sees what the young, for all their standing and eagerness, cannot see.
literal: The thing an elder sitting on the ground saw with his eyes, a child standing upright will not see it.
usage: Said to check a youngster who thinks his own view is complete, and to honour the elder's judgement.
igbo: ihe okenye nọ n’ala were hụ, nwatakịrị kwụrụ ọtọ ọ gaghị ahụ ya.

meaning: A sensible person catches the point of a proverb at once, but a fool, told the very same thing, only turns his face away into the bush.
literal: If a proverb is told to one who knows, he knows; but if it is told to a fool, he puts his head into the bush.
usage: Said with a shrug when a pointed remark lands on someone who will not hear it.
igbo: A tụọrọ ọmara ọ mara, mana a tụọrọ ofeke o tinnye isi n’ọhịa.

meaning: What is not in a creature's nature will never grow on it; do not expect a person or thing to take on what it simply does not have.
literal: A lizard does not grow hair.
usage: A flat dismissal when someone keeps expecting what a person has never had.
igbo: ngwere anaghị agba ajị.

meaning: Size up your own strength before you take a thing on; know what you can swallow before you swallow it.
equivalent: Don't bite off more than you can chew.
literal: Before a person swallows an udara seed, he ought first to know how strong it is.
usage: A warning to someone about to take on more than he can handle.
igbo: tupu mmadụ eloo mkpụrụ ụdara, o kwesịrị ka ọ mara otu ike ya ha.

meaning: [uncertain] One who puts his ear to the ground, listening in on others, hears what was meant to sting him; overheard talk brings hurt.
literal: A person who puts his ear to the ground hears ụya agbịsị [unclear].
usage: A caution against eavesdropping and the wounds it brings.
igbo: onye tọọ ntị n’ala, ọ nụ ụya agbịsị.

meaning: The one who needs something must bow his head to get it; nothing is given to the stiff-necked.
literal: If a kid goat kneels both knees on the ground, it sucks its mother's breast.
usage: Said to someone too proud to ask, or to excuse the humility of a person who must beg for help.
igbo: nwa ewu gbuo ikpere naabọ n’ala, ọ ńụọ nne ya ara.

meaning: What a father truly leaves his child is ọfọ — the truth and uprightness he lived by — not property.
literal: Ọfọ is the bone the father set aside for the child.
usage: Said of a parent's moral legacy, or to urge a child to walk in the father's uprightness.
igbo: ọfọ bụ ọkpụkpụ nna tafọọrọ nwa.

meaning: [uncertain] A fool never notices what is going on around him; even the plainest thing done in his presence escapes him.
literal: A fool does not know when the firewood ụkwa was split [unclear].
usage: A jibe at someone oblivious to what everyone else can see.
igbo: ofeke anaghị ama mgbe e kere nkụ ụkwa.

meaning: [uncertain] Every creature lives and behaves after its own kind; each goes its own way and keeps its own manner.
literal: Every animal dwells in its own ọwarị [unclear].
usage: Said when people differ in their habits and each must be allowed his own way.
igbo: anụmanụ ọbụla na-akpa n’ọwarị ya.

meaning: When the sign that should follow an act does not appear, the cause lies out of sight; something has gone wrong where the spirits are.
literal: If sacrifice is offered and the vulture is not seen, one knows that something has happened at the home of the spirits.
usage: Said when an expected result fails to come and people suspect a hidden cause.
igbo: A chụchaa aja ma a hụghị udele a maara na ihe mere na be ndị mmụọ.

meaning: A child may not know what is wrapped in a bundle, yet the bundle still preys on his mind; people can worry about what they do not understand.
literal: A child does not know what is tied in a bundle; the thought of the tied bundle is eating him.
usage: Used to tease or describe someone, especially a child, who frets over a matter whose contents they cannot know.
igbo: Nwata amaghị ihe e kechiri na ngwugwu, uche ngwugwwu e kere ana-agụ ya

meaning: When an experienced diviner performs a sacrifice properly, the spirits receive it as if directly from his hand; practiced skill gets the result.
literal: If the old dibia, performing sacrifice clearly, performs sacrifice, it is as if he put the sacrifice into the hands of the spirits.
usage: Said to praise practiced skill or to insist that a rite done by an expert carries full force.
igbo: Ma, ochie dibia ịchụ aja doro anya chụọ aja, ọ dị ka o nyere ndị mmụọ aja n’aka

meaning: [uncertain] The line is fragmentary and the key words are unclear; it appears to contrast absent things with gestures of self-reliance, but the proverb's point cannot be recovered reliably.
literal: Mother, abịa does not exist; one knocks a hand on the chest. Iyi does not exist; one drinks with knee and hand.
usage: Not usable as given; the text is too corrupt to place.
igbo: Nne, abịa adịghị adị, a kụwa aka n’obi. Iyi adịghị adị, a ńụwa ikpere aka

meaning: One man's meat is another man's poison.
equivalent: One man's meat is another man's poison.
literal: Whoever eats this, eats this; this one did not kill him, this one killed him.
usage: Used when explaining that the same food, medicine, or experience harms one person and spares another.
igbo: onye rie nke a, rie nke a, nke a egbughị ya, nke a egbuo ya

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is garbled, especially 'nyụọ ọgụ akpana' and 'nyụchie ala'; the proverb's sense cannot be reliably recovered.
