literal: The chick that is in the nest fights akpana; if it is in the tree or on the ground, it covers the ground.
usage: Not usable as given; the wording is too corrupt to place.
igbo: Nwa nnụnụ nọ n’ufe nyụọ ọgụ akpana, o bere ebere n’osisi maọbụ n’ala, ọ nyụchie ala

meaning: When you find a corpse, bury it; do not press too hard to learn what killed it, because too many questions can frighten people out of doing what must be done.
literal: Whoever saw a corpse should bury the corpse, but let him not ask what killed the corpse, because if people ask fully what killed the corpse, perhaps fear will not allow people to bury it.
usage: Used to counsel against over-questioning when a necessary duty must be carried out.
igbo: onye hụrụ ozu lie ozu, ma ya ajụla ihe gburu ozu, maka na mmadụ jupụtachaa ihe gburu ozu, ike kwe, egwu agaghị ekwe ndị mmadụ lie ya

meaning: Better to stay hungry than to eat your fill and then collapse by the roadside; it is wiser to endure want now than to be undone by indulgence.
literal: Instead of I will fill my belly and then lie down on the road, let me fast.
usage: Said to urge restraint, especially about eating or enjoying something in a way that will later cripple you.
igbo: kama m ga-eriju afọ were dachie ụzọ, ka m buru ọnụ.

meaning: You reap what you sow.
equivalent: You reap what you sow.
literal: What a person throws into the market is what will be bought for him.
usage: Used to warn that people will be treated according to what they themselves put forward.
igbo: ihe onye tụrụ n’ahịa ka a ga-azụtara ya.

meaning: Whoever enjoys the meat is the one who must pay the debt; the beneficiary bears the cost.
literal: Any person who ate the lamb is the one who owes the debt.
usage: Used to fix responsibility on those who benefited from something, especially when payment or blame is being assigned.
igbo: Onye ọbụla riri amụ ebulu ji ibi ụgwọ.

meaning: Eating without asking or refusing leads to dying without sickness; indiscriminate eating can kill suddenly.
literal: Not refusing or asking, taking and eating leads to, without being sick, dying.
usage: Used as a warning against eating anything offered without caution or permission.
igbo: ajụghị ajụ were rie na-ebute a rịaghị arịa were nwụọ.

meaning: The seed a person plants is what it becomes; you become what you sow.
equivalent: As you sow, so shall you reap.
literal: The seed a person planted is what it is becoming.
usage: Used to warn that a person's present actions determine the outcome they will meet.
igbo: Mkpurụ onye kurụ ka ọ na-aghọrọ.

meaning: [uncertain] The line is corrupt and the phrase 'ka okpu ata' is unclear; the proverb's sense cannot be reliably recovered.
literal: The ear will hear what is not named, like a cap chews.
usage: Not usable as given; the wording is too corrupt to place.
igbo: ntị ga-anụ ihe anaghị aha ka okpu ata.

meaning: [uncertain] The Igbo is unclear, especially 'ihie uto di ya n'ukwu'; it seems to say something about a woman's attractiveness or nature, but the exact point is not recoverable.
literal: However a woman is, something sweet is on her leg.
usage: Not usable as given; the expression is too unclear to place.
igbo: Etu obuna nwanyi n'adi ihie uto di ya n'ukwu.

meaning: A man does not refuse a breast; men do not turn down what is offered to them.
literal: A man does not refuse breast.
usage: Used jokingly or knowingly when a man accepts an offer or attention, especially from a woman.
igbo: Nwoke anaghi aju ara.

meaning: [uncertain] The wording is fragmentary and 'kpere otele ya ahiri' is unclear; the proverb's sense cannot be reliably recovered.
literal: It is with one hand that one kpere its otele ahiri.
usage: Not usable as given; the text is too unclear to place.
igbo: Ona abu ewere otu aka kpere otele ya ahiri.

meaning: [uncertain] Once a person has stripped away their own dignity in the open, others stop giving them the regard they once had.
literal: A woman takes off her cloth; no one gives her a thought.
usage: Thrown at someone who has shamed themselves in public and still expects the old deference.
igbo: Nwanyi yipu akwa anaghi eche ya eche.

meaning: [uncertain] The line is damaged and no reliable sense can be drawn from the text as given; it seems to concern a brief window of time and what was sought in it.
literal: It is a small day that we chased, and there was 'nchi'.
usage: Too damaged in this text to place confidently in speech.
igbo: Ubochi nta ka anyi chua na owere nchi.

meaning: No one is without an equal; whenever you are born, someone of your own standing is born too, so do not carry yourself as though you stand alone.
literal: The one who was born learns his fellow.
usage: Said to deflate a young person who thinks no one can match him, or to console someone who feels alone in a struggle.
igbo: Onye amuru ya amuta ibe-ya.

meaning: The timid keep their lives safe by staying close to the strong.
literal: A person of fear holds his life with a person of strength.
usage: Said, often wryly, of someone who survives by clinging to a powerful patron.
igbo: Onye ujo, ji ndu ya na onye ike.

meaning: [uncertain] The line is badly garbled; it appears to be a caution at a hearing or family meeting not to pass judgement carelessly, since the judgement may come back to the one passing it.
literal: Case judged — 'atụ nna be aghọrọ', 'nna be lenu' — see whether the case is yours!!
usage: A caution offered in a dispute, urging care because the matter at hand may yet land on the speaker.
igbo: Atuo ikpe atu nnabe aghoro, nnabe lenu ma atu odi gi!!

meaning: [uncertain] One does not put one's body or one's gifts to a use that degrades them.
literal: One does not use the buttocks to dance the prostitute's dance.
usage: A rebuke to someone parading their body or their gifts in a way that cheapens them.
igbo: Anaghi eji amu ukwu eyi akwuna egwu.

meaning: Settling one obligation does not finish the matter; what you use to clear a debt today is what you will need again for the next one.
literal: The thing one uses to pay a debt once is for another time!
usage: Said after a debt is paid, to remind the payer that clearing one account does not exhaust the demands ahead.
igbo: Ihe a na eji akwu ugwo otu, wu maka mgbe ozo!

meaning: A promise to do a thing 'next time' is not something to be relied on.
literal: Another time, a woman is a lie.
usage: Said half in jest when someone's promise to do a thing 'next time' is plainly empty.
igbo: Mgbe ozo nwanyi bu asi.

meaning: [uncertain] One does not cast off what belongs to one, or one's own head, merely because it is wounded or has turned difficult.
literal: One does not abandon the head, even if it broke and refused.
usage: Said when someone is tempted to turn their back on their own family or their own place because of its faults.
igbo: Anaghi ahapu isi, gbawara otula aju.

meaning: Once the share has been handed round, everyone can see who is being called on to pay; the one who takes the benefit is the one who carries the cost.
literal: If a share is put into the hand, one knows the one called for payment.
usage: Said to settle an argument over who should foot a bill, once the benefit has already been shared out.
igbo: E kee oke na aka, a mara onye a kporo ugwo!

meaning: [uncertain] The line is garbled beyond recovery with the text as given.
literal: Ivedi entered 'aba', 'abago'.
usage: Too damaged in this text to place confidently in speech.
igbo: Ivedi bara aba abago.

meaning: People declare that a thing is beyond them until their own interest is touched; the old woman who says she cannot run runs when a goat makes off with her cocoyam.
literal: The old woman said she does not run; was it not when a goat carried off her cocoyam that she was heard?
usage: Used to cut through a claim of weakness made by someone whose appetite proves otherwise.
igbo: Agadi nwayi si na ya adahi agba oso, obu hi mgbe ewu buru ede anuru ya?

meaning: The fearful one turns up brave and loud only after the fighting is finished.
literal: If the fight is finished, the person of fear comes in!
usage: Thrown at someone who appears brave and vocal once the danger has already passed.
igbo: E gboo ogu, onye ujo ana abaa!

meaning: What a person gives away is what comes back to feed them; the giving hand is the hand that eats.
literal: Give a thing, eat a thing.
usage: Said to encourage a giver at the moment they are tempted to hold back.
igbo: Enye ife erie ife.

meaning: A fearful heart never takes the lead; the one who is afraid will not go in front.
literal: If the belly is afraid, it will not lead the way.
usage: Said when fear keeps someone from stepping forward to lead, or to prod a timid person onward.
igbo: O buru na afo na atu ujo, ogaghi ebu uzo.
Onye ivedi ana m anu ife ina ekwu Ochiooooooo.
meaning: [uncertain] The line is too corrupt to fix a sense; it seems to involve someone speaking out of anger and being heard out, ending in a cry ('Ochiooooooo').
literal: A person with anger — I am hearing what you are saying — Ochiooooooo.
usage: Recorded as a broken fragment; a speaker could not reliably reach for it in this form.

igbo: Ogologo amu anaghi egosi dimkpa.
meaning: Being big is not the same as being a man; mere size proves nothing about strength or worth.
equivalent: It's not the size that matters
literal: A long penis does not show a strong man.
usage: Thrown at someone who boasts of size or bulk as if it were proof of ability.

igbo: Kpim kpim kpim bu onye ike n'ahu.
meaning: [uncertain] Probably about repeated small beats or steps amounting to bodily strength, but the ideophone 'kpim kpim kpim' is not attested in this wording.
literal: Kpim kpim kpim is a strong person in the body.
usage: Recorded as a fragment; not reliably usable as it stands.

igbo: Nwanyi isi mkpe si amu, kele wu anya!
meaning: [uncertain] Corrupt; it seems to concern a woman, her head or breast, and looking with the eye, but no reliable sense can be recovered.
literal: Woman, head 'mkpe', says from the breast — look, it is the eye!
usage: Recorded as a fragment; a speaker could not reliably reach for it.

igbo: Nwanyi ngwa si ma oluru di ma olughi di na ihie oma abani obuna onu ihie ga ekpere ya oku.
meaning: [uncertain] Corrupt and truncated; it appears to weigh whether a woman has married or has not, and what good or ill her mouth brings her, but the sense cannot be fixed.
literal: A hasty woman says whether she married a husband or did not marry a husband; a good thing ... it is her mouth that the thing will call fire to.
usage: Recorded as a broken line; not reliably usable as it stands.

igbo: E biri, a kwuo, wu e biri, e bite!
meaning: [uncertain] Reads roughly as 'it is lived-and-spoken, it is lived-and-arrived at', but the second half is corrupt and the point cannot be fixed.
literal: It lived, it was said — that is it lived, let it live!
usage: Recorded as a fragment; a speaker could not reliably reach for it.

igbo: Ikpata ego na nwatakiri, obodo ana akuru gi aka. Ijebe eje obodo esoro gi jebe.
meaning: When a young person does well, the whole town claps for him and his success becomes the community's own; wherever he goes, his people go with him.
literal: To earn money in childhood, the town is clapping for you. Wherever you go, the town follows and goes.
usage: Said to encourage a young earner who has won public goodwill, or to remind the successful that their standing is communal.

igbo: Ejula na asugbu onwe ya osi ona asunye oku.
meaning: [uncertain] Something like 'the snail destroys itself while claiming it is feeding the fire' — ruining yourself and calling it help; the verbs in the line are corrupt.
literal: The snail is killing itself; it says it is pouring into the fire.
usage: Recorded with corrupt spelling; a speaker would use it to mock someone wrecking himself while claiming to help.

igbo: A naghi aju nwamkpi ebe o rahuru, ka ma, o bu ma o tetekwara!
meaning: [uncertain] Roughly: nobody asks the young he-goat where it slept, only whether it has woken up now — judge a person by the present, not by past hardship.
literal: One does not ask the young he-goat where it slept; rather, is it that it has woken up too!
usage: Used to wave aside questions about someone's past struggles and point at how they are doing now.

igbo: Onye goro ogo be ngwere n'achi uche na aka.
meaning: [uncertain] Corrupt; it seems to involve someone who has taken up an in-law tie 'at the lizard's place' and watches it warily, but no clear sense can be recovered.
literal: The one who married an in-law at the lizard's place, keeping watch in the hand.
usage: Recorded as a fragment; not reliably usable.

igbo: Okenye ona alu ogu ikpe omuma?
meaning: An elder does not fight a quarrel that carries blame; a person of standing keeps out of disgraceful disputes.
literal: An elder — is he fighting a fight of a case of blame?
usage: Said to rebuke an older person who has let himself be dragged into a shameful squabble.

igbo: Ewu kpaba ike ere ya n'afia.
meaning: The goat that grows strong and fat is the one taken to market; being capable or prosperous is what gets a person called on and used.
literal: If a goat becomes strong, it is sold in the market.
usage: Said when someone's usefulness or prosperity draws demands that he is then expected to meet.

igbo: Okenye na eliba aku elibe ma nwatakiri na ere aku n'afia.
meaning: [uncertain] Corrupt; it sets an elder against a child over 'aku' (wealth or palm kernels) in the market, but the verbs are unclear and the point cannot be fixed.
literal: The elder is ... the wealth ..., but a small child is selling wealth in the market.
usage: Recorded as a fragment; a speaker could not reliably reach for it.
